uni-cse-algorithms.title: Design and Analysis of Algorithms (B.Tech CSE)
uni-cse-algorithms.description: Unit-by-unit Design and Analysis of Algorithms: recurrences and the Master theorem, divide and conquer, greedy methods with MST and Dijkstra, dynamic programming, backtracking and string matching, and NP-completeness — with C, C++ and Java code activities and GATE-style exams.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Analysis of Algorithms and Recurrences
courses.summary: Correctness via loop invariants, best/worst/average case, asymptotic notation proofs, solving recurrences by substitution, recursion tree and the Master theorem, and amortised analysis. Covers topics commonly taught in B.Tech Design and Analysis of Algorithms courses.
outcomes: Learners can prove correctness with a loop invariant
Learners can solve recurrences with the recursion-tree method and the Master theorem
Learners can tell when the Master theorem does not apply
Learners can perform aggregate and accounting amortised analysis

story.title: The bug that passed every test

scenes.text: Dev's max-finding function passes all 20 sample tests but fails on an array of negative numbers in the contest.
He learns to state what is true at the start of every iteration — a loop invariant — and the bug becomes obvious: he initialised max to 0.

steps.title: What an algorithm is
steps.body: A finite, unambiguous sequence of steps that takes input and produces correct output for **every** valid input and terminates. We analyse it for correctness, time and space.

steps.title: Loop invariant proofs
steps.body:
Show three things:
- **Initialisation**: true before the first iteration.
- **Maintenance**: if true before an iteration, it stays true after it.
- **Termination**: when the loop ends, the invariant gives the desired result.

steps.title: Solved example: maximum
steps.body:
`m = A[0]; for i = 1..n−1: if A[i] > m: m = A[i]`
- Invariant: at the start of iteration i, m = max(A[0..i−1]).
- Init: i = 1, m = A[0] ✔. Maintenance: comparing with A[i] gives max(A[0..i]) ✔.
- Termination: i = n → m = max(A[0..n−1]) ✔.
Setting m = 0 breaks initialisation for all-negative arrays.

steps.title: Solved example: best, worst, average
steps.body:
Linear search for x in n items.
- Best: x first → 1 comparison.
- Worst: absent or last → n.
- Average (present, uniform position): (1+2+…+n)/n = (n+1)/2 → Θ(n).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing an invariant that is true but useless at termination.
- Testing only typical inputs; always test empty, one element, duplicates, negatives.
- Equating 'average case' with 'expected for random input' without stating the distribution.

activity.prompt: Read n and n integers (possibly all negative). Print the maximum. Initialise correctly!
activity.hint: Start with the first element, not 0.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a step of a loop-invariant proof?
quiz.why: A loop-invariant proof has three logical steps: initialisation, maintenance and termination. Compilation is a programming step, not part of the proof.

quiz.q: Average comparisons for successful linear search
quiz.why: On average the target is in the middle, so the mean position is (1 + 2 + … + n)/n = (n + 1)/2 comparisons.
By definition an algorithm must finish after a finite number of steps. It need not be O(1), recursive or use arrays.

quiz.q: Invariant for insertion sort at start of iteration i
quiz.why: At the start of iteration i of insertion sort, the prefix A[0..i−1] holds the same elements as before, but sorted. The whole array is not sorted yet.
If max starts at 0 and all values are negative, the loop never replaces it, so it wrongly returns 0, which is not in the array.

scenes.text: Ira draws the calls made by merge sort as a tree: one call at the top, two below, four below that.
Adding the work level by level, she sees n per level and log n levels.

steps.title: Recursion tree
steps.body:
Draw each call with its non-recursive cost, sum each level, then sum the levels.

T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n: each level costs n, there are log₂n + 1 levels → **Θ(n log n)**.

steps.title: Solved example: T(n) = 3T(n/4) + n²
steps.body:
- Level 0: n². Level 1: 3(n/4)² = (3/16)n². Level i: (3/16)^i n².
- Geometric series with ratio < 1 → dominated by the root.
- **T(n) = Θ(n²)**.

steps.title: Solved example: substitution
steps.body:
Prove T(n) = 2T(⌊n/2⌋) + n is O(n log n).
- Guess T(n) ≤ c n log n. Assume true for n/2.
- T(n) ≤ 2c(n/2)log(n/2) + n = c n log n − c n + n ≤ c n log n when c ≥ 1. ✔

T(n) = T(n−1) + n → unroll: n + (n−1) + … + 1 = Θ(n²).

steps.title: Solved example: unbalanced split
steps.body:
T(n) = T(n/3) + T(2n/3) + n.
- Every level costs at most n.
- Longest path: n → (2/3)n → … → height log₃⁄₂ n.
- **Θ(n log n)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Proving T(n) ≤ cn + n and concluding O(n) — the constant must not grow.
- Forgetting the leaves' cost: a^(log_b n) = n^(log_b a) leaves.
- Summing only the first two levels.

activity.prompt: Read n (a power of 2). Compute T(n) with T(1)=1 and T(n)=2T(n/2)+n exactly (recursively), and print it. (For n=8: 32.)
activity.hint: Closed form: n log₂ n + n.

quiz.why: Each level of the recursion tree does n work and there are log n levels, so T(n) = Θ(n log n). It is the merge-sort recurrence.
Each call does 1 unit of work and makes one call on n−1, so there are n steps in total: T(n) = Θ(n).
Each step does constant work and halves the input, so there are log n steps, as in binary search: Θ(log n).

quiz.q: Number of leaves in the recursion tree of T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n)
quiz.why: The tree has depth log_b n and branches a ways each level, so there are a^(log_b n) = n^(log_b a) leaves.
The work per level shrinks by a factor of 3/16 per level (3 × (n/4)² = 3n²/16), which is less than 1, so the root's n² dominates.

scenes.text: With 10 recurrences in a GATE mock and 15 minutes left, Om cannot draw ten trees.
The Master theorem compares f(n) with n^(log_b a) and gives each answer in seconds.

steps.title: Statement
steps.body:
For T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), a ≥ 1, b > 1, let p = log_b a.
- **Case 1**: f(n) = O(n^(p−ε)) → T = Θ(n^p).
- **Case 2**: f(n) = Θ(n^p log^k n), k ≥ 0 → T = Θ(n^p log^(k+1) n).
- **Case 3**: f(n) = Ω(n^(p+ε)) and a f(n/b) ≤ c f(n) for some c < 1 → T = Θ(f(n)).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
- T = 9T(n/3) + n: p = 2, f = n smaller → **Θ(n²)**.
- T = T(2n/3) + 1: a=1, b=3/2, p = 0, f = Θ(1) = n⁰ → Case 2 → **Θ(log n)**.
- T = 3T(n/4) + n log n: p ≈ 0.79, f larger, regularity holds → **Θ(n log n)**.
- T = 2T(n/2) + n log n: p = 1, f = n log n (k=1) → **Θ(n log² n)**.
- T = 7T(n/2) + n² (Strassen): p = log₂7 ≈ 2.81 → **Θ(n^2.81)**.

steps.title: When it does NOT apply
steps.body:
- a not constant (T = nT(n/2) + n), or b ≤ 1.
- Subtraction recurrences like T(n) = T(n−1) + n (use unrolling).
- f(n) negative, or the gap is not polynomial in the basic version: T = 2T(n/2) + n/log n (gap is a log factor; extended theorem gives Θ(n log log n)).

steps.title: Change of variables
steps.body: T(n) = 2T(√n) + log n. Let m = log n, S(m) = T(2^m): S(m) = 2S(m/2) + m → Θ(m log m) → **T(n) = Θ(log n · log log n)**.

activity.prompt: Read integers a, b, d for T(n) = aT(n/b) + n^d (a≥1, b≥2, d≥0). Print CASE1, CASE2 or CASE3 by comparing a with b^d (a > b^d → CASE1, equal → CASE2, less → CASE3).
activity.hint: With f(n)=n^d, compare log_b a with d, i.e. a with b^d.

quiz.why: Here n^(log₂4) = n² and f(n) = n grows slower, so the leaves dominate: Θ(n²) by case 1 of the master theorem.
Here n^(log₂4) = n² matches f(n) = n², so each level does equal work and there are log n levels: Θ(n² log n), case 2.
Here f(n) = n³ grows faster than n^(log₂4) = n², and the regularity condition holds, so the root dominates: Θ(n³), case 3.
The master theorem handles T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n), where the input is divided by b. T(n−1) + n shrinks by subtraction, so it does not apply.
Substitute m = log n, so T(2^m) = 2T(2^(m/2)) + m. Let S(m) = T(2^m): S(m) = 2S(m/2) + m = Θ(m log m), so T(n) = Θ(log n log log n).

scenes.text: A dynamic array doubles its capacity when full. Occasionally an append copies thousands of items.
Neel shows his team that spread over all appends, each costs only about 3 units — amortised O(1).

steps.title: Idea
steps.body:
Amortised cost = total cost of a worst-case **sequence** of n operations ÷ n. No probability involved — it is a guarantee on sequences.

Methods: **aggregate**, **accounting** (bank credits), **potential** (Φ function).

steps.title: Solved example: doubling array (aggregate)
steps.body:
n appends starting from capacity 1.
- Copies happen at sizes 1, 2, 4, …, < n → total copies < 2n.
- Plus n writes → total < 3n.
- Amortised **O(1)** per append.

steps.title: Solved example: binary counter (accounting)
steps.body:
Increment a k-bit counter n times.
- Bit 0 flips every time, bit 1 every 2nd, bit i every 2^i-th.
- Total flips ≤ n(1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + …) < 2n → amortised **O(1)**.
- Accounting: charge 2 per increment — 1 to set a bit, 1 saved to reset it later.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing amortised with average-case (random input).
- Growing by a constant (+10) instead of a factor — gives O(n) amortised.
- Letting the bank balance go negative in the accounting method.

steps.title: Where you meet it
steps.body: C++ `vector::push_back`, Java `ArrayList.add`, hash table resizing, splay trees, union–find with path compression (nearly O(1) amortised).

activity.prompt: Read n. Simulate n appends to an array that starts with capacity 1 and doubles when full. Print the total number of element copies made during resizes.
activity.hint: When size == cap, copy size elements and double cap.

quiz.q: Amortised cost of push_back with doubling
quiz.why: Doubling copies a total of less than 2n elements over n appends, so the average (amortised) cost per push_back is O(1), even though a single resize costs O(n).
Amortised analysis gives a bound on the average cost per operation over any worst-case sequence. It needs no probability or random input, unlike average-case analysis.

quiz.q: Growing an array by +100 each time gives amortised append
quiz.why: Growing by a fixed +100 means about n/100 resizes, each copying up to n items, so the total copies are Θ(n²/100) and the amortised cost per append is O(n), not O(1).

quiz.q: Total bit flips for n increments of a binary counter
quiz.why: Bit i flips once every 2^i increments, so the total flips are n(1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + …) < 2n.

quiz.q: Which is an amortised analysis method?
quiz.why: The three amortised analysis methods are aggregate, accounting and potential. Branch and bound, greedy and memoisation are different techniques.

questions.q: T(n)=8T(n/2)+n²
questions.why: Here n^(log₂8) = n³ is larger than f(n) = n², so the leaves dominate: Θ(n³) (master theorem case 1).
Here n^(log₂1) = n⁰ = 1 and f(n) = n is larger, so the root dominates: Θ(n), case 3. The halving makes a geometric series 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + … that sums to about 2n.
Here n^(log₂2) = n and f(n) = 1 is smaller, so the leaves dominate: Θ(n), case 1.

questions.q: T(n)=T(n−1)+n²
questions.why: Unrolling gives 1² + 2² + … + n² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1)/6, which is Θ(n³).
Each call makes two calls for n−1 in the Tower of Hanoi style, so the cost doubles each level: 2ⁿ − 1 = Θ(2ⁿ).
Each step takes the square root of n, so it takes log log n steps to get down to a constant, with cost 1 per step: Θ(log log n).

questions.q: T(n)=16T(n/4)+n² log n
questions.why: Here n^(log₄16) = n², and f(n) = n² log n is n² times log^k n with k = 1. That's the extended case 2, giving Θ(n² log^(k+1) n) = Θ(n² log² n).

questions.q: Assertion: Master theorem cannot solve T(n)=2^n T(n/2)+n. Reason: a must be a constant.
questions.why: The assertion is true: the master theorem needs a constant number of subproblems, and here a = 2ⁿ changes with n. The reason is true and explains the assertion.

questions.q: Amortised cost per operation of a stack with multipop (n operations total)
questions.why: Every element is pushed once and can be popped at most once, so n operations cost O(n) in total. The amortised cost per operation is O(1), even though one multipop can be expensive.

questions.q: Loop: for(i=1;i<=n;i++) for(j=i;j<=n;j+=i) x++; total
questions.why: For each i, the inner loop runs about n/i times. The total is n(1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … + 1/n) = n·Hₙ = Θ(n log n).

questions.q: Case: a library's add() sometimes takes 50 ms when it resizes but usually 1 µs. The documented cost 'amortised O(1)' means
options: the average over random data is O(1)
any n adds take O(n) total
each add is O(1) worst case
questions.why: 'Amortised O(1)' is a guarantee over a sequence: any n adds take O(n) total, even if a few are slow. It isn't a worst-case bound for each add or an average over random data.

questions.q: Strassen's recurrence T(n)=7T(n/2)+n² gives exponent
questions.why: Here n^(log₂7) ≈ n^2.81 beats f(n) = n², so case 1 applies and T(n) = Θ(n^(log₂7)) ≈ n^2.81. That's better than the n³ of the naive method.

questions.q: Recursion tree for T(n)=T(n/3)+T(2n/3)+n has height
questions.why: The longest path takes the larger piece, shrinking by 2/3 each level, so the height is log_(3/2) n = Θ(log n). Each level costs at most n.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of growth?
options: log n < √n < n < n log n
questions.why: Among these functions, log n grows slowest, then √n, then n, then n log n, which is the standard order.
Here n^(log₃3) = n and f(n) = n/2 is the same order, so each level does equal work and there are log n levels: Θ(n log n), case 2.

questions.q: Number of copies to reach size 2^k by doubling from capacity 1
questions.why: Doubling from 1 to 2^k copies 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2^(k−1) = 2^k − 1 items in total.

questions.q: The best-case time of an algorithm is
options: the minimum cost over inputs of size n
questions.why: The best-case time is the smallest cost over all inputs of size n. It is not the average and not an amortised bound.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Divide and Conquer
courses.summary: The divide-and-conquer paradigm: binary search and its variants, merge sort with inversion counting, quicksort and randomised selection, fast exponentiation, Karatsuba and Strassen multiplication, maximum subarray and closest pair.
outcomes: Learners can design a divide-and-conquer algorithm and write its recurrence
Learners can count inversions in O(n log n)
Learners can find the k-th smallest element in expected linear time
Learners can explain Karatsuba and Strassen speed-ups

lessons.title: Paradigm, fast power and binary search variants

scenes.text: RSA on a phone computes numbers like 7^65537 mod m. Multiplying 65,536 times would drain the battery.
Squaring repeatedly needs only about 17 multiplications.

steps.title: Divide, conquer, combine
steps.body:
1. **Divide** into smaller subproblems of the same kind.
2. **Conquer** each recursively (solve directly when small).
3. **Combine** the answers.

Recurrence: T(n) = aT(n/b) + D(n) + C(n).

steps.title: Solved example: peak element
steps.body:
Find any i with A[i] ≥ neighbours. Look at mid: if A[mid] < A[mid+1], a peak exists on the right; otherwise on the left (including mid). O(log n).
- [1, 3, 20, 4, 1, 0]: mid=2 → 20 > 4 → go left → peak 20 at index 2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Computing x^(n/2) twice (T(n) = 2T(n/2)+1 = O(n)!). Store it once.
- Overflow in (a·b) mod m — use 64-bit or __int128.
- Calling every recursive algorithm divide and conquer (subproblems must be independent and smaller by a fraction).

activity.prompt: Read x, n, m and print x^n mod m using fast exponentiation (n up to 10^18).
activity.hint: Process bits of n from least significant; square x each step.

quiz.why: Fast exponentiation squares x and halves n each step, so it needs only about log n multiplications, not n.
2^10 = 1024. Dividing by 1000 leaves a remainder of 1024 − 1000 = 24.

quiz.q: Which step combines sub-answers in merge sort?
quiz.why: Merge sort splits the array, sorts each half, then merges the two sorted halves. The merge step is the combine step of divide and conquer.

quiz.q: Peak finding by binary search costs
quiz.why: Look at the middle element and move toward the larger neighbour, which always leaves a peak in the remaining half. Halving each step gives O(log n).

quiz.q: Calling pow(x,n/2) twice per level gives
quiz.why: Calling pow(x, n/2) twice gives T(n) = 2T(n/2) + 1, which solves to O(n). Calling it once and reusing the result gives O(log n).

scenes.text: A movie site compares your ranking of 1,000 films with your friend's. The number of pairs you disagree on measures similarity.
Counting those pairs one by one is 5 lakh checks; merge sort counts them while sorting.

steps.title: Inversions via merge sort
steps.body:
When merging L and R, if R[j] < L[i], then R[j] is smaller than **all remaining** elements of L: add (len(L) − i) inversions.

T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) = **O(n log n)**.

steps.title: Solved example: maximum subarray
steps.body:
D&C: best of left half, right half, and the best crossing the middle (extend left from mid and right from mid+1). T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n = O(n log n).

Kadane's algorithm does it in O(n): cur = max(x, cur + x), best = max(best, cur).
- [−2, 1, −3, 4, −1, 2, 1, −5, 4] → **6** (4, −1, 2, 1).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding 1 instead of (len(L) − i) per cross inversion.
- Using int for the count: n = 10⁵ can give ~5·10⁹ inversions → use long long.
- Kadane with best initialised to 0 when all numbers are negative.

activity.prompt: Read n and n integers. Print the number of inversions using merge sort (O(n log n)).
activity.hint: Add m-i+1 when taking from the right half.

quiz.why: An inversion is a pair out of order. In [3, 1, 2], (3, 1) and (3, 2) are inversions, while (1, 2) is fine. That is 2.
Maximum inversions occur for a reversed array, where every pair is out of order: C(n, 2) = n(n−1)/2.
Kadane's algorithm keeps a running best sum while making a single pass over the array, so it takes O(n) time.
The divide-and-conquer solution solves each half recursively and scans for the best subarray crossing the middle in O(n), so T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n.
A subarray must contain at least one element. When all numbers are negative the best choice is the single largest element, −1, not 0.

scenes.text: HR needs the median salary of 50,000 employees for a report — but not a full sorted list.
Quickselect partitions once and recurses into one side only, giving the answer in linear expected time.

steps.title: Quickselect
steps.body:
To find the k-th smallest: partition around a pivot at position p.
- k = p → done; k < p → recurse left; k > p → recurse right.
- Expected **O(n)** with a random pivot (T(n) = T(n/2) + n on average); worst O(n²).

steps.title: Median of medians (deterministic)
steps.body:
Groups of 5 → median of each → recursively find the median of those medians → use as pivot. It guarantees at least ~3n/10 elements on each side.

T(n) ≤ T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + O(n) → **O(n)** worst case (since 1/5 + 7/10 < 1).

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Find the 3rd smallest of [7, 10, 4, 3, 20, 15] (k = 2, 0-based), pivot = last = 15.
- Partition → [7, 10, 4, 3, **15**, 20], p = 4. k < p → left part [7, 10, 4, 3].
- Pivot 3 → [**3**, 10, 4, 7], p = 0. k > p → right part [10, 4, 7].
- Pivot 7 → [4, **7**, 10] at global index 2 = k → answer **7**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Recursing into both sides (that is quicksort, O(n log n)).
- Mixing 0-based k with 1-based 'k-th smallest'.
- Groups of 3 in median of medians do not give linear time (1/3 + 2/3 = 1).

activity.prompt: Read n, k (1-based) and n integers. Print the k-th smallest using quickselect (Lomuto partition, last element pivot).
activity.hint: Keep narrowing [l, r] around the target index.

quiz.why: Randomised quickselect recurses into only one side of the partition. The expected sizes shrink geometrically, giving n + n/2 + n/4 + … = O(n) expected time. Sorting would cost O(n log n).

quiz.q: Worst case of quickselect with bad pivots
quiz.why: If every pivot is the smallest or largest element, each partition removes just one item. Work is n + (n−1) + … + 1 = O(n²).

quiz.q: Median of medians uses groups of
quiz.why: Median of medians splits the input into groups of 5. Five is the smallest odd size where the recurrence still adds up to linear time (7 also works, 3 does not).
Finding the pivot is a recursive call on n/5 group medians, and the pivot guarantees that the remaining side has at most about 7n/10 elements. Add n for partitioning: T(n) = T(n/5) + T(7n/10) + n.
Sort the list to get 1, 4, 5. The second smallest is the middle value, 4. The value 1 is the smallest and 5 the largest.

scenes.text: A crypto library multiplies 2,048-bit numbers millions of times a day.
Karatsuba's trick saves one multiplication out of four at every level — and that compounds.

steps.title: Karatsuba
steps.body:
x = a·10^m + b, y = c·10^m + d.
xy = ac·10^(2m) + ((a+b)(c+d) − ac − bd)·10^m + bd → **3** multiplications instead of 4.

T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n) = Θ(n^(log₂3)) ≈ **Θ(n^1.585)**.

steps.title: Strassen
steps.body: Multiplies 2×2 block matrices with **7** multiplications instead of 8 (and 18 additions). T(n) = 7T(n/2) + Θ(n²) = Θ(n^2.807). Practical only for large n; numerically less stable.

steps.title: Closest pair of points
steps.body:
Sort by x, split at the median line, solve both halves → δ = min. Check only points within δ of the line, sorted by y; each needs comparing with at most 7 next points.
- T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) → **O(n log n)** (vs O(n²) brute force).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing Karatsuba's exponent as log₂4 = 2.
- Saying Strassen uses 7 additions (it is 7 multiplications).
- Re-sorting by y in every call of closest pair (gives O(n log² n)).

activity.prompt: Read two non-negative integers x and y (each < 10^9). Multiply using ONE level of Karatsuba with m = 10^4 split (a = x/10^4, b = x%10^4, etc.) and print the product. Use long.
activity.hint: xy = ac·M² + ((a+b)(c+d) − ac − bd)·M + bd.

quiz.why: Karatsuba does three multiplications of half-size numbers instead of four, by computing (a+b)(c+d) and reusing ac and bd.
The recurrence T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n) has leaves n^(log₂3) ≈ n^1.585, which dominate the linear work, so the time is Θ(n^1.585). That beats the schoolbook n².
Strassen's method multiplies 2×2 blocks using 7 multiplications rather than the usual 8, trading them for extra additions.

quiz.q: Closest pair by D&C runs in
quiz.why: Divide and conquer splits the points by x, solves each half, then checks a narrow strip in linear time. T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) gives O(n log n).

quiz.q: Points compared per strip point (classic bound)
quiz.why: For each point in the strip only the next few points (at most 7) in y-order can be closer than the best distance d, because a packing argument limits how many points fit in a d × 2d box.

questions.q: Recurrence of binary search
questions.why: Binary search does constant work, then continues in just one half, so T(n) = T(n/2) + 1. This gives O(log n).
5³ = 125. Dividing 125 by 13: 13 × 9 = 117, and 125 − 117 = 8, so the remainder is 8.

questions.q: Multiplications in fast power for n = 16 (squarings only)
questions.why: Repeated squaring gives x² → x⁴ → x⁸ → x¹⁶, which is 4 squarings. Each squaring doubles the exponent, so log₂16 = 4.

questions.q: Inversions in [1, 5, 4, 3, 2]
questions.why: Only the last four values 5, 4, 3, 2 are out of order, in reverse. Every pair among them is an inversion: C(4,2) = 6. The leading 1 is smaller than all, so adds none.
The best run is 2 − 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. Adding −9 and then 4 would only reduce the total, and 4 alone is smaller than 6.

questions.q: Karatsuba: 21 × 43 middle term (a+b)(c+d) − ac − bd
questions.why: With 21 = (2,1) and 43 = (4,3): (a+b)(c+d) = 3 × 7 = 21, ac = 8 and bd = 3, so the middle term ad + bc = 21 − 8 − 3 = 10. Check: 2·3 + 1·4 = 10.

questions.q: Median-of-medians with groups of 7 gives
questions.why: With groups of 7, the recurrence is T(n) = T(n/7) + T(5n/7) + O(n). The fractions add to 1/7 + 5/7 = 6/7 < 1, so the total is linear.

questions.q: Assertion: quickselect is faster than sorting to find the median on average. Reason: it recurses into only one side.
questions.why: The assertion is true: average quickselect is O(n), while sorting is O(n log n). The reason is true and explains it, because following just one side after each partition gives the geometric sum.

questions.q: Strassen exponent
questions.why: Strassen's recurrence T(n) = 7T(n/2) + O(n²) leads to Θ(n^(log₂7)) ≈ n^2.81, which is why the exponent is log₂7.

questions.q: Case: you need the 10 smallest of 10⁸ readings without full sorting. Best
questions.why: Quickselect finds the 10th smallest in expected linear time and leaves the smaller elements on one side. Sorting just those 10 is cheap, so this beats sorting all 10⁸ readings.

questions.q: D&C for finding max and min together uses comparisons about
questions.why: Compare elements in pairs first: 1 comparison per pair, then the winners compete for max and the losers for min. That costs about n/2 + 2(n/2 − 1) = 3n/2 − 2 comparisons, beating 2n − 2.

questions.q: T(n)=3T(n/2)+n is
questions.why: Here n^(log₂3) ≈ n^1.585 is larger than f(n) = n, so the leaves dominate: Θ(n^(log₂3)) by case 1.

questions.q: Closest pair brute force complexity
questions.why: Brute force compares every pair of points: n(n−1)/2 pairs, which is O(n²).

questions.q: Which problem is NOT naturally divide and conquer?
questions.why: Merge sort, closest pair and Karatsuba all split into subproblems and combine. Kadane's algorithm is a single left-to-right scan with a running sum, which is dynamic programming or greedy.

questions.q: Number of multiplications in naive recursive 2-split integer multiply recurrence
questions.why: Splitting each number in two gives four half-size products (ac, ad, bc, bd) plus linear additions: T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n, which is Θ(n²). Karatsuba cuts it to three.

questions.q: Expected comparisons of randomised quickselect are at most about
questions.why: Randomised quickselect makes at most about 4n comparisons in expectation (about 3.39n for the median), so it is linear. n log n or n² would be too large.

questions.q: Fast power of x^n with n having b bits uses multiplications at most
questions.why: An n with b bits needs b squarings plus at most one extra multiplication for each 1 bit, so at most 2b multiplications in total.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Greedy Algorithms, MST and Shortest Paths
courses.summary: The greedy-choice property and exchange arguments, activity selection, fractional knapsack, Huffman coding, job sequencing with deadlines, minimum spanning trees (Kruskal with union–find, Prim) and single-source shortest paths (Dijkstra).
outcomes: Learners can prove a greedy choice with an exchange argument
Learners can build a Huffman code and compute its cost
Learners can run Kruskal and Prim and state their complexities
Learners can run Dijkstra and explain why negative edges break it

lessons.title: Greedy method, activity selection and fractional knapsack

scenes.text: Fest week: 12 clubs want the only seminar hall at overlapping times. The coordinator wants to host as many events as possible.
Picking the event that finishes earliest, again and again, turns out to be optimal.

steps.title: When greedy works
steps.body:
Two properties:
- **Greedy-choice property**: a locally best choice is part of some optimal solution.
- **Optimal substructure**: after the choice, the rest is a smaller instance of the same problem.

Proof tool: **exchange argument** — swap an optimal solution's choice with the greedy one without making it worse.

steps.title: Solved example: fractional knapsack
steps.body:
Capacity 50; items (value, weight): (60,10), (100,20), (120,30). Ratios 6, 5, 4.
- Take item 1 fully (10 kg, 60), item 2 fully (20 kg, 100) → 30 kg used.
- Take 20/30 of item 3 → 80.
- Total **240**. Greedy by ratio is optimal for *fractional*, not 0/1 (0/1 optimum here is 220).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sorting activities by start time or duration (both can fail).
- Applying ratio-greedy to 0/1 knapsack.
- Assuming greedy coin change always works (coins {1, 3, 4}, amount 6: greedy 4+1+1 = 3 coins, optimal 3+3 = 2).

activity.prompt: Read n and n pairs (start finish). Print the maximum number of non-overlapping activities (an activity may start exactly when the previous finishes).
activity.hint: Sort by finish time; take an activity if it starts at or after the last finish.

quiz.why: Activity selection sorts by finish time. Choosing the activity that ends earliest leaves the most room for the rest, which is the greedy choice.
In fractional knapsack, take items in decreasing value-to-weight ratio, so every kilogram carries the most value possible.

quiz.q: Greedy coin change fails for coins {1,3,4}, amount
quiz.why: For amount 6, greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 (three coins) but 3 + 3 uses only two. So greedy fails for these coins at 6.

quiz.q: The proof technique for greedy correctness
quiz.why: The exchange argument shows that swapping an optimal solution's choice for the greedy one never makes it worse, which proves greedy is correct.
Sorting by ratio costs O(n log n), and the filling loop is only O(n), so sorting dominates the total.

scenes.text: A file of 100,000 characters uses only six letters, with 'a' appearing 45% of the time.
Giving frequent letters shorter codes, Huffman's tree saves about a quarter of the space over fixed 3-bit codes.

steps.title: Huffman's algorithm
steps.body:
Put each symbol in a min-heap by frequency. Repeat n−1 times: remove the two smallest, create a parent with their sum, insert it. Left edge = 0, right = 1.

Produces an optimal **prefix code** (no code is a prefix of another). Time O(n log n).

steps.title: Solved example: job sequencing
steps.body:
Jobs (profit, deadline): J1 (100,2), J2 (19,1), J3 (27,2), J4 (25,1), J5 (15,3). Unit time each.
- Sort by profit: J1, J3, J4, J2, J5. Put each in the latest free slot ≤ deadline.
- J1 → slot 2, J3 → slot 1, J4 none, J2 none, J5 → slot 3.
- Profit = 100 + 27 + 15 = **142**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Merging the two *largest* frequencies.
- Forgetting that the cost (sum of freq × depth) equals the sum of all internal node weights — a quick check: 14+25+30+55+100 = 224 ✔.
- In job sequencing, putting a job in the *earliest* slot instead of the latest.

activity.prompt: Read n frequencies. Print the total cost of the Huffman code (sum of internal node weights).
activity.hint: Each merge adds a+b to the cost.

quiz.why: Huffman coding repeatedly merges the two lowest-frequency nodes, so the rarest symbols end up deepest in the tree with the longest codes.

options: no codeword is a prefix of another
quiz.why: A prefix code means no codeword is the start of another, so a bit stream can be decoded without ambiguity.
Merge 1 + 1 = 2 (cost 2), then 2 + 1 = 3 (cost 3). The total cost is 2 + 3 = 5.
A heap gives each extract-min and insert in O(log n), and there are n − 1 merges, so the total is O(n log n).

quiz.q: Job sequencing places a job in
options: the latest free slot before its deadline
quiz.why: In job sequencing, each job goes into the latest free slot on or before its deadline. That leaves earlier slots free for other jobs.

lessons.title: Minimum spanning trees: Kruskal and Prim

scenes.text: A state power board must connect 8 villages with cable. Each possible link has a cost.
The cheapest network that connects everyone without loops is a minimum spanning tree.

steps.title: Cut property
steps.body: For any cut of the graph, the lightest edge crossing it belongs to some MST. Both Kruskal and Prim follow from it. An MST has exactly V − 1 edges; it is unique if all weights are distinct.

steps.title: Kruskal
steps.body:
Sort edges by weight; add an edge if it joins two different components (check with **union–find**).
- Time O(E log E) = O(E log V).
- Union by rank + path compression makes each find nearly O(1) (inverse Ackermann).

steps.title: Prim
steps.body:
Grow one tree from a start vertex; repeatedly add the lightest edge leaving the tree.
- With a binary heap: O(E log V). With an adjacency matrix and arrays: O(V²) — good for dense graphs.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Vertices A–E. Edges: A-B 1, B-C 4, A-C 3, B-D 2, C-D 5, D-E 7, C-E 6.
- Kruskal: A-B 1 ✔, B-D 2 ✔, A-C 3 ✔, B-C 4 ✗ (cycle), C-D 5 ✗, C-E 6 ✔.
- MST weight = 1 + 2 + 3 + 6 = **12**, 4 edges ✔.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the MST contains the shortest path between every pair (it does not).
- Adding an edge that creates a cycle in Kruskal.
- Thinking the heaviest edge can never be in an MST — it must be if it is a bridge.

activity.prompt: Read V, E and E edges (u v w, 0-based). Print the total weight of the MST using Kruskal with union–find.
activity.hint: Add an edge only if find(u) != find(v).

quiz.q: Edges in an MST of 10 vertices
quiz.why: A spanning tree on V vertices has V − 1 edges, so a 10-vertex MST has 9. More edges would make a cycle.
Kruskal adds edges in weight order and must test quickly whether an edge would form a cycle, which the union–find structure does.

quiz.q: Prim with adjacency matrix runs in
quiz.why: With an adjacency matrix, Prim scans an array of V entries for the minimum on each of V steps, giving O(V²).

quiz.q: If all edge weights are distinct, the MST is
quiz.why: If all edge weights are distinct, there is no tie in the cut or cycle rules, so the MST is unique.
A minimum spanning tree connects all vertices with the smallest possible total edge weight. It doesn't minimise path lengths or diameter.

scenes.text: A food delivery app must find the fastest route from the restaurant to every customer zone.
Dijkstra's algorithm settles the nearest unsettled zone each time, like water spreading through pipes.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body:
dist[s] = 0, others ∞. Repeatedly extract the unvisited vertex u with smallest dist; **relax** each edge (u, v, w): if dist[u] + w < dist[v], update.
- Binary heap: O((V + E) log V). Array: O(V²).
- Requires **non-negative** weights.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Edges (directed): S→A 4, S→B 1, B→A 2, A→C 1, B→C 5.
- Settle S (0): A = 4, B = 1.
- Settle B (1): A = min(4, 3) = 3, C = 6.
- Settle A (3): C = min(6, 4) = 4.
- Settle C (4). Final: S 0, A 3, B 1, C 4.

steps.title: Why negative edges break it
steps.body:
S→A 2, S→B 3, B→A −2. Dijkstra settles A at 2, but S→B→A = 1. Once settled, A is never fixed.

Use **Bellman–Ford** (Unit 4) for negative edges.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding a constant to all edges to remove negatives — it changes which path is shortest (paths with more edges get penalised).
- Forgetting to skip stale heap entries (`if d > dist[u] continue`).
- Using int when path sums can overflow.

activity.prompt: Read V, E, E directed edges (u v w) and a source s. Print the shortest distance to every vertex (space separated), or INF if unreachable.
activity.hint: Skip heap entries whose distance is larger than the current best.

quiz.why: Dijkstra needs non-negative edge weights, so once a vertex is settled its distance can't be improved later.
With a binary heap, each edge may cause a decrease-key and each vertex an extract-min, each O(log V): O((V + E) log V).
Relaxing edge (u, v) means checking whether dist[u] + w < dist[v] and, if so, updating dist[v] to the shorter route.

quiz.q: For negative edges (no negative cycles) use
quiz.why: Bellman–Ford handles negative edge weights (as long as there is no negative cycle). Dijkstra, Prim and Kruskal don't solve this problem.

quiz.q: Dijkstra on an unweighted graph behaves like
quiz.why: With all weights equal, the nearest unsettled vertex is the next one in breadth-first order, so Dijkstra behaves like BFS.

questions.q: Greedy is optimal for which problem?
questions.why: Greedy is optimal for fractional knapsack, because the exchange argument works. For 0/1 knapsack, longest path and TSP it can fail.

questions.q: Huffman cost for frequencies 5, 10, 20, 40
questions.why: Merge 5 + 10 = 15, 15 + 20 = 35, 35 + 40 = 75. The cost is the sum of the merged weights: 15 + 35 + 75 = 125.

questions.q: Fractional knapsack, W=10, items (v,w): (10,5), (8,4), (6,6). Max value
questions.why: Ratios are 2, 2 and 1. Take the first two items (weight 9, value 18), then 1 kg of the third: 1/6 of value 6 gives 1. Total 19.
Sort by finish time: take (1,3), then (4,6) since it starts after 3, then (6,8). The others overlap, so the maximum is 3.

questions.q: Kruskal time
questions.why: Kruskal sorts the edges in O(E log E) and union–find work is nearly linear, so sorting dominates.

questions.q: Assertion: Prim and Kruskal give the same MST weight. Reason: all MSTs of a graph have equal total weight.
questions.why: The assertion is true: both algorithms give an MST of the same weight. The reason is true and explains it, because all minimum spanning trees have the same minimum total weight.

questions.q: Graph with 6 vertices, distinct weights. Edges in MST
questions.why: A spanning tree on 6 vertices has V − 1 = 5 edges.

questions.q: Dijkstra from S: S→A 7, S→B 2, B→A 3, A→C 1, B→C 8. dist(C)
questions.why: dist(B) = 2; relaxing B→A gives A = 2 + 3 = 5 (better than 7). Then A→C gives C = 5 + 1 = 6, which beats B→C (2 + 8 = 10), so dist(C) = 6.

questions.q: Case: a network has a link with weight −3 (a rebate) but no negative cycles. Which algorithm is safe?
questions.why: With a negative edge weight (but no negative cycle), Bellman–Ford is correct. Dijkstra can give wrong answers, and Kruskal and Prim are for spanning trees.

questions.q: Job sequencing (profit,deadline): (20,2), (15,2), (10,1), (5,3), (1,3). Max profit
questions.why: Take profits in descending order: 20 goes in slot 2, 15 in slot 1, 10 has deadline 1 but slot 1 is taken, so skip it. 5 goes in slot 3, and 1 is out. Total 20 + 15 + 5 = 40.

questions.q: Union–find with union by rank and path compression: amortised cost per op
questions.why: With union by rank and path compression, each operation costs O(α(n)) amortised, where α is the inverse Ackermann function, which is below 5 for any practical n.

questions.q: Which statement about MSTs is false?
options: The MST path between two vertices is always the shortest path
The lightest edge is always in some MST
A bridge is in every MST
questions.why: The false statement is that the MST path is always the shortest path. An MST minimises total weight, not distances between pairs, so it can differ from a shortest-path tree.

questions.q: Greedy coin change is optimal for Indian denominations 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 2000 because
questions.why: Indian coin denominations form a canonical system, where taking the largest coin first always gives the fewest coins. Greedy doesn't work for every system, e.g. {1, 3, 4}.

questions.q: Huffman: maximum code length for n symbols
questions.why: The deepest leaf of a Huffman tree with n symbols can be at depth n − 1, as for Fibonacci-like frequencies that form a chain.

questions.q: Prim's with binary heap on a dense graph (E≈V²)
questions.why: Prim's algorithm with a binary heap runs in O(E log V). With E ≈ V² this becomes O(V² log V), worse than the array version's O(V²).

questions.q: Dijkstra visits vertices in order of
questions.why: Dijkstra always extracts the vertex with the smallest tentative distance, so vertices are finalised in non-decreasing order of distance.

questions.q: Fixed-length code for 6 symbols needs bits per symbol
questions.why: With 6 symbols we need ⌈log₂6⌉ = 3 bits, since 2 bits only distinguish 4 symbols.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Dynamic Programming
courses.summary: Overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure, memoisation vs tabulation, 0/1 knapsack, longest common subsequence, edit distance, matrix-chain multiplication, coin change, and graph DP: Bellman–Ford and Floyd–Warshall.
outcomes: Learners can define DP states, transitions and base cases
Learners can fill LCS, knapsack and matrix-chain tables by hand
Learners can reconstruct an optimal solution from a table
Learners can run Bellman–Ford and Floyd–Warshall and detect negative cycles

scenes.text: A puzzle asks: in how many ways can you climb 40 stairs taking 1 or 2 steps? Siya's recursive program runs for minutes.
She stores each answer the first time she computes it. The program now finishes instantly.

steps.title: Two properties
steps.body:
- **Overlapping subproblems**: the same subproblem recurs (unlike merge sort).
- **Optimal substructure**: an optimal solution contains optimal solutions of subproblems.

Recipe: define the **state**, write the **recurrence**, set **base cases**, choose an **order** of evaluation, then (optionally) **reconstruct**.

steps.title: Top-down vs bottom-up
steps.body:
- **Memoisation** (top-down): recursion + cache; computes only needed states.
- **Tabulation** (bottom-up): fill a table in dependency order; no recursion overhead; easy space optimisation.
Both have time = (#states) × (work per state).

steps.title: Solved example: stairs
steps.body:
ways(n) = ways(n−1) + ways(n−2), ways(0) = 1, ways(1) = 1.
- 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 … ways(5) = **8**.
- O(n) time and O(1) space with two variables. ways(40) = 165580141.

steps.title: Solved example: minimum coins
steps.body:
Coins {1, 3, 4}, amount 6. dp[x] = 1 + min dp[x − c].
- dp: 0, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, **2** → 3 + 3.
- Time O(amount × coins).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- States that don't capture all needed information (wrong answers).
- Filling the table in an order that reads uncomputed cells.
- Using DP when subproblems don't overlap — no gain over divide and conquer.

activity.prompt: Read the number of coin types k, the k coin values, and an amount A (≤ 10000). Print the minimum number of coins to make A, or -1 if impossible.
activity.hint: dp[0]=0; dp[x]=1+min over coins.

quiz.why: Dynamic programming needs overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure. Greedy choice is a different property.
ways(n) = ways(n−1) + ways(n−2), starting 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13. So ways(6) = 13, a Fibonacci number shifted by one.
Memoisation stores results of recursive calls in a cache, so each subproblem is solved once. It is the top-down form of DP.
Using coins 3 and 4 gives 7 with two coins. A greedy choice of 4 + 1 + 1 + 1 would need four.
DP running time is estimated as the number of states times the work per state.

scenes.text: Before a Himalayan trek, Arnav can carry 10 kg and must pick gear to maximise usefulness; items can't be split.
In a bioinformatics lab his sister compares two DNA strings to find their longest common subsequence. Both use 2-D tables.

steps.title: 0/1 knapsack
steps.body:
K[i][w] = best value using the first i items with capacity w.
- K[i][w] = K[i−1][w] if wᵢ > w
- else max(K[i−1][w], vᵢ + K[i−1][w − wᵢ])
Time O(nW) — **pseudo-polynomial** (W is a number, not input length).

steps.title: Solved example: knapsack
steps.body:
W = 50; (v, w): (60,10), (100,20), (120,30).
- Options: items 2 + 3 → 50 kg, value **220**; 1 + 3 → 180; 1 + 2 → 160.
- Answer 220 (greedy by ratio would give 160 here).

steps.title: LCS
steps.body:
L[i][j] for prefixes X[1..i], Y[1..j]:
- if X[i] = Y[j]: L[i−1][j−1] + 1
- else max(L[i−1][j], L[i][j−1])
Time and space O(mn); length alone in O(min(m,n)) space.

steps.title: Solved example: LCS
steps.body:
X = ABCBDAB, Y = BDCABA.
- Filling the 7×6 table gives L = **4**; one LCS is BCBA (others: BDAB, BCAB).
- Reconstruct by walking back from L[7][6]: diagonal on a match, else move toward the larger neighbour.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing subsequence (not contiguous) with substring (contiguous).
- In the 1-D knapsack optimisation, looping w upward (that solves *unbounded* knapsack). Loop w **downward** for 0/1.
- Calling O(nW) polynomial.

activity.prompt: Read two strings X and Y (no spaces). Print the length of their longest common subsequence.
activity.hint: Row 0 and column 0 are all zeros.

quiz.why: The 0/1 knapsack table has n rows and W columns, each filled in O(1), so the time is O(nW).
'AC' appears in 'ABC' in order (skipping B), so the longest common subsequence is 2.

quiz.q: For 0/1 knapsack with a 1-D array, iterate capacity
quiz.why: With a single array for 0/1 knapsack, loop capacity downward so each item is used at most once. Going upward would reuse the same item.
O(nW) depends on the numeric value of W, not the number of bits in it, so it is pseudo-polynomial, exponential in the input length.
The common subsequence G, T, A, B appears in order in both strings, giving length 4 (GTAB).

scenes.text: A graphics engine multiplies four transformation matrices. One bracketing takes 26,000 multiplications, another 4,500.
Meanwhile, the spell checker asks how many edits turn 'kitten' into 'sitting'. Both are interval/sequence DPs.

steps.title: Matrix chain
steps.body:
Matrices A₁…Aₙ, Aᵢ is p[i−1] × p[i].
m[i][j] = min over k (i ≤ k < j) of m[i][k] + m[k+1][j] + p[i−1]·p[k]·p[j], m[i][i] = 0.
Fill by increasing chain length. Time **O(n³)**, space O(n²).

steps.title: Edit distance
steps.body: D[i][j] = min(D[i−1][j] + 1 (delete), D[i][j−1] + 1 (insert), D[i−1][j−1] + [xᵢ ≠ yⱼ] (replace/match)), D[i][0] = i, D[0][j] = j. Time O(mn).

steps.title: Solved example: kitten → sitting
steps.body:
- k→s (replace), e→i (replace), insert g at end.
- Edit distance = **3**.
- 'sunday' → 'saturday' = 3 (insert a, insert t, replace n→r).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using p[i]·p[k]·p[j] instead of p[i−1]·p[k]·p[j].
- Filling the matrix-chain table row by row (needs diagonal/length order).
- Forgetting the base row/column of the edit-distance table.

activity.prompt: Read n (number of matrices) and n+1 dimensions p0..pn. Print the minimum number of scalar multiplications.
activity.hint: Outer loop over chain length, then start i, then split k.

quiz.why: The matrix-chain table has about n² cells and each tries up to n split points, so the time is O(n³).

quiz.q: Cost of multiplying a 2×3 by a 3×4 matrix
quiz.why: Multiplying a p×q by a q×r matrix takes p·q·r scalar multiplications: 2 × 3 × 4 = 24.
'cat' and 'cut' differ only in the middle letter, so one replacement turns one into the other: distance 1.
Turning a string of i characters into the empty string takes i deletions, so D[i][0] = i.

quiz.q: Number of ways to parenthesise 4 matrices
quiz.why: The number of ways to parenthesise n matrices is the Catalan number C(n−1). For 4 matrices that is C₃ = 5.

scenes.text: A trader converts rupees → dollars → euros → rupees and ends with more money than she started with.
In a graph of −log(exchange rates), that profit is a negative cycle, and Bellman–Ford can detect it.

steps.title: Bellman–Ford
steps.body:
Relax **all** edges V − 1 times. If a V-th pass still improves some distance → a negative cycle is reachable.
- Time **O(VE)**. Works with negative edges.
- DP view: d_k(v) = shortest path using at most k edges.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Edges: S→A 4, S→B 5, B→A −3, A→C 2.
- Pass 1 (in this edge order): A = 4, B = 5, A = 2 (via B), C = 4.
- Pass 2–3: no change. Final: S 0, A 2, B 5, C 4.

steps.title: Floyd–Warshall
steps.body:
All-pairs shortest paths: for k in 1..n, for i, for j: d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]).
- Time **O(V³)**, space O(V²). k must be the outermost loop.
- Negative cycle ⇔ some d[i][i] < 0 at the end.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting k as the inner loop in Floyd–Warshall.
- Relaxing only V − 2 times or stopping early without checking.
- Adding to ∞ and overflowing — check d[u] < INF before relaxing.

activity.prompt: Read V, E, E directed edges (u v w, weights may be negative) and source s. Run Bellman–Ford. If a negative cycle is reachable print NEGATIVE CYCLE, else print distances (INF if unreachable), space separated.
activity.hint: An improvement on pass V means a negative cycle.

quiz.why: Bellman–Ford relaxes every edge, V − 1 times, so it takes O(VE).
Floyd–Warshall has three nested loops over V vertices, so it runs in O(V³).

quiz.q: In Floyd–Warshall, the outermost loop is over
quiz.why: The outermost loop is over k, the intermediate vertex allowed on paths. After round k, paths may use vertices 1..k as intermediates.

quiz.q: A negative cycle in Floyd–Warshall shows as
quiz.why: If there is a negative cycle, going around it lowers the cost, so some d[i][i] becomes negative.
A shortest simple path has at most V − 1 edges, so V − 1 passes of relaxation are enough.

questions.q: Which is NOT solved by DP typically?
questions.why: Activity selection is solved by a simple greedy algorithm (earliest finish time), so DP isn't needed. Matrix chain, edit distance and LCS are classic DP.

questions.q: LCS length of 'ABCDGH' and 'AEDFHR'
questions.why: 'A', 'D', 'H' appear in both strings in the same order, giving an LCS of length 3 (ADH).

questions.q: 0/1 knapsack W=7, items (v,w): (1,1), (4,3), (5,4), (7,5). Max value
questions.why: Capacity 7: items (4,3) and (5,4) weigh 7 and give value 9. The item (7,5) with (1,1) gives 8, so 9 is the maximum.

questions.q: Matrix chain p=[5,10,3,12,5,50,6] — number of DP cells with i<j
questions.why: With n = 6 matrices there is one cell for each pair i < j: C(6,2) = 15.

questions.q: Edit distance 'sunday' → 'saturday'
questions.why: The classic edit distance between 'sunday' and 'saturday' is 3: insert 'a', insert 't', and replace 'n' with 'r'.

questions.q: Assertion: 0/1 knapsack is NP-hard yet solvable in O(nW). Reason: O(nW) is exponential in the number of bits of W.
questions.why: Both statements are true. Knapsack is NP-hard, yet O(nW) is only pseudo-polynomial: W takes log W bits, so nW is exponential in the input length. R explains how both can hold.

questions.q: Minimum coins for 11 with {1, 5, 6, 9}
questions.why: Use coins 5 and 6 to make 11, which takes just two coins. A greedy 9 + 1 + 1 would need three.

questions.q: Cost of (AB)C with A 10×100, B 100×5, C 5×50
questions.why: A·B costs 10 × 100 × 5 = 5000 and gives a 10×5 matrix. Multiplying by C (5×50) costs 10 × 5 × 50 = 2500. Total 7500.

questions.q: Case: route planning needs distances between all 300 city pairs, with some negative toll rebates but no negative cycles. Simplest choice
questions.why: All-pairs shortest paths with negative edges but no negative cycles is what Floyd–Warshall handles in O(V³), which is simple and fine for 300 cities. Dijkstra can't be used with negative edges.

questions.q: Number of subproblems in LCS of lengths m and n
questions.why: The LCS table has one cell for each pair of prefix lengths, from 0 to m and 0 to n, so (m + 1)(n + 1) subproblems.

questions.q: Space-optimised LCS length needs
questions.why: Each row depends only on the previous row, so you only keep two rows of length min(m, n) + 1, which is O(min(m, n)) space.

questions.q: Longest increasing subsequence of [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18] has length
questions.why: One increasing subsequence is 2, 3, 7, 18, of length 4. No increasing subsequence of length 5 exists.

questions.q: LIS can be found in
questions.why: With patience sorting, keep a 'tails' array and use binary search for each element, which gives O(n log n).

questions.q: Bellman–Ford: after k passes, d(v) is at most the shortest path using
questions.why: After k passes of Bellman–Ford, d(v) is no more than the shortest distance using at most k edges. This is the DP invariant.

questions.q: Ways to climb 7 stairs with steps of 1 or 2
questions.why: ways(n) = ways(n−1) + ways(n−2) with ways(1) = 1 and ways(2) = 2: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21. So ways(7) = 21.

questions.q: Number of distinct parenthesisations of 5 matrices
questions.why: The number of ways to parenthesise n matrices is the Catalan number C(n−1), so for 5 matrices C₄ = 14.

questions.q: Memoised fib(n) time
questions.why: Memoisation computes each fib(k) once for k up to n, each in O(1), so the total is O(n). The plain recursive version is exponential.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Backtracking, Branch and Bound and String Matching
courses.summary: State-space trees, backtracking for N-Queens, subset sum and graph colouring, branch and bound with bounding functions, and string matching: naive, Rabin–Karp and Knuth–Morris–Pratt.
outcomes: Learners can draw a state-space tree and prune it
Learners can solve N-Queens and subset sum by backtracking
Learners can apply a bounding function in branch and bound
Learners can compute the KMP prefix function and match in O(n + m)

scenes.text: At the chess club, Rohan tries to place 8 queens so that none attack each other. Random tries fail.
He places one queen per row and steps back the moment a conflict appears. Solutions start appearing quickly.

steps.title: Backtracking
steps.body:
Build a solution one component at a time; after each choice, test feasibility (the **bounding/constraint** check). If infeasible, undo the last choice and try the next one.

The search space is a **state-space tree**; pruning cuts whole subtrees.

steps.title: Solved example: 4-Queens
steps.body:
Rows 1–4, one queen per row; column c conflicts if same column or |r₁−r₂| = |c₁−c₂|.
- Row 1 col 1 → row 2 col 3 → row 3: none safe → backtrack; row 2 col 4 → row 3 col 2 → row 4: none → backtrack…
- First solution: columns **(2, 4, 1, 3)**; the other is (3, 1, 4, 2). 4-Queens has 2 solutions; 8-Queens has 92.

steps.title: Cost
steps.body: Worst case is exponential (N! placements for N-Queens with the one-per-row trick), but pruning makes typical runs far smaller. Use column and diagonal boolean arrays for O(1) safety checks: diagonals r+c and r−c+N−1.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to undo state (unmark column/diagonal) after the recursive call.
- Checking only one diagonal direction.
- Counting rotations/reflections as different or the same without saying which.

activity.prompt: Read N (1 ≤ N ≤ 10). Print the number of solutions to the N-Queens problem.
activity.hint: Mark, recurse, unmark.

quiz.why: The 8-Queens puzzle has 92 solutions in total, and 12 distinct ones when rotations and reflections are treated as the same.

quiz.q: Backtracking abandons a partial solution when
quiz.why: Backtracking abandons (prunes) a partial solution as soon as it violates a constraint, since no completion can be valid.

quiz.q: Two queens at (r1,c1),(r2,c2) share a diagonal if
quiz.why: Two queens share a diagonal when their row difference equals their column difference in magnitude, |r₁ − r₂| = |c₁ − c₂|, since the diagonal slope is ±1.
4-Queens has exactly two solutions: columns (2, 4, 1, 3) and (3, 1, 4, 2), which are mirror images.

quiz.q: The search space in backtracking is drawn as
quiz.why: Backtracking explores a state-space tree, in which each level is a choice and each branch is one option.

lessons.title: Subset sum, graph colouring and Hamiltonian cycles

scenes.text: The exam cell must schedule papers so that no student has two papers in the same slot.
Papers become vertices, clashes become edges, and slots become colours — a graph colouring problem.

steps.title: Subset sum
steps.body:
Given positive numbers and target T, choose a subset summing to T. Sort ascending; at each element include or exclude.

Prune: if current sum + next element > T (sorted) stop that branch; if current sum + all remaining < T stop.

steps.title: m-colouring
steps.body:
Assign colours 1..m to vertices in order; a colour is valid if no already-coloured neighbour has it. The smallest such m is the **chromatic number**.
- Bipartite graphs: 2. Planar graphs: ≤ 4 (four-colour theorem). Kₙ: n.

steps.title: Hamiltonian cycle
steps.body: Visit every vertex exactly once and return. Backtrack by extending a path with an unvisited neighbour; at depth V check an edge back to the start. (Euler circuit — every *edge* once — is easy: all degrees even and connected.)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing Hamiltonian (vertices) with Eulerian (edges).
- Not sorting before using the 'next element too big' prune.
- Claiming every planar graph needs 4 colours (it needs *at most* 4).

activity.prompt: Read n, n positive integers and target T. Print YES if some subset sums to T, else NO (backtracking or DP).
activity.hint: Prune when the sum exceeds T.

quiz.why: K₅ has an edge between every pair of vertices, so all 5 need different colours: χ(K₅) = 5.
A Hamiltonian cycle goes through every vertex exactly once and returns to its start. Visiting every edge once is an Euler circuit.

quiz.q: An Euler circuit exists in a connected graph iff
quiz.why: By Euler's theorem, a connected graph has an Euler circuit exactly when every vertex has even degree.

quiz.q: Chromatic number of a cycle of 6 vertices
quiz.why: An even cycle is bipartite, so two colours (alternating around the cycle) suffice. Fewer isn't possible since it has edges.
The subset-sum DP fills an n × T boolean table (items by target sums), so it takes O(nT).

scenes.text: A medical representative must visit 5 hospitals and return to base by the shortest route.
Branch and bound discards any partial route whose optimistic estimate is already worse than the best full route found.

steps.title: Idea
steps.body:
Like backtracking but for **optimisation**. Each node gets a **bound** (lower bound for minimisation, upper bound for maximisation). If the bound is no better than the best complete solution so far (the incumbent), prune.

Exploration orders: FIFO (BFS), LIFO (DFS), **least-cost (best-first)** using a priority queue.

steps.title: Solved example: 0/1 knapsack bound
steps.body:
W = 10; items sorted by ratio: (40, 4), (42, 7), (25, 5), (12, 3) → ratios 10, 6, 5, 4.
- Root bound (fractional): 40 + (6/7)·42 = 76.
- Include item 1, exclude item 2: bound = 40 + 25 + (1/3)·12 = 69; leaf {1, 3} gives 65.
- Other branches have bound ≤ 65 or are infeasible → optimum **65**.

steps.title: Solved example: TSP lower bound
steps.body: A simple bound: for each city, (sum of its two cheapest incident edges)/2, summed over cities. Any branch whose bound ≥ the best tour cost so far is pruned. Better bounds (e.g. reduced cost matrix) prune more.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a bound that is not optimistic — you may prune the true optimum.
- Mixing up upper and lower bounds for max vs min problems.
- Expecting polynomial time — the worst case is still exponential.

activity.prompt: Read n, W and n items (value weight). Print the best 0/1 knapsack value using DFS branch and bound with a fractional-knapsack upper bound (items pre-sorted by value/weight in your code).
activity.hint: Prune when the optimistic bound cannot beat the best so far.

quiz.q: Branch and bound is mainly for
quiz.why: Branch and bound is used for optimisation problems. It uses bounds on the best achievable cost to prune branches.
Least-cost branch and bound always expands the most promising live node, which needs a priority queue (best-first search).

quiz.q: A bound for a maximisation problem must be
quiz.why: For maximisation, the bound must be an optimistic upper bound, never below the true best of that branch, so a pruned branch can't hide a better answer.

quiz.q: Worst-case time of B&B for TSP
quiz.why: Branch and bound for TSP can still explore exponentially many nodes in the worst case, because pruning isn't guaranteed to cut much.

quiz.q: Fractional knapsack value is used in 0/1 B&B as
quiz.why: Allowing fractions relaxes the problem, so the fractional knapsack value is at least as large as any 0/1 answer. It is an upper bound for pruning.

lessons.title: String matching: naive, Rabin–Karp and KMP

scenes.text: A server log has 50 crore characters; the SRE searches for an error code thousands of times a day.
KMP never moves backwards in the text, so each search is a single linear sweep.

steps.title: Naive and Rabin–Karp
steps.body:
- **Naive**: try every shift; O((n − m + 1)m) worst case.
- **Rabin–Karp**: rolling hash of the window; compare strings only when hashes match. Expected O(n + m), worst O(nm) with many spurious hits. Great for multiple patterns.

steps.title: KMP prefix function
steps.body:
π[q] = length of the longest proper prefix of P[0..q] that is also a suffix of it. On a mismatch after q matched characters, jump to q = π[q−1] instead of restarting.
- Build π in O(m); match in O(n). Total **O(n + m)**.

steps.title: Solved example: π for ABABACA
steps.body:
P = A B A B A C A
- π = 0 0 1 2 3 0 1
- e.g. at index 4 (ABABA), 'ABA' is both a prefix and suffix → 3; at index 5, 'C' breaks it → 0.

steps.title: Solved example: Rabin–Karp hash
steps.body:
Base 10, mod 13, text digits 31415, pattern 15 → p = 15 mod 13 = 2.
- Windows: 31 → 5, 14 → 1, 41 → 2 (spurious hit, 41 ≠ 15), 15 → 2 ✔ match at shift 3.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the full string (not *proper* prefix) in π, giving π[q] = q+1.
- Forgetting to verify characters after a Rabin–Karp hash match.
- Negative values when removing the leading digit of a rolling hash — add mod before taking %.

activity.prompt: Read a text T and a pattern P (no spaces). Print all 0-based starting indices where P occurs in T (space separated) using KMP, or -1 if none.
activity.hint: After a full match, continue with q = pi[m-1] to find overlaps.

quiz.why: KMP builds the prefix function in O(m) and scans the text in O(n) without backing up, so the total is O(n + m).
For 'AAAA' each prefix has a border as long as one less than itself: the values are 0, 1, 2, 3.
Rabin–Karp is O(n + m) on average, but if many windows have the same hash (spurious hits), each needs an O(m) check, so the worst case is O(nm).

options: a mismatch at the first character
quiz.why: A spurious hit is when the hash of a window equals the pattern hash although the strings differ, so a character-by-character check is needed.

quiz.q: Naive matching worst-case comparisons for n=10, m=3
quiz.why: There are n − m + 1 = 8 alignments, each costing up to m = 3 comparisons, so at most 8 × 3 = 24.

questions.q: Solutions to 6-Queens
questions.why: 6-Queens has exactly 4 solutions.

questions.q: 5-Queens solutions
questions.why: 5-Queens has 10 solutions (and 2 distinct ones up to symmetry).

questions.q: Chromatic number of a tree with ≥ 2 vertices
questions.why: A tree has no cycles, so it is bipartite and can be coloured with just 2 colours.

questions.q: Chromatic number of a 5-cycle
questions.why: A 5-cycle is an odd cycle, which isn't bipartite, so 2 colours aren't enough, but 3 are.

questions.q: KMP prefix function of 'AABAAAB'
questions.why: Compute each position's longest border: A=0, A=1, B=0, A=1, A=2, A=2 (the third A can't extend because the next is B), B=3. That gives 0 1 0 1 2 2 3.

questions.q: Assertion: backtracking can be exponential. Reason: pruning removes some but not necessarily most branches.
questions.why: Both are true. Pruning cuts only some branches, so in the worst case the search tree is still exponential. The reason explains why backtracking can be exponential.

questions.q: Euler circuit exists for degrees (connected) 2, 2, 4, 2, 2
questions.why: All degrees (2, 2, 4, 2, 2) are even and the graph is connected, so an Euler circuit exists.

questions.q: Euler path (not circuit) requires exactly how many odd-degree vertices
questions.why: An Euler path that is not a circuit starts at one odd-degree vertex and ends at another, so exactly 2 vertices have odd degree.

questions.q: Subset of {1, 4, 6, 9} summing to 10
Rabin–Karp mod 11, base 10: hash of '26'
questions.why: The window '26' has value 2 × 10 + 6 = 26, and 26 mod 11 = 4 (since 22 + 4 = 26).

questions.q: Case: a plagiarism checker must look for 10,000 phrase patterns in each essay. Best
options: Rabin–Karp with a hash set of pattern hashes
questions.why: With many patterns, Rabin–Karp can compute rolling hashes of all windows once and look each one up in a hash set of pattern hashes, instead of scanning the text for each pattern.

questions.q: Branch and bound with FIFO order resembles
questions.why: A FIFO order explores live nodes level by level, like breadth-first search. LIFO would act like DFS and least-cost like best-first.

questions.q: Which problem is NOT typically solved by backtracking?
questions.why: Shortest paths with non-negative weights are solved efficiently in polynomial time by Dijkstra, so backtracking isn't the natural method. N-Queens, Sudoku and graph colouring are classic backtracking.

questions.q: KMP: after a full match with π[m−1] = 2, the next comparison continues with q =
questions.why: After a full match, KMP doesn't restart at 0. π[m−1] = 2 means the last 2 matched characters are also a prefix, so it continues with q = 2.

questions.q: Naive matching worst case for text 'AAAA…A' (n) and pattern 'AA…AB' (m)
questions.why: For text AAA…A and pattern AA…AB, each of the n − m + 1 shifts matches m − 1 characters before failing on the last, giving Θ((n − m + 1)m).

questions.q: Planar graphs are colourable with at most
questions.why: By the four-colour theorem, every planar graph can be coloured with at most 4 colours.

questions.q: State-space tree of subset sum with n items has leaves
questions.why: Each of the n items is either included or excluded, so there are 2ⁿ leaves in the state-space tree.

courses.title: Unit 6 · P, NP, NP-Completeness and Approximation
courses.summary: Decision vs optimisation problems, the classes P, NP, NP-hard and NP-complete, polynomial-time reductions, Cook–Levin theorem, classic NP-complete problems, and coping strategies: approximation algorithms, heuristics and special cases.
outcomes: Learners can define P, NP, NP-hard and NP-complete precisely
Learners can verify a certificate in polynomial time
Learners can explain the direction of a reduction
Learners can analyse the 2-approximation for vertex cover

story.title: Easy to check, hard to find

scenes.text: Checking a filled Sudoku takes a minute. Solving a hard blank one can take hours.
Whether every quickly-checkable problem is also quickly-solvable is the famous P vs NP question — still open.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Decision problem**: answer yes/no (e.g. 'Is there a tour of cost ≤ k?').
- **P**: solvable in polynomial time by a deterministic algorithm.
- **NP**: a 'yes' answer has a **certificate** checkable in polynomial time (equivalently, solvable in polynomial time by a non-deterministic machine).
- P ⊆ NP. Whether P = NP is unknown.

steps.title: Solved example: verifying
steps.body:
- **Subset sum**: certificate = the chosen subset; add it up in O(n) → in NP.
- **Hamiltonian cycle**: certificate = vertex order; check each vertex appears once and each consecutive pair is an edge → O(V) → in NP.
- **Shortest path ≤ k**: in P (Dijkstra) — and therefore also in NP.

steps.title: co-NP
steps.body: Problems whose 'no' answers have short certificates, e.g. 'Is this formula unsatisfiable?'. Primality (PRIMES) is in P (AKS, 2002).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'NP' does **not** mean 'not polynomial'; it means non-deterministic polynomial.
- Saying NP problems 'cannot' be solved in polynomial time — that is unproven.
- Confusing optimisation versions with decision versions.

activity.prompt: Certificate checker: read V, E, the E undirected edges, then a sequence of V vertices. Print VALID if it is a Hamiltonian cycle (every vertex exactly once and consecutive vertices, including last→first, adjacent), else INVALID.
activity.hint: Checking is polynomial even though finding is hard.

quiz.why: NP stands for non-deterministic polynomial time: problems whose solutions can be verified in polynomial time.

quiz.q: Which is known to be true?
quiz.why: P ⊆ NP is known: a problem that can be solved quickly can also be verified quickly. Whether P = NP is still open.

quiz.q: A certificate for subset sum is
quiz.why: A certificate for subset sum is the subset itself, and you can verify it by adding its numbers in polynomial time.
PRIMES is in P, shown by the AKS algorithm, which tests primality in polynomial time.

options: is there a tour of cost ≤ k?
quiz.why: The decision version asks a yes/no question: is there a tour of cost at most k? The optimisation version asks for the cheapest tour.

story.title: If I can solve that, I can solve this

scenes.text: A team lead says: 'Our scheduling task is just graph colouring in disguise.'
That one sentence — a reduction — tells them their problem is at least as hard as colouring.

steps.title: Polynomial reduction A ≤p B
steps.body:
A polynomial-time function f maps instances of A to instances of B with x ∈ A ⇔ f(x) ∈ B.
- If B ∈ P then A ∈ P.
- If A is NP-hard then B is NP-hard.
**Direction matters**: to prove B hard, reduce a *known hard* problem A **to** B.

steps.title: Classes
steps.body:
- **NP-hard**: every NP problem reduces to it (may not be in NP; e.g. halting problem, optimisation TSP).
- **NP-complete**: NP-hard **and** in NP.
- **Cook–Levin theorem**: SAT is NP-complete (the first one).
- If any NP-complete problem is in P, then P = NP.

steps.title: Solved example: Independent Set ≤p Vertex Cover
steps.body:
S is an independent set in G ⇔ V − S is a vertex cover.
- So G has an independent set of size ≥ k ⇔ G has a vertex cover of size ≤ V − k.
- The map (G, k) → (G, V − k) is polynomial. Vertex cover is therefore NP-hard (given Independent Set is).

steps.title: Chain of classic reductions
steps.body: SAT → 3-SAT → Independent Set → Vertex Cover → Set Cover; 3-SAT → 3-Colouring; 3-SAT → Subset Sum; Vertex Cover → Hamiltonian Cycle → TSP.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reducing the new problem to SAT and claiming it is NP-hard (wrong direction — that only shows it is in NP).
- Forgetting to show membership in NP when claiming NP-complete.
- Using an exponential-time reduction.

activity.prompt: Brute-force check: read V, E, edges and k. Print YES if there is a vertex cover of size ≤ k (try all subsets; V ≤ 15), else NO.
activity.hint: Every edge must have at least one endpoint in the chosen set.

quiz.q: To prove B is NP-hard, reduce
options: a known NP-hard problem to B
B to a problem in P
B to a known NP-hard problem
quiz.why: To show B is NP-hard, reduce a known NP-hard problem to B: if B were easy, so would that problem be. The reverse direction proves nothing about B's hardness.
Cook and Levin proved that SAT is NP-complete, the first problem shown to be so.
NP-complete means a problem is in NP and also NP-hard.
If S is an independent set, every edge has at least one end outside S, so V − S covers all edges, which makes it a vertex cover. The reverse also holds.
The halting problem is undecidable, so it is not in NP, but every NP problem reduces to it, which makes it NP-hard.

scenes.text: Exam timetabling, register allocation in compilers and map colouring all look different.
Underneath, they are the same NP-complete graph colouring problem.

steps.title: The famous list
steps.body:
- **SAT / 3-SAT** (2-SAT is in P!)
- **Clique**, **Independent Set**, **Vertex Cover**
- **Hamiltonian Cycle/Path**, **TSP (decision)**
- **3-Colouring** (2-colouring is in P)
- **Subset Sum**, **0/1 Knapsack (decision)**, **Partition**
- **Set Cover**, **Exact Cover**

steps.title: Solved example: easy vs hard twins
steps.body:
- Euler circuit (P) vs Hamiltonian cycle (NP-complete)
- Shortest path (P) vs longest simple path (NP-hard)
- 2-SAT (P, via implication graph SCCs) vs 3-SAT (NP-complete)
- 2-colouring (P, BFS) vs 3-colouring (NP-complete)
- Minimum spanning tree (P) vs Steiner tree (NP-hard)

steps.title: Solved example: 3-SAT check
steps.body:
(x₁ ∨ ¬x₂ ∨ x₃) ∧ (¬x₁ ∨ x₂ ∨ x₃) ∧ (¬x₃ ∨ x₁ ∨ x₂). Try x₁ = T, x₂ = T, x₃ = F:
- Clause 1: T ✔. Clause 2: x₂ = T ✔. Clause 3: ¬x₃ = T ✔ → **satisfiable**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling 2-SAT or 2-colouring NP-complete.
- Saying knapsack has no polynomial algorithm — it has a pseudo-polynomial one.
- Forgetting that NP-hardness is about the worst case; many real instances are easy.

activity.prompt: Read n variables and m clauses; each clause has 3 integers (positive i = x_i, negative = NOT x_i, 1-based). Print SAT if some assignment satisfies all clauses (brute force, n ≤ 15), else UNSAT.
activity.hint: Bit v of mask is the value of x_(v+1).

quiz.why: 2-SAT is in P: build the implication graph and check strongly connected components. Hamiltonian cycle, 3-SAT and 3-colouring are NP-complete.
Longest simple path is NP-hard because it includes Hamiltonian path as a special case.
The decision version of Clique is one of Karp's 21 NP-complete problems. Sorting, MST and Euler circuit are in P.

quiz.q: Brute force SAT on n variables tries
quiz.why: Each of the n variables can be true or false independently, giving 2ⁿ assignments to try by brute force.

quiz.q: Register allocation in compilers maps to
quiz.why: Register allocation is modelled as colouring an interference graph, where variables that live at the same time must get different registers.

lessons.title: Coping with hardness: approximation and heuristics

scenes.text: A logistics start-up can't wait for an exact TSP solution for 5,000 stops every night.
They use an algorithm guaranteed to be within 1.5× of optimal on metric distances, then polish it with local search.

steps.title: Approximation ratio
steps.body:
An algorithm is a ρ-approximation if its cost is within a factor ρ of the optimum for **every** input (≤ ρ·OPT for minimisation).

Other strategies: exact exponential algorithms for small n, DP on special structure (trees), parameterised algorithms, ILP solvers, heuristics (greedy, local search, simulated annealing).

steps.title: Solved example: vertex cover 2-approximation
steps.body:
Repeat: pick any uncovered edge (u, v), add **both** u and v, delete all edges touching them.
- The picked edges form a matching M; any cover needs ≥ |M| vertices (one per edge) → OPT ≥ |M|.
- We output 2|M| ≤ 2·OPT → **ratio 2**.
- Path 1–2–3–4: pick (1,2), then (3,4) → {1,2,3,4} (size 4); OPT = {2,3} (size 2).

steps.title: Solved example: metric TSP
steps.body:
- MST-doubling: walk the MST twice and shortcut repeated vertices (triangle inequality) → **2-approximation**.
- Christofides: MST + minimum perfect matching on odd-degree vertices → **1.5-approximation**.
- Without the triangle inequality, no constant-factor approximation exists unless P = NP.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a heuristic an approximation algorithm without a proven ratio.
- Adding only one endpoint of the chosen edge in the vertex-cover algorithm (no guarantee).
- Ignoring that greedy set cover gives an H(n) ≈ ln n ratio, not a constant.

steps.title: In industry
steps.body: Delivery routing, chip layout, crew scheduling and ad allocation all solve NP-hard problems daily using ILP solvers, approximation and heuristics, with exact methods for small sub-problems.

activity.prompt: Read V, E and E edges (in the given order). Run the 2-approximation for vertex cover (scan edges in order; if neither endpoint is in the cover, add both). Print the size of the cover.
activity.hint: Add both endpoints of an uncovered edge.

quiz.q: Ratio of the matching-based vertex-cover algorithm
quiz.why: Take a maximal matching and use both endpoints of every matched edge. This gives a cover of size at most twice the optimum, because any cover needs one endpoint of each matched edge.
Christofides' algorithm uses an MST plus a minimum matching on odd-degree vertices, giving a tour at most 1.5 times optimal for metric TSP.
For general (non-metric) TSP, no constant-factor approximation is possible unless P = NP, since one could solve Hamiltonian cycle with it.
The greedy set cover algorithm picks the set covering the most uncovered elements, and its guarantee is about the harmonic number H_n ≈ ln n.

quiz.q: A heuristic differs from an approximation algorithm because it
quiz.why: A heuristic may work well in practice but has no proven worst-case guarantee, while an approximation algorithm comes with a provable bound.

questions.q: If an NP-complete problem is solved in polynomial time, then
questions.why: Every NP problem reduces in polynomial time to an NP-complete one, so a polynomial algorithm for one of them would solve all of NP quickly, giving P = NP.

questions.q: Which is NOT known to be NP-complete?
questions.why: Clique, 3-SAT and subset sum are NP-complete. Graph isomorphism isn't known to be NP-complete or in P, and a quasi-polynomial algorithm exists.

questions.q: Assertion: every problem in P is in NP. Reason: a polynomial algorithm can verify by solving.
questions.why: A is true: P ⊆ NP. R is true and explains it, because a polynomial algorithm can ignore any certificate and just solve the problem to verify the answer.

questions.q: A ≤p B and B ∈ P. Then
questions.why: If A reduces in polynomial time to B and B is solvable in polynomial time, then combine the reduction with B's algorithm to solve A in polynomial time.

questions.q: A ≤p B and A is NP-hard. Then
questions.why: If an NP-hard problem A reduces to B, then solving B would solve A, so B must be at least as hard: B is NP-hard.

questions.q: Max independent set of a 5-cycle has size
questions.why: In a 5-cycle no two chosen vertices can be adjacent, so the largest independent set has ⌊5/2⌋ = 2 vertices.

questions.q: Min vertex cover of a 5-cycle
questions.why: The complement of a maximum independent set is a minimum vertex cover, so it is 5 − 2 = 3.

questions.q: Case: a startup claims a polynomial exact algorithm for general TSP, tested on 50 cities. Correct response
options: Ask for a proof; tests prove nothing about all inputs
questions.why: Success on 50 cities proves nothing about all inputs. A truly polynomial exact TSP algorithm would show P = NP, so the claim needs a proof.

questions.q: Vertex-cover 2-approx on a star with 5 leaves outputs size
questions.why: The algorithm picks one edge, say centre–leaf, adds both its endpoints, and every edge of the star is covered. That is 2 vertices (the optimum is 1), within the factor of 2.

questions.q: 2-SAT is solved using
questions.why: 2-SAT is solved by building the implication graph and finding strongly connected components. If x and ¬x lie in the same component, it's unsatisfiable.

questions.q: Which pair is (P, NP-complete)?
questions.why: Euler circuit (every edge once) is solvable in polynomial time, so it is in P, while Hamiltonian cycle (every vertex once) is NP-complete.

questions.q: Optimisation TSP is
questions.why: Optimisation TSP asks for the cheapest tour and isn't a yes/no question, so it isn't in NP. It's NP-hard, since the decision version is NP-complete.

questions.q: Vertex cover can be solved in polynomial time on
questions.why: In bipartite graphs, König's theorem links minimum vertex cover to maximum matching, which is polynomial. For general graphs it's NP-hard.

questions.q: MST-doubling TSP approximation ratio (metric)
questions.why: Double the MST edges, then shortcut the walk to get a tour. The tour is at most 2 × MST weight, and MST ≤ OPT, so it is within a factor of 2.

questions.q: Cook–Levin theorem states
questions.why: The Cook–Levin theorem states that SAT is NP-complete, which was the first problem proven to be NP-complete.

questions.q: Subset sum is
questions.why: Subset sum is NP-complete, but the O(nT) DP is pseudo-polynomial, so it's only weakly NP-complete: easy when the numbers are small.

questions.q: A certificate for 'graph is 3-colourable'
questions.why: A proposed colouring is a short certificate: checking every edge to see its ends have different colours takes polynomial time.

courses.title: Algorithms · Revision & Practice
