quiz.why: Automatic (local) variables live on the stack, in the frame of the function that declared them.

questions.q: The & operator gives…
questions.why: The & operator gives the address of its operand. The * operator gives the value at an address.

questions.q: Dereferencing a NULL pointer results in…
questions.why: Dereferencing a NULL pointer is undefined behaviour. In practice it usually crashes, but the language doesn't promise any result.

questions.q: If double *d = 1000 (8-byte double), d + 2 is…
questions.why: Adding 2 to a double* moves it by 2 × 8 = 16 bytes: 1000 + 16 = 1016.

questions.q: `int a[]={1,2,3,4}; int *p=a+1; printf("%d", p[1]);` prints…
questions.why: p = a + 1 points to a[1], so p[1] is *(p + 1) = a[2] = 3.

questions.q: Which allocates memory for 10 ints, zero-filled?
questions.why: calloc(10, sizeof(int)) allocates space for 10 ints and sets it all to zero. malloc(10) allocates only 10 bytes and doesn't clear them.

questions.q: `int (*f)(int)` declares f as…
options: Pointer to function taking int, returning int
questions.why: In int (*f)(int), the parentheses make f a pointer, to a function that takes an int and returns an int.

questions.q: Output: `int x=10, *p=&x, **q=&p; **q = 20; printf("%d", x);`
questions.why: q points to p, p points to x, so **q is x. Assigning 20 to it changes x to 20.
&a is a pointer to the whole array, so &a + 1 points just past the array. Cast to int* and subtract 1, you get a[4], which is 5.

questions.q: Assertion: `free(p); free(p);` is harmless. Reason: free checks whether memory was already freed.
questions.why: Both parts are false. Freeing the same pointer twice is undefined behaviour, and free doesn't keep track of what was already freed.

questions.q: Case: a function `int* make(void){ int v = 5; return &v; }` sometimes prints garbage. Cause?
questions.why: v is a local variable and it no longer exists after the function returns, so the returned pointer dangles. Use malloc or a static variable instead.

questions.q: `int a[]={10,20,30}; int *p=a; int y = ++*p;` y and a[0] are…
questions.why: ++*p increments the int that p points to, so a[0] becomes 11, and the expression's value is 11, so y = 11 and a[0] = 11.

questions.q: `int a[]={10,20,30}; int *p=a; int y = *++p;` y is…
questions.why: *++p first moves p to a[1], then dereferences it. So y = 20.

questions.q: With `char *s = "GATE";` what does `printf("%s", s + 2);` print?
questions.why: s + 2 points to the character at index 2, which is 'T', so printf prints the rest of the string, 'TE'.

questions.q: Difference q − p where p = &a[2], q = &a[7] (int a[10])?
questions.why: Pointer subtraction gives the number of elements between them, not bytes: &a[7] − &a[2] = 5.

questions.q: Which declaration is 'array of 3 pointers to functions returning int'?
questions.why: In int (*f[3])(void), f[3] is an array of 3 elements, and each element is a pointer to a function taking no arguments and returning int.

questions.q: On a 64-bit machine, `sizeof(int *)` and `sizeof(char *)` are typically…
questions.why: Pointer size depends on the machine's address width, not on the type it points to. On a 64-bit system, both are 8 bytes.

questions.q: `int *p = malloc(4 * sizeof(int)); p = malloc(8 * sizeof(int));` What problem occurs?
options: Memory leak of the first block
questions.why: The second malloc overwrites p, so the address of the first block is lost and it can never be freed. That's a memory leak.

questions.q: Given `int m[3][4]` and `int (*p)[4] = m;`, `*(*(p + 2) + 1)` refers to…
questions.why: p points to rows of 4 ints. p + 2 is row 2, *(p + 2) is that row, and adding 1 then dereferencing gives column 1, so the element is m[2][1].

courses.title: Unit 6 · Structures, Unions, Enums, Preprocessor and File Handling Concepts
courses.summary: User-defined types (struct, union, enum, typedef), structure padding and sizeof, self-referential structures, the preprocessor and macros, bit manipulation, and the standard file-handling API (fopen/fprintf/fscanf/fclose) explained conceptually.
outcomes: Learners can define and use structures, arrays of structures and pointers to structures
Learners can compute sizeof for structs with padding and for unions
Learners can write safe macros and use conditional compilation
Learners can describe file modes and the file-handling workflow

scenes.text: Harsh keeps name, roll number and CGPA in three separate arrays. Sorting by CGPA scrambles them.
Bundling them into one struct Student keeps each record together, so sorting moves whole records.

steps.title: Defining and using a struct
steps.body:
```
struct Student { int roll; char name[20]; float cgpa; };
struct Student s = {1, "Asha", 8.7f};
typedef struct Student Student;   // now 'Student s2;' works
```
- Member access: `s.roll`; through a pointer: `p->roll` ≡ `(*p).roll`.
- Structs can be assigned (`s2 = s;` copies all members) and passed/returned by value.
- Structs cannot be compared with `==`; compare member by member.

steps.title: Nested and self-referential structs
steps.body:
- Nested: `struct Date { int d, m, y; }; struct Emp { char name[20]; struct Date doj; };` → `e.doj.y`.
- Self-referential: `struct Node { int data; struct Node *next; };` — a struct may contain a **pointer** to its own type (not an instance of itself). This is the basis of linked lists and trees.

steps.title: Solved example: topper from an array of structs
steps.body:
Student s[3] = {{1,"Asha",8.7},{2,"Ben",9.1},{3,"Chi",8.9}};
- best = 0.
- i = 1: 9.1 > 8.7 → best = 1.
- i = 2: 8.9 > 9.1? No.
- Topper: **Ben (roll 2)**. Print with `s[best].name`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Missing semicolon after the closing brace of a struct definition.
- `p.roll` when p is a pointer (use `p->roll`).
- Assigning strings: `s.name = "Ravi";` is illegal; use `strcpy(s.name, "Ravi");`.
- Passing large structs by value repeatedly — pass a pointer (const if read-only).

activity.prompt: Define `struct P { char name[20]; int marks; };`. Read n then n lines of `name marks`; print the name with the highest marks (first one on ties).
activity.hint: Track the index of the best record; use > (not >=) to keep the first on ties.

quiz.q: Access member x through pointer p to a struct?
quiz.why: For a pointer to a struct, p->x means (*p).x, so it dereferences the pointer and selects the member.

quiz.q: Can two structs be compared with ==?
quiz.why: C doesn't define == for structures. You must compare the members one by one (or use memcmp with care).

quiz.q: A struct can contain a member of type…
quiz.why: A struct can't contain an instance of itself, since it would be infinitely large. It can contain a pointer to itself, which is how linked lists are built.

quiz.q: `s2 = s1;` for two structs of the same type…
quiz.why: Assigning one struct to another of the same type copies all of its members.

options: Create an alias for a type
quiz.why: typedef gives a new name (an alias) to an existing type. It doesn't create a new type or allocate memory.

scenes.text: Kunal expects his struct of a char and an int to take 5 bytes, but sizeof says 8.
The compiler inserted padding so the int sits on a 4-byte boundary, which the CPU reads faster.

steps.title: Alignment and padding
steps.body:
Typical rule (4-byte int, 8-byte double): each member starts at an offset that is a multiple of its alignment, and the total size is a multiple of the largest member alignment.

- `struct A { char c; int i; };` → c at 0, padding 1–3, i at 4 → **8**.
- `struct B { char c; double d; char e; };` → c 0, d 8, e 16, total rounded to 24.
- Reordering largest-first: `{ double d; char c; char e; }` → 16.

Padding is implementation-defined; these values are for common 64-bit systems.

steps.title: Unions and enums
steps.body:
- **union**: all members share the same memory; size = largest member (plus padding). Only one member is meaningful at a time.
- `union U { int i; char c[4]; float f; };` → sizeof 4.
- **enum**: named integer constants. `enum Day { MON, TUE, WED = 10, THU };` → MON = 0, TUE = 1, WED = 10, THU = 11.
- **Bit-fields**: `struct F { unsigned ready : 1; unsigned mode : 3; };` packs flags into bits; you cannot take the address of a bit-field.

steps.title: Solved example: sizeof questions
steps.body:
Assume char 1, short 2, int 4, double 8 bytes with natural alignment.
- `struct { char a; short b; char c; }` → a 0, b 2, c 4, size rounded to multiple of 2 → **6**.
- `struct { int x; char y; }` → 5 rounded up to **8**.
- `union { double d; int a[3]; }` → largest member 12, rounded to multiple of 8 → **16**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding member sizes and ignoring padding.
- Writing one union member and reading another, expecting a portable conversion (type punning has subtle rules).
- Assuming enum values must be consecutive or start at 1.

activity.prompt: Print the values of an enum `enum Level { LOW, MID = 5, HIGH, MAX = 20 };` as `LOW MID HIGH MAX` numbers on one line: expected `0 5 6 20`.
activity.hint: An enumerator without a value is one more than the previous one.

quiz.q: sizeof a union is at least…
quiz.why: All members of a union share the same memory, so a union is at least as big as its largest member.

quiz.q: `enum E { A, B = 4, C };` C equals…
quiz.why: Enumerators count up from the previous value. A = 0, B = 4, so C = 4 + 1 = 5.

quiz.q: Typical sizeof `struct { char c; int i; }` with 4-byte int?
quiz.why: The int must be aligned to 4 bytes, so 3 padding bytes are inserted after the char. The size is 1 + 3 + 4 = 8.

quiz.q: Can you take the address of a bit-field member?
quiz.why: Bit-fields may not start on a byte boundary, so they have no address and you can't use & on them.

quiz.q: Reordering struct members from largest to smallest usually…
quiz.why: Ordering members from largest to smallest usually needs less padding between them, so the struct gets smaller.

lessons.title: The preprocessor, macros and bit manipulation

scenes.text: Om defines #define SQ(x) x*x and SQ(2+3) gives 11 instead of 25.
Text substitution produced 2+3*2+3. Parentheses around every parameter and the whole body fix it.

steps.title: Directives
steps.body:
- `#include <file>` (system path) vs `#include "file"` (local first).
- `#define PI 3.14159` — object-like macro; `#define MAX(a,b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b))` — function-like.
- `#undef`, `#if`, `#ifdef`, `#ifndef`, `#elif`, `#else`, `#endif` — conditional compilation.
- **Include guards**: `#ifndef MYLIB_H` / `#define MYLIB_H` … `#endif` prevent double inclusion.
- Operators: `#x` makes a string, `a##b` pastes tokens. Predefined: `__FILE__`, `__LINE__`, `__DATE__`.

steps.title: Solved example: macro traps
steps.body:
`#define SQ(x) x*x`
- SQ(2+3) → 2+3*2+3 = **11**.
- `#define SQ(x) ((x)*(x))` → 25. ✓
- But SQ(i++) → ((i++)*(i++)) modifies i twice → undefined. Prefer an `inline` function for such cases.

`#define DOUBLE(x) (x)+(x)` then `10 * DOUBLE(3)` → 10*(3)+(3) = **33**, not 60. Wrap the whole body in parentheses.

steps.title: Bit manipulation toolkit
steps.body:
- Set bit k: `x | (1u << k)`
- Clear bit k: `x & ~(1u << k)`
- Toggle bit k: `x ^ (1u << k)`
- Test bit k: `(x >> k) & 1`
- Is power of two: `x && !(x & (x - 1))`
- Count set bits (Kernighan): `while (x) { x &= x - 1; c++; }` — runs once per set bit.
- Swap without temp: `a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b;` (fails if a and b are the same object).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Missing parentheses in macros.
- A space between macro name and '(' in the definition makes it object-like: `#define F (x) x` is not a function-like macro.
- Shifting a signed negative number or shifting by ≥ the width of the type — undefined.

activity.prompt: Read an unsigned integer x. Print the number of set bits, and `yes` or `no` for whether x is a power of two, on two lines.
activity.hint: x & (x-1) clears the lowest set bit; keep a copy of x for the second test.

quiz.why: The macro just replaces text: SQ(1+1) becomes 1+1*1+1. Multiplication goes first, so it is 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, not 4. Wrap macro parameters in parentheses.

options: Prevent multiple inclusion of a header
quiz.why: Include guards (#ifndef / #define / #endif) stop a header from being included twice in the same file, which avoids redefinition errors.

quiz.q: Expression to test whether bit 3 of x is set?
quiz.why: Shift bit 3 down to position 0 with x >> 3, and mask with & 1 to get just that bit. Non-zero means it is set.
x − 1 flips the lowest set bit and all zeros below it. ANDing with x clears just the lowest set bit. This is Kernighan's trick.
Macros are expanded by the preprocessor, before the compiler sees the code.

scenes.text: Ananya's marks program loses all data when it closes, so she must re-type it every time.
She learns to write records to a file with fprintf and read them back with fscanf next time.

steps.title: The FILE workflow
steps.body:
- `FILE *fp = fopen("marks.txt", "r");` — returns NULL if it fails (always check).
- Modes: `"r"` read (must exist), `"w"` write (creates/truncates), `"a"` append, `"r+"` read/write (must exist), `"w+"` read/write (truncates), `"a+"` read/append; add `b` for binary (`"rb"`).
- Text I/O: `fprintf`, `fscanf`, `fgets`, `fputs`, `fgetc`, `fputc`.
- Binary I/O: `fwrite(&rec, sizeof rec, 1, fp)`, `fread(...)`.
- Positioning: `fseek(fp, offset, SEEK_SET|SEEK_CUR|SEEK_END)`, `ftell`, `rewind`.
- `fclose(fp)` flushes buffers and releases the file.

steps.title: Solved example: count lines in a file
Command-line arguments
steps.body:
`int main(int argc, char *argv[])`
- argc = number of arguments including the program name.
- argv[0] = program name, argv[1]… = arguments, argv[argc] = NULL.
- `./sum 3 4` → argc = 3, argv[1] = "3". Convert with `atoi` or `strtol`.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Not checking fopen for NULL.
- Opening with "w" when you meant to keep existing data (it truncates).
- `while (!feof(fp))` loops — they run one extra time; test the return value of the read function instead.
- Storing fgetc's result in a char.

activity.prompt: Simulate reading a file from standard input: count characters, words (separated by spaces/newlines) and lines until EOF, and print them as `chars words lines`. Use getchar like fgetc.
activity.hint: A word starts when you see a non-space character while 'in' is 0.

quiz.q: Mode that creates a file or erases an existing one?
quiz.why: Mode "w" opens a file for writing, creating it if it doesn't exist and truncating (erasing) it if it does. "a" appends instead.
fopen returns NULL if it can't open the file, so you should always check for it before using the file pointer.

quiz.q: Why store fgetc's result in an int?
options: To tell EOF apart from valid characters
quiz.why: EOF is a negative int value that doesn't correspond to a valid character. Storing the result in a char could confuse EOF with a real character, so use an int.
argv[0] is the program name, then 'a' and 'b'. That is 3 arguments, so argc is 3.

quiz.q: Function to move to the end of a file?
quiz.why: fseek(fp, 0, SEEK_END) moves the file position to the end. rewind goes to the start and ftell only reports the position.

questions.q: Operator to access a member through a struct pointer?
questions.why: For a pointer p to a struct, the -> operator accesses a member: p->m. The dot operator is for a struct variable.

questions.q: File mode "a" means…
questions.why: Mode "a" opens a file for appending: new data is written at the end and existing content stays.

questions.q: Typical sizeof `union { int i; double d; char c; }` on 64-bit?
questions.why: A union's size is that of its largest member. The double is 8 bytes, so the size is 8.

questions.q: `enum { R = 2, G, B = 7, Y };` values of G and Y?
questions.why: R = 2, so G = 3, and B = 7 is set explicitly, so Y = 8.

questions.q: With `#define ADD(a,b) a+b`, value of `3 * ADD(2,4)`?
questions.why: The macro substitutes text without parentheses, so 3 * ADD(2,4) becomes 3 * 2 + 4. By precedence this is 6 + 4 = 10, not 3 × 6 = 18.

questions.q: Typical sizeof `struct { char a; double b; int c; }` (8-byte double, 4-byte int)?
questions.why: char a at offset 0; the double b needs 8-byte alignment so it starts at 8; int c at 16. The total of 20 is padded to a multiple of 8, giving 24.

questions.q: Typical sizeof `struct { double b; int c; char a; }`?
questions.why: double b at 0, int c at 8, char a at 12. That's 13 bytes, padded to a multiple of 8 for the double, so 16.

questions.q: Expression to clear bit 2 of x?
questions.why: To clear bit 2, AND with the inverted mask: x & ~4. OR sets a bit, XOR toggles it, and x & 4 only tests it.

questions.q: Number of loop iterations of Kernighan's bit count for x = 0b10110010?
questions.why: Each iteration x &= x − 1 removes one set bit. The pattern 10110010 has four 1 bits, so the loop runs 4 times.

questions.q: Assertion: a struct may contain a member of its own type. Reason: the compiler can compute its size recursively.
questions.why: It may only contain a pointer to its own type; a self-instance would have infinite size.

questions.q: Case: A program reads a file with `while(!feof(fp)) { fscanf(fp, "%d", &x); sum += x; }` and the last number is added twice. Fix?
questions.why: feof only becomes true after a read has already failed, so the loop body runs once more with a stale x. Loop on the return value instead: while (fscanf(...) == 1).

questions.q: `x && !(x & (x-1))` is true for x =…
questions.why: x & (x − 1) is 0 only for powers of two (one set bit), and x && makes sure x isn't 0. Of the options, only 16 is a power of two.

questions.q: What does `#x` do inside a macro body?
options: Converts argument x to a string literal
questions.why: In a macro, #x is the stringizing operator. It turns the macro argument into a string literal, as in #define STR(x) #x.

questions.q: For `./calc 10 20 +`, argv[3] is…
questions.why: argv[0] is the program name "./calc", argv[1] is "10", argv[2] is "20", and argv[3] is "+".

questions.q: Which is FALSE about structures in C?
options: They can be passed by value
They can be returned from functions
questions.why: Structs can be passed by value, assigned and returned from functions, but == isn't defined for them. That's the false statement.

questions.q: Output: `unsigned x = 5; x ^= (1u << 1); printf("%u", x);`
questions.why: 1u << 1 is 2 (binary 0010). XOR with x = 5 (0101) gives 0111 = 7. The bit flips on.

questions.q: `#define MUL(a,b) ((a)*(b))` — value of MUL(1+2, 3+4)?
questions.why: The parameters are parenthesised, so MUL(1+2, 3+4) expands to ((1+2)*(3+4)) = 3 × 7 = 21. Without the parentheses it would become 1+2*3+4 = 11.

questions.q: Typical sizeof `struct { char a; short b; int c; char d; }` (short 2, int 4)?
questions.why: a at 0, short b at 2, int c at 4, char d at 8. That's 9 bytes, padded to a multiple of 4 (the largest alignment), so 12.

courses.title: Programming in C · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: One-page cheat sheets for every unit, a set of output-prediction drills, and two mock papers mixing all units at GATE and end-semester level.
outcomes: Learners can recall key rules of every unit quickly
Learners can predict outputs of tricky C snippets
Learners can attempt a full mock paper under time pressure

scenes.text: It is 10 pm before the C exam. Pooja has no time to reread notes.
She revises one compact sheet per unit and solves five tricky snippets.

steps.title: Unit 1 essentials
steps.body:
- Build: preprocess → compile → assemble → link.
- sizeof(char) = 1; int usually 4; signed overflow = UB; unsigned wraps mod 2ⁿ.
- Octal 0…, hex 0x…; 'A' = 65.
- Integer division truncates toward zero; sign of % follows dividend.
- && and || short-circuit; assignment and ?: are right-associative.
- %d %u %ld %lld %f (printf double) %lf (scanf double) %c %s %p %zu.

steps.title: Unit 2 essentials
steps.body:
- else pairs with nearest unmatched if.
- switch: integer type, constant labels, fall-through without break.
- do-while runs ≥ 1 time; for(;;) is infinite.
- Iteration counts: i *= k loops → log_k n; nested i, j ≤ i → n(n+1)/2.
- break exits innermost loop; continue jumps to the update (for).

steps.title: Unit 3 essentials
steps.body:
- Call by value; use pointers to modify caller variables.
- Storage: auto (garbage), static (0, persists), extern (declared elsewhere), register (no &).
- Recursion = base case + progress; frames on the stack.
- Hanoi 2ⁿ − 1; naive fib calls C(n) = 1 + C(n−1) + C(n−2).

steps.title: Drill with answers
steps.body:
- `printf("%d", 5 > 3 > 1);` → (1) > 1 → **0**.
- `int i = 3; printf("%d", i << 2 | 1);` → 12 | 1 = **13**.
- `int x = 7; x = x++ ;` — undefined behaviour in C before C11 sequencing rules too; avoid.
- `for (i = 0; i < 10; i += 3);` final i = **12**.

statements.s: sizeof(int) is always 4 bytes.
do-while executes its body at least once.
statements.why: The test is at the end.

statements.s: A static local variable is re-initialised on every call.
In C, -7 / 2 equals -3.
A switch can test a float value.

quiz.why: Comparison operators go left to right. 5 > 3 is 1, and then 1 > 1 is 0, so the result is 0, not true as maths would suggest.

quiz.q: Default value of an uninitialised auto variable?
quiz.why: An uninitialised auto variable holds an indeterminate (garbage) value. Only static and global variables are zero-initialised.
i goes 0, 3, 6, 9, then 12. Since 12 < 10 is false, the loop stops with i = 12.
'Undefined reference' is reported by the linker, when a symbol can't be resolved. Syntax and type errors come from the compiler.
Tower of Hanoi needs 2ⁿ − 1 moves: 2⁶ − 1 = 64 − 1 = 63.

scenes.text: Pointers still scare Imran. He decides to master just six identities.
With those six rules, every pointer question in the mock suddenly looks familiar.

steps.title: Unit 4 essentials
steps.body:
- addr(a[i]) = B + i·w; row-major A[i][j] = B + (i·C + j)·w; column-major = B + (j·R + i)·w.
- Arrays decay to pointers when passed; pass n separately.
- Bubble sort: n(n−1)/2 comparisons worst, O(n) best with flag, stable.
- Strings end with '\0'; strcmp for comparison; sizeof vs strlen.

steps.title: Unit 5 essentials
steps.body:
- a[i] ≡ *(a+i) ≡ i[a]; p + k moves k elements.
- *p++ (use, then move), (*p)++ (increment value), ++*p, *++p.
- &a + 1 skips the whole array.
- int *a[5] (array of pointers) vs int (*a)[5] (pointer to array).
- malloc (garbage) / calloc (zeros) / realloc (use temp) / free (then NULL).

steps.title: Unit 6 essentials
steps.body:
- Struct size includes padding; total is a multiple of the largest alignment.
- Union size = largest member (rounded).
- enum values continue from previous + 1.
- Macros: parenthesise parameters and body.
- Bits: set |, clear & ~, toggle ^, test >> & 1; x & (x−1) clears lowest set bit.
- fopen modes r/w/a/+/b; check NULL; loop on read return values.

steps.title: Drill with answers
steps.body:
- `char s[] = "GATE"; printf("%c", *(s + 3));` → **E**.
- `int a[] = {2,4,6}; int *p = a; p++; printf("%d", *p * 2);` → **8**.
- sizeof `struct { int a; char b; }` → **8** (typical).

activity.prompt: Match each declaration to its meaning.
pairs: pointer to an array of 4 ints

quiz.why: s + 1 points to the second character of 'CODE', so printf with %s prints from there to the end: 'ODE'.

quiz.q: Row-major address of A[1][2] in int A[3][3], base 100, w 4?
calloc differs from malloc because it…
quiz.why: calloc sets the allocated memory to zero. malloc leaves it holding garbage.
CUBE(1+1) expands to 1+1*1+1*1+1. Multiplications go first, so it is 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4, not 8.

quiz.q: Typical sizeof `struct { char c[3]; int i; }`?
quiz.why: The 3 chars take 3 bytes, then 1 byte of padding so the int starts at offset 4. With the 4-byte int the total is 8.

lessons.title: Mock paper strategy and practice set

scenes.text: Yash used to get stuck on one hard pointer question and run out of time.
Now he does a first pass of easy questions, marks the hard ones, and returns to them later. His score rises by 15 marks.

steps.title: Exam strategy
steps.body:
- Pass 1: definitions, syntax, single-step outputs (aim for 40% of marks fast).
- Pass 2: tracing loops and recursion — write variable tables.
- Pass 3: pointer and memory puzzles — draw boxes and arrows.
- In programs: write the function signature, base cases and edge cases (n = 0, negative numbers, empty strings).

steps.title: Answer-writing for theory questions
steps.body:
- Define the term in one line.
- Give syntax.
- Give a short code example with output.
- Mention one advantage and one pitfall.

Example: 'Explain static storage class' → definition, syntax, counter example, 'persists across calls / not thread-safe as shared state'.

steps.title: Worked long question
steps.body:
Q: Write a function to remove duplicates from a sorted array in place and return the new length.
- Step 1: if n == 0 return 0.
- Step 2: k = 1; for i = 1 to n−1: if a[i] != a[k−1] then a[k++] = a[i].
- Step 3: return k.
- {1,1,2,3,3,3,4} → {1,2,3,4}, length **4**. Time O(n), space O(1).

steps.title: Last-minute traps
steps.body:
- Integer division inside averages.
- Missing break in switch.
- String compare with ==.
- Missing '\0' space.
- Off-by-one loop bounds.

activity.prompt: Remove duplicates from a sorted array in place. Read n and n sorted integers; print the new length, then the unique elements.
activity.hint: Keep a write index k; copy a[i] only when it differs from the last kept value.

quiz.q: Best first step when a recursion question looks hard?
quiz.why: Drawing the recursion tree lets you see each call and its result, which avoids tracing mistakes. Guessing isn't reliable.

quiz.q: Time complexity of in-place dedup of a sorted array?
quiz.why: A sorted array's duplicates sit next to each other, so one pass with two indices removes them in place in O(n).

quiz.q: Which edge case is most often forgotten in array functions?
quiz.why: The empty case (n = 0) is the one most often forgotten. Array functions may then read a[0] or a[n−1], which is out of range.

quiz.q: Average of ints a and b without truncation?
quiz.why: (a+b)/2 is integer division and drops the fraction. Dividing by 2.0 makes it floating-point, so the half is kept.
strcmp(s, t) == 0 compares the characters of the two strings. s == t only compares addresses.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q1. Which header declares printf?
questions.why: printf is declared in <stdio.h>, the standard input/output header.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q2. Output: `int a = 10; printf("%d", a++ + 5);`
questions.why: a++ gives the old value 10 in the expression, then increments a. So 10 + 5 = 15 is printed.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q3. Iterations: `for(i=2;i<=50;i*=2)`
questions.why: i takes 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and 64 fails i <= 50. That's 5 iterations.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q4. `char *p = "hello"; printf("%c", p[strlen(p)-1]);`
questions.why: strlen(p) is 5, so p[4] is the last character of 'hello', 'o'. p[5] would be '\0'.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q5. Return of `int f(int n){ return n<=0 ? 0 : n%2 + f(n/2); }` for n = 29?
questions.why: The function adds n%2 at each halving, which sums the binary digits of n. 29 is 11101, which has four 1 bits, so it returns 4.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q6. Typical sizeof `struct { char a; int b; char c; }`?
questions.why: a at 0, int b needs alignment so it is at 4, c at 8. That's 9 bytes, padded to a multiple of 4, giving 12.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q7. `int a[] = {1,2,3,4,5}; int *p = a + 4; printf("%d", p - a);`
questions.why: Pointer subtraction counts elements, not bytes: p − a with p = a + 4 gives 4.

questions.q: Mock 1 · Q8. Which causes a memory leak?
options: Reassigning the only pointer to a malloc'd block
questions.why: A leak happens when the last pointer to a malloc'd block is overwritten, because the block becomes unreachable and can't be freed. free(NULL) is harmless.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q1. Value of 0x10 + 010 + 10?
questions.why: 0x10 is 16, 010 is octal = 8, and 10 is 10. The sum is 16 + 8 + 10 = 34.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q2. `switch(1){ case 1: x+=1; case 2: x+=2; default: x+=3; }` with x = 0 gives x =
questions.why: The value 1 matches case 1: x = 1. With no break it falls through to case 2 (x = 3) and then default (x = 6).

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q3. Recursive calls (including the first) for `f(n){ if(n>1){ f(n-1); f(n-1);} }` with n = 4?
questions.why: C(n) = 1 + 2C(n−1) with C(1) = 1. That gives 1, 3, 7, 15 for n = 1 to 4, so f(4) makes 15 calls.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q4. `int x = 0; if (x++ || ++x) ; printf("%d", x);`
questions.why: x++ gives 0 (false) and x becomes 1. Since the left side of || is false, ++x runs, making x = 2.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q5. Column-major address of A[2][3] in A[4][5], base 0, w = 2?
questions.why: Column-major address = (col × rows + row) × size = (3 × 4 + 2) × 2 = 14 × 2 = 28.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q6. `const int *p` and `int *const q` — which can be re-pointed?
questions.why: const int *p points to a const int, but p itself can be moved. int *const q is a constant pointer that can't be re-pointed. So only p can be re-pointed.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q7. Case: A queue program crashes only after many runs; Valgrind reports 'invalid read of size 4' after free. Bug type?
questions.why: Valgrind reporting an invalid read after free means the program is using memory it already freed. That's a use-after-free bug.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q8. Output: `int a=3, b=4; int *p=&a, *q=&b; *p ^= *q; *q ^= *p; *p ^= *q; printf("%d %d", a, b);`
questions.why: This is the XOR swap: a ^= b, b ^= a, a ^= b exchanges the two values without a temporary. So a = 4 and b = 3.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q9. With `int a = -1; unsigned b = 1;`, `a > b` is…
questions.why: a is converted to unsigned, so −1 becomes a huge value (UINT_MAX), which is greater than 1. The result is 1.

questions.q: Mock 2 · Q10. Which is NOT valid C?
questions.why: An array name isn't a modifiable lvalue, so you can't assign to it. int a[3]; a = NULL; is invalid, while the other declarations are fine.

uni-cse-cloud.title: Cloud Computing
uni-cse-cloud.description: Cloud concepts, virtualisation and containers, core compute/storage/network services, serverless and DevOps, and security, identity, cost and reliability — vendor-neutral with AWS, Azure and Google Cloud examples.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Cloud Concepts and Models
courses.summary: The NIST definition of cloud computing, service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS), deployment models, economics (CapEx vs OpEx) and global infrastructure. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can state the five essential characteristics of cloud computing
Learners can classify services as IaaS, PaaS, SaaS or FaaS
Learners can compare public, private, hybrid and multi-cloud deployments
Learners can explain regions, availability zones and edge locations

scenes.text: Every year a university's results website crashes when lakhs of students log in at 10 am.
Moving to the cloud, it scales out to 50 servers for two hours and back to 2 — paying only for what it used.

steps.title: NIST's five essential characteristics
steps.body:
The US National Institute of Standards and Technology (SP 800-145) defines cloud by:

- **On-demand self-service** — provision without calling a person.
- **Broad network access** — over standard networks from many devices.
- **Resource pooling** — multi-tenant shared hardware.
- **Rapid elasticity** — scale out/in quickly, appearing unlimited.
- **Measured service** — usage is metered and billed.

steps.title: Why organisations adopt cloud
steps.body:
- **CapEx → OpEx**: no up-front data-centre purchase; pay-as-you-go.
- Elasticity and global reach in minutes.
- Economies of scale lower unit cost.
- Managed services reduce operational work.
- Trade-offs: vendor lock-in, data-residency rules, variable bills, need for new skills.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Elasticity vs scalability.** Scalability = ability to handle growth (add resources). Elasticity = **automatically** adding and removing resources as demand changes. The results website shows elasticity.

**Example 2. Cost comparison.** On-premises: buy 50 servers for peak = ₹1.5 crore + running costs, idle 360 days a year. Cloud: 2 servers always + 48 extra for ~40 hours a year → a small fraction of the cost.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking cloud is always cheaper — steady, predictable workloads can be cheaper on reserved capacity or on-premises.
- 'Cloud = someone else's computer' ignores managed services and automation.
- Forgetting to switch off resources (idle resources still cost money).

activity.prompt: Match each NIST characteristic to its example.
pairs: Create a VM from a web console in 2 minutes
Use the app from a phone or laptop
Many customers share the same physical hosts
Billed per second of compute used

quiz.q: Which is NOT a NIST essential characteristic?
quiz.why: NIST's five essential characteristics are on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service. 'Unlimited free storage' isn't one of them.

quiz.q: Moving from buying servers to monthly bills is a shift from…
quiz.why: Buying servers is a capital expense (CapEx). Paying a monthly bill for use is an operating expense (OpEx), so the shift is CapEx to OpEx.

quiz.q: Automatically adding and removing capacity with demand is…
quiz.why: Elasticity means capacity grows and shrinks automatically with demand, so you pay only for what you need.

quiz.q: A drawback of public cloud can be…
quiz.why: Public cloud services can be proprietary, which makes moving away hard. That's vendor lock-in.
Many customers (tenants) sharing the same physical infrastructure is resource pooling, one of NIST's characteristics.

lessons.title: Service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, FaaS

scenes.text: Make pizza at home (on-premises), buy a frozen one and bake it (IaaS), order delivery (PaaS), or eat at a restaurant (SaaS).
The more 'as a service', the less you manage yourself.

steps.title: Who manages what
steps.body:
- **IaaS**: provider runs hardware, network, virtualisation; you manage OS, runtime, apps, data. (Virtual machines: EC2, Azure VMs, Compute Engine.)
- **PaaS**: provider also runs OS and runtime; you deploy code and data. (App Service, Elastic Beanstalk, App Engine, managed databases.)
- **SaaS**: complete application; you manage users and data settings. (Email, office suites, CRM.)
- **FaaS / serverless**: you upload functions that run on events and bill per invocation (Lambda, Azure Functions, Cloud Functions).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Classify.** A VM where you install Linux and MySQL → IaaS. A managed PostgreSQL service → PaaS (DBaaS). Web email → SaaS. A function that resizes images when uploaded → FaaS.

**Example 2. Patching.** Who patches the OS? IaaS → **you**. PaaS → **provider**. SaaS → **provider**.

steps.title: Choosing a model
steps.body: Prefer the highest-level service that meets your needs (less operations work); drop to IaaS when you need OS-level control, special software or lift-and-shift migration.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking SaaS means the provider is responsible for your data's correctness and access settings — you still own users, permissions and data.
- Calling any website 'SaaS'.
- Assuming serverless means no servers exist (they are just managed for you).

activity.prompt: Classify each offering.

items.text: Virtual machine with your own OS config
Managed web-app hosting where you push code
Virtual network and disks you configure

quiz.why: In IaaS the provider runs the hardware, networking and hypervisor. The customer manages the guest OS, middleware and applications.

quiz.q: A managed database service is typically…
quiz.why: A managed database service gives you a ready-made platform, with the provider handling the servers and database software. That's PaaS.

quiz.q: Serverless functions are billed mainly by…
quiz.why: Serverless functions are billed per invocation and for the time and memory they use, not for idle servers.

quiz.q: OS patching in PaaS is done by…
quiz.why: In PaaS the provider manages the platform, including OS patching. The customer manages just the application and data.
IaaS has the lowest level of abstraction, so the customer controls the most, down to the operating system.

scenes.text: A bank must keep core transaction data in its own controlled environment but wants cloud elasticity for its mobile app.
It chooses hybrid cloud: private for the core, public for the app front end, connected securely.

steps.title: The four (+1) models
steps.body:
- **Public cloud**: shared provider infrastructure, open to any customer.
- **Private cloud**: dedicated to one organisation, on-premises or hosted.
- **Hybrid cloud**: private + public connected, workloads can move between them.
- **Community cloud**: shared by organisations with common concerns (e.g. government departments).
- **Multi-cloud**: using several public providers (avoid lock-in, best-of-breed, resilience).

steps.title: Data residency and compliance
steps.body: Laws and regulators may require certain data to stay within a country or meet specific controls. In India, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 governs personal data, and sector regulators (for example for banking and payments) may add rules. Providers offer in-country regions to help customers comply — but compliance remains the customer's responsibility too.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body: **Example 1.** A start-up with no hardware → public cloud. **Example 2.** A defence lab with strict isolation → private cloud. **Example 3.** A retailer bursts to public cloud during festive sales while keeping inventory systems in its data centre → hybrid ('cloud bursting').

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing hybrid (private + public) with multi-cloud (several public providers).
- Assuming private cloud is automatically more secure — security depends on how it is run.
- Ignoring network latency and egress costs between environments.

a.text: A hospital chain must keep patient records in India under strict controls but wants a scalable public website and appointment app. Which deployment model?

choices.label: Public cloud for everything in any region
choices.feedback: Data residency and controls need careful planning — region choice matters.

choices.label: Hybrid: controlled environment (or in-country region with strict controls) for records, public cloud for the app

b.text: Records might be stored outside India without the right controls — a compliance risk. Reconsider regions and controls.

c.text: Patient data stays under strict control while the app scales during busy seasons.

quiz.q: Using AWS and Azure together is…
quiz.why: Using more than one public cloud provider, such as AWS and Azure, is multi-cloud. Hybrid means mixing private and public.

quiz.q: On-premises private cloud + public cloud integrated is…
quiz.why: A hybrid cloud integrates an on-premises private cloud with a public cloud.

options: Overflowing peak load from private to public cloud
quiz.why: Cloud bursting means sending extra load to a public cloud when a private cloud runs out of capacity at peak times.

quiz.q: Shared by several organisations with common requirements…
quiz.why: A community cloud is shared by several organisations that have similar needs, such as common security or compliance rules.

options: No — it depends on operations and controls
quiz.why: A private cloud is not automatically secure. Security depends on how it is configured and operated, with good controls and practices.

lessons.title: Global infrastructure: regions, zones and edge

scenes.text: Heavy rain floods one data centre in a city.
An app spread across three availability zones keeps running — users never notice.

steps.title: Building blocks
steps.body:
- **Region**: a geographic area containing multiple data centres (e.g. a Mumbai or Pune region).
- **Availability Zone (AZ)**: one or more physically separate data centres within a region with independent power, cooling and networking, connected by low-latency links.
- **Edge locations / points of presence**: used by CDNs and DNS to serve content close to users.
- Region choice affects latency, price, available services and data residency.

steps.title: Availability maths
steps.body:
Availability = uptime / total time. 99.9% ('three nines') allows about **8.76 hours** downtime per year; 99.99% about **52.6 minutes**.

Independent redundant components: availability = 1 − (1 − a)ⁿ. Components in series: multiply availabilities.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Two independent zones each 99%: 1 − 0.01² = **99.99%**.

**Example 2. Series.** Web tier 99.9% and database 99.9% both required: 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ **99.8%**.

**Example 3.** 99.95% per month (30 days = 43,200 min) → 0.05% × 43,200 ≈ **21.6 minutes** allowed downtime.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Running everything in a single AZ.
- Assuming SLAs cover your whole app — they apply per service, and your design determines the total.
- Choosing a far-away region for Indian users (higher latency).
- Forgetting that data transfer between regions often costs money.

activity.prompt: Compute the availability of 3 independent redundant replicas each 99% available, and of two 99.9% services in series. Print both as percentages rounded to 4 decimals.
activity.starter:
a = 0.99
# parallel = 1 - (1-a)^3
# series = 0.999 * 0.999
print(round(parallel * 100, 4), round(series * 100, 4))
activity.solution:
a = 0.99
parallel = 1 - (1 - a) ** 3
series = 0.999 * 0.999
print(round(parallel * 100, 4), round(series * 100, 4))
activity.hint: Parallel: 1 − product of failure probabilities; series: product of availabilities.

options: Isolated data centre(s) within a region
quiz.why: An availability zone is one or more isolated data centres within a region. Spreading across zones protects against a single data-centre failure.
99.9% availability allows 0.1% downtime. 0.001 × 8760 hours in a year = 8.76 hours.
The system fails only if both replicas fail: 0.1 × 0.1 = 0.01. So availability is 1 − 0.01 = 99%.
Edge locations cache content close to users, which lowers latency in content delivery.

options: Latency, price, services and data residency
quiz.why: Region choice affects latency to users, price, which services are available, and where data is stored (data residency rules).

questions.q: Which document is the classic definition of cloud computing?
questions.why: NIST Special Publication 800-145 gives the standard definition of cloud computing, with five characteristics, three service models and four deployment models.

questions.q: Pay-as-you-go pricing reflects…
questions.why: Pay-as-you-go pricing depends on the provider measuring usage, which is the measured service characteristic.

questions.q: Web email for a company is…
questions.why: Web email delivered as a complete application is software as a service (SaaS).

questions.q: You install your own OS patches on a…
questions.why: On an IaaS virtual machine you manage the guest OS, including patches. In PaaS, FaaS and SaaS the provider does.

questions.q: Assertion: Cloud is always cheaper than on-premises. Reason: Cloud uses pay-as-you-go pricing.
questions.why: The assertion is false: cloud isn't always cheaper, as steady heavy workloads can cost more than owning hardware. The reason is true, since pay-as-you-go is how cloud is billed, but it doesn't make cloud always cheaper.

questions.q: Hybrid cloud combines…
questions.why: A hybrid cloud combines a private cloud and a public cloud, which work together.

questions.q: Three independent 95% components in parallel →
questions.why: A parallel system fails only if all three components fail: 0.05³ = 0.000125. Availability = 1 − 0.000125 = 0.999875 = 99.9875%.

questions.q: 99.99% availability allows about how much downtime per year?
questions.why: 99.99% allows 0.01% downtime: 0.0001 × 525 600 minutes per year ≈ 52.6 minutes.

questions.q: Case: an app must survive a single data-centre failure with minimal latency. Best design?
options: Deploy across multiple AZs in one region
questions.why: Deploying across multiple availability zones in one region survives a single data-centre failure and keeps latency low, as the zones are close together.

questions.q: Which is an example of rapid elasticity?
options: Auto-scaling group grows during a sale
questions.why: Rapid elasticity means capacity scales up and down quickly with demand, such as an auto-scaling group growing during a sale.

questions.q: Case: a government department wants to share infrastructure with other departments with common security needs. Model?
questions.why: A community cloud is shared by organisations with common needs, such as several government departments with similar security rules.

questions.q: Series availability of 99.95% load balancer, 99.9% app, 99.9% DB ≈
questions.why: For components in series, multiply the availabilities: 0.9995 × 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 0.9975 = 99.75%. The system is less available than any single part.

questions.q: Which is FaaS?
options: A function running when an image is uploaded
questions.why: Function as a service (FaaS) runs a function in response to an event, such as an image upload, without managing servers.

questions.q: Monthly SLA 99.9% over 30 days allows ≈
questions.why: 30 days = 43 200 minutes. The SLA allows 0.1% of that: 0.001 × 43 200 = 43.2 minutes.

questions.q: Case: users in India complain of slow load times for an app hosted in another continent. Cheapest first fix?
options: Use a CDN and/or deploy in a nearby region
questions.why: Slow loading for distant users is mainly caused by network distance (latency). The cheapest first fix is to bring content closer with a CDN or a nearby region. Bigger VMs or more laptop RAM don't shorten the distance.

questions.q: Which statement about data residency is correct?
options: Customers must choose regions/controls to meet their legal obligations
questions.why: Data residency is a shared obligation: the provider offers regions and controls, but the customer must choose them so that their legal duties are met. It applies to all service models and in India too.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Virtualisation, Containers and Kubernetes
courses.summary: Hypervisors and virtual machines, containers and Docker images, container orchestration with Kubernetes, and how these power cloud services.
outcomes: Learners can compare type 1 and type 2 hypervisors
Learners can explain how containers differ from VMs
Learners can write and reason about a simple Dockerfile
Learners can describe Kubernetes pods, deployments, services and scaling

scenes.text: A college lab server runs at 8% CPU most of the day.
With a hypervisor it hosts ten isolated virtual machines, each with its own OS.

steps.title: Hypervisor types
steps.body:
A **hypervisor** (virtual machine monitor) creates and runs virtual machines.

- **Type 1 (bare-metal)**: runs directly on hardware — KVM, Xen, Hyper-V, VMware ESXi. Used in data centres.
- **Type 2 (hosted)**: runs as an app on a host OS — VirtualBox, VMware Workstation. Used on laptops.
- Hardware support (Intel VT-x, AMD-V) makes virtualisation efficient.

steps.title: Techniques
steps.body:
- **Full virtualisation**: guest OS unmodified.
- **Paravirtualisation**: guest uses special drivers/calls for speed.
- Live migration moves a running VM between hosts.
- **Overcommitment**: allocating more virtual CPUs/RAM than physical, relying on not all being busy.
- Snapshots capture VM state for backup or rollback.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Consolidation.** 20 physical servers averaging 10% CPU → consolidate to about 3 hosts at ~67% each (leaving headroom).

**Example 2. Overcommit ratio.** A host with 32 physical cores runs VMs totalling 96 vCPUs → overcommit **3:1**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking VMs share the same OS kernel (they don't; each has its own).
- Over-aggressive overcommitment causing 'noisy neighbour' slowdowns.
- Treating snapshots as backups (they usually live on the same storage).

activity.prompt: Type 1 or Type 2 hypervisor?

quiz.why: A type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor runs directly on the hardware. A type 2 hypervisor runs on top of a host operating system.
Each virtual machine runs its own guest operating system with its own kernel, which gives strong isolation. Containers share the host kernel.
Overcommit ratio = virtual CPUs allocated ÷ physical cores = 192/64 = 3, so 3:1.

quiz.q: Moving a running VM between hosts is…
quiz.why: Live migration moves a running VM from one host to another with little or no downtime.
VT-x (Intel) and AMD-V are CPU extensions that make virtualisation faster and safer. HDMI, Wi-Fi and USB-C are unrelated.

scenes.text: Ravi's app runs on his laptop but fails on the server because of a different library version.
Packaged as a Docker image with all dependencies, it runs the same everywhere.

steps.title: Containers vs VMs
steps.body:
Containers package an app with its dependencies and run as **isolated processes sharing the host kernel** (Linux namespaces for isolation, cgroups for resource limits).

- Start in seconds, megabytes in size, high density.
- Weaker isolation than VMs (shared kernel) — in multi-tenant clouds they often run inside VMs or sandboxed runtimes.

steps.title: Images and Dockerfiles
steps.body:
An **image** is a read-only stack of layers; a **container** is a running instance with a thin writable layer. Images live in registries.

Typical Dockerfile:
- `FROM python:3.12-slim`
- `WORKDIR /app`
- `COPY requirements.txt .` then `RUN pip install -r requirements.txt`
- `COPY . .`
- `CMD ["python", "app.py"]`
Ordering matters for layer caching: copy dependency files before source code.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Caching.** If only app.py changes, layers up to `RUN pip install` are reused, so rebuilds are fast. If you `COPY . .` before installing, every code change re-installs dependencies.

**Example 2. Commands.** `docker build -t myapp:1.0 .` → `docker run -p 8080:5000 myapp:1.0` maps host port 8080 to container port 5000.

steps.title: Common mistakes (including security)
steps.body:
- Putting secrets in images (anyone who pulls the image can read them) — use runtime secrets.
- Running as root inside containers; add a non-root `USER`.
- Using `latest` tags in production (not reproducible).
- Huge images: use slim bases and multi-stage builds; scan images for known vulnerabilities.

activity.prompt: Order the Dockerfile instructions for best layer caching.

quiz.why: Containers share the host operating system's kernel and are isolated as processes. They don't have a guest OS of their own.
Namespaces isolate what a container can see (processes, network, filesystem), and cgroups limit the resources it can use. Together they make containers possible.
In -p host:container, port 8080 on the host is forwarded to port 5000 inside the container.

quiz.q: Why copy requirements.txt before the source code?
quiz.why: Docker caches each layer. Dependencies change rarely, so copying requirements.txt and installing first lets that layer be reused when only the source code changes.
Images can be shared and inspected, so secrets must not be baked in. Inject them at run time through a secrets mechanism.

scenes.text: A food-delivery app runs 500 containers. Some crash, traffic spikes at dinner, new versions ship daily.
Kubernetes keeps the desired number running, restarts failures and rolls out updates gradually.

steps.title: Core objects
steps.body:
- **Cluster**: control plane (API server, scheduler, controller manager, etcd store) + worker **nodes** (kubelet, container runtime).
- **Pod**: smallest deployable unit — one or more tightly coupled containers sharing network and storage.
- **Deployment**: declares desired replicas and handles rolling updates/rollbacks via ReplicaSets.
- **Service**: stable virtual IP/DNS name that load-balances to matching pods (ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer).
- **Ingress**: HTTP routing from outside. **ConfigMap/Secret** for configuration. **Namespace** for isolation.

steps.title: Declarative desired state
steps.body:
You describe *what* you want in YAML (e.g. replicas: 3); controllers continuously reconcile actual state to desired state.

- **Liveness probe**: restart if unhealthy. **Readiness probe**: send traffic only when ready.
- **Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA)**: desired = ⌈current × currentMetric / targetMetric⌉.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. HPA.** 4 pods at 90% average CPU, target 60% → ⌈4 × 90/60⌉ = **6** pods.

**Example 2. Self-healing.** Deployment wants 3 replicas; a node dies taking 1 pod → the controller schedules a new pod elsewhere → back to 3.

**Example 3. Rolling update.** maxUnavailable 1, maxSurge 1 with 4 replicas → at most 5 pods during the update and at least 3 serving.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Running a single replica for a critical service.
- No resource requests/limits (pods starve or get evicted).
- Missing readiness probes (traffic hits pods still starting).
- Treating Secrets as encrypted by default — enable encryption at rest and restrict access with RBAC.

activity.prompt: Implement the HPA formula desired = ceil(current * metric / target) and print results for (4, 90, 60) and (10, 30, 60).
activity.starter:
import math
def desired(current, metric, target):
    # formula
    pass
print(desired(4, 90, 60), desired(10, 30, 60))
activity.hint: Use math.ceil.

quiz.why: A pod is the smallest deployable unit in Kubernetes. It wraps one or more containers that share network and storage.

quiz.q: Which object gives pods a stable network endpoint?
quiz.why: A Service gives a group of pods one stable address and DNS name, even when individual pods come and go.
Kubernetes keeps all its cluster state in etcd, a distributed key-value store.
The HPA formula is desired = ceil(current × currentUtilisation / target) = ceil(3 × 100/50) = 6 pods.

options: Pod receives no traffic until ready
quiz.why: If a readiness probe fails, the pod is taken out of the Service's endpoints, so it gets no traffic until it is ready again. It isn't restarted, which is what a liveness probe does.

story.title: Running Kubernetes is a job in itself

scenes.text: A small team spends half its time upgrading and patching its self-built Kubernetes cluster.
Moving to a managed Kubernetes service, the provider runs the control plane; the team focuses on the app.

steps.title: Options
steps.body:
- **VMs** with auto-scaling groups / scale sets — full control.
- **Managed Kubernetes**: EKS (AWS), AKS (Azure), GKE (Google) — provider runs the control plane.
- **Serverless containers**: run a container without managing nodes (e.g. AWS Fargate, Azure Container Apps, Cloud Run).
- **Container registries**: ECR, ACR, Artifact Registry.

steps.title: Purchase options for compute
steps.body:
- **On-demand**: flexible, highest unit price.
- **Reserved / savings plans**: commit 1–3 years for large discounts on steady usage.
- **Spot / preemptible**: spare capacity at big discounts but can be reclaimed with short notice — for fault-tolerant batch jobs.
- Right-size instances using monitoring data.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Choose.** Nightly video transcoding that can restart → spot. A database running 24×7 for 3 years → reserved. A new app with unknown traffic → on-demand + auto-scaling.

**Example 2. Cost.** On-demand ₹10/hour × 730 h = ₹7,300/month. A 40% reserved discount → ₹4,380/month.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using spot instances for stateful, can't-interrupt workloads.
- Buying reservations before understanding steady usage.
- Forgetting managed services still require you to secure workloads and configure access.

activity.prompt: Match workload to purchase option.

quiz.q: In managed Kubernetes, the provider runs…
quiz.why: In managed Kubernetes (like EKS, AKS or GKE), the provider runs and maintains the control plane. You still manage your workloads and, often, the worker nodes.
Spot instances are cheap but can be reclaimed at short notice, so they suit fault-tolerant, interruptible work such as batch jobs, not critical single VMs.
On-demand cost is 20 × 730 = ₹14,600. A 30% discount leaves 70%: 14,600 × 0.7 = ₹10,220.

options: You don't manage the underlying nodes
quiz.why: With serverless containers you run containers without managing the servers underneath, as the provider handles the nodes.
A container registry stores and distributes container images, as Docker Hub or a cloud registry does.

questions.q: VirtualBox on Windows is a…
questions.why: VirtualBox is installed on top of a host OS like Windows, so it is a type 2 (hosted) hypervisor.

questions.q: Containers start faster than VMs mainly because…
options: They boot no separate OS kernel
questions.why: A container doesn't boot its own operating system kernel, since it shares the host's. That's why containers start in seconds while VMs take longer.

questions.q: cgroups provide…
questions.why: cgroups (control groups) limit and account for resources such as CPU and memory used by a container.

questions.q: Assertion: Containers provide stronger isolation than VMs. Reason: Containers share the host kernel.
questions.why: The assertion is false: containers generally give weaker isolation than VMs. The reason is true and is exactly why: containers share the host kernel, so a kernel flaw can affect them all.

questions.q: Which Dockerfile order rebuilds fastest after a code change?
options: Copy deps file, install, then copy code
questions.why: Copy the dependency file, install, and only then copy the code. The install layer stays cached when only code changes, so rebuilds are fast.

questions.q: Kubernetes object that maintains N replicas and rolling updates?
questions.why: A Deployment keeps the desired number of replicas running and performs rolling updates and rollbacks.

questions.q: HPA: 5 pods at 80% CPU, target 50% →
questions.why: desired = ceil(5 × 80/50) = ceil(8) = 8 pods.

questions.q: HPA: 6 pods at 20%, target 60% →
questions.why: desired = ceil(6 × 20/60) = ceil(2) = 2 pods, so the HPA scales down.

questions.q: A liveness probe failing causes…
questions.why: If the liveness probe fails, Kubernetes concludes the container is stuck and restarts it. A failing readiness probe only removes it from traffic.

questions.q: Case: secrets were baked into a public container image. Best immediate actions?
options: Rotate the secrets and rebuild without them; use a secret store
questions.why: Once a secret is in a public image, assume it is compromised. Rotate it, rebuild the image without it, and keep secrets in a secret store. Renaming or re-tagging doesn't help.

questions.q: Rolling update of 10 replicas with maxUnavailable 2, maxSurge 3: max pods at once?
questions.why: maxSurge 3 allows up to 3 extra pods above the desired count, so the maximum is 10 + 3 = 13.

questions.q: Same: min pods available?
questions.why: maxUnavailable 2 means at most 2 of the 10 pods can be down, so at least 10 − 2 = 8 must stay available.

questions.q: Which purchase option suits an interruptible ML training job with checkpoints?
questions.why: A training job with checkpoints can resume after an interruption, so spot instances give a big discount at low risk.

questions.q: 48 cores, VMs total 120 vCPUs → overcommit?
questions.why: Overcommit = 120 vCPUs / 48 cores = 2.5, which is 2.5:1.

questions.q: Case: pods receive traffic while still loading a 2-minute cache, causing errors. Fix?
questions.why: A readiness probe keeps a pod out of the Service until it has finished loading, so no traffic reaches it too early. A liveness probe would restart it instead.

questions.q: Which is NOT part of the Kubernetes control plane?
questions.why: The control plane includes the API server, scheduler, controller manager and etcd. The kubelet runs on every worker node, so it isn't part of the control plane.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Core Services: Compute, Storage, Networking, Databases
courses.summary: Block, file and object storage; virtual networks, subnets, load balancers, DNS and CDNs; managed relational and NoSQL databases; scaling patterns. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can choose block, file or object storage for a workload
Learners can design a VPC/VNet with public and private subnets
Learners can explain load balancers, DNS and CDNs
Learners can choose between relational and NoSQL managed databases and scaling approaches

scenes.text: An ed-tech start-up stores videos on a VM's disk and runs out of space every month.
Moving videos to object storage gives virtually unlimited capacity and cheaper archive tiers.

steps.title: Three storage types
steps.body:
- **Block storage**: raw volumes attached to a VM (EBS, Azure Managed Disks, Persistent Disk) — for OS disks and databases; low latency.
- **File storage**: shared network file system (EFS, Azure Files, Filestore) — many servers mount the same folders.
- **Object storage**: objects (data + metadata + key) in buckets/containers via HTTP APIs (S3, Azure Blob, Cloud Storage) — massively scalable, ideal for media, backups, data lakes, static websites.

steps.title: Tiers, durability, lifecycle
steps.body:
- Access tiers: hot/standard → cool/infrequent → archive (cheapest storage, slower and costlier retrieval).
- **Lifecycle rules** move or delete objects automatically by age.
- Durability vs availability: object stores advertise very high durability (data not lost) through replication across devices/zones; availability is whether you can access it right now.
- Versioning protects against accidental overwrite/deletion.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Choose.** MySQL data files → block. Shared uploads folder for 6 web servers → file. 2 TB of user photos → object.

**Example 2. Lifecycle cost.** 10 TB of videos: 1 TB watched often (hot), 9 TB older than 90 days → move 9 TB to a cool tier at, say, half the price — storage bill drops by about 45%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leaving buckets publicly readable by accident — many data leaks start this way. Block public access by default and grant least-privilege access.
- Archiving data that is read frequently (retrieval charges).
- No versioning or backups for important data.
- Assuming block volumes survive instance deletion (check settings).

activity.prompt: Pick the storage type.

items.text: Shared home folders for a lab cluster

quiz.q: Best for storing millions of user photos?
quiz.why: Object storage scales to huge numbers of items and is accessed over HTTP, so it suits millions of photos. Block storage is for VM disks.

quiz.q: Many servers mounting the same folder need…
quiz.why: When many servers need to mount the same folder, use file storage (a shared file system such as NFS or SMB).
Lifecycle rules automatically move objects to cheaper tiers or delete them as they age, which saves cost.

quiz.q: Archive tiers are cheap for storage but…
quiz.why: Archive tiers are cheap per GB but retrieving data is slow and may cost extra, so use them for rarely read data.

options: Block public access; grant least privilege
quiz.why: A safe default is to block public access and grant only the permissions needed (least privilege). Public buckets are a common cause of data leaks.

lessons.title: Virtual networks, subnets and security groups

story.title: The database on the public internet

scenes.text: A student project's database had a public IP and an open port — it was found by automated scanners within hours.
Redesigned: web servers in a public subnet, database in a private subnet reachable only from the web tier.

steps.title: VPC / VNet basics
steps.body:
A virtual network is your isolated network in the cloud with a CIDR range (e.g. 10.0.0.0/16).

- **Subnets** split it (per AZ): **public** subnets route to an internet gateway; **private** subnets do not.
- **NAT gateway** lets private instances reach the internet for updates without being reachable from it.
- **Route tables** decide where traffic goes.
- Peering / VPN / dedicated links connect networks and on-premises sites.

steps.title: Firewalls in the cloud
steps.body:
- **Security groups / NSGs**: instance-level rules, typically stateful (return traffic allowed automatically).
- **Network ACLs**: subnet-level, often stateless (must allow both directions).
- Principle of **least privilege**: open only needed ports to needed sources (e.g. DB port only from the web tier's security group).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. CIDR sizes.** /16 → 2¹⁶ = 65,536 addresses; /24 → 256. A /16 can hold 256 /24 subnets. (Clouds reserve a few addresses per subnet — e.g. 5 on AWS, so a /24 gives 251 usable.)

**Example 2. Three-tier design.** Load balancer in public subnets → app servers in private subnets → database in isolated private subnets; DB security group allows its port only from the app security group.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Allowing admin ports (SSH/RDP) from 0.0.0.0/0 — use a bastion, VPN or managed session access with MFA.
- Overlapping CIDR ranges that prevent future peering.
- Putting databases in public subnets.
- Forgetting NACLs are stateless.

activity.prompt: Compute the number of addresses in a CIDR block and how many /24 subnets fit in a /16. Print both for prefix 20.
activity.starter:
prefix = 20
# addresses = 2 ** (32 - prefix)
# subnets_24 = how many /24 fit in this /20
print(addresses, subnets_24)
activity.solution:
prefix = 20
addresses = 2 ** (32 - prefix)
subnets_24 = 2 ** (24 - prefix)
print(addresses, subnets_24)
activity.hint: A /20 has 2^12 addresses; it splits into 2^(24−20) /24 blocks.

quiz.why: A /24 leaves 32 − 24 = 8 host bits, so 2⁸ = 256 addresses.

quiz.q: Private subnet instances reach the internet for updates via…
quiz.why: A NAT gateway lets instances in a private subnet make outbound connections (for updates) without being reachable from the internet.
Security groups are stateful: if inbound traffic is allowed, the reply traffic is allowed automatically. Network ACLs are typically stateless.

quiz.q: Best place for a production database?
options: Private subnet, access only from app tier
quiz.why: A production database should sit in a private subnet, reachable only from the application tier, to minimise exposure.

quiz.q: Opening SSH to 0.0.0.0/0 is risky because…
options: Anyone on the internet can try to connect
quiz.why: 0.0.0.0/0 means every address on the internet, so anyone can try to connect to SSH and attempt to break in. Limit it to trusted IP addresses.

scenes.text: An online store expects 20× normal traffic during a festival sale.
A load balancer spreads requests across many servers, and a CDN serves images from cities near shoppers.

steps.title: Load balancers
steps.body:
- **Layer 4** (TCP/UDP): fast, routes by IP/port.
- **Layer 7** (HTTP/HTTPS): routes by path/host/header, terminates TLS, can add a web application firewall.
- Algorithms: round robin, least connections, weighted, IP hash.
- **Health checks** remove unhealthy targets.
- Combine with auto-scaling for elasticity; sticky sessions only when unavoidable (prefer stateless apps).

steps.title: DNS and CDN
steps.body:
- **DNS** maps names to addresses; records: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), TXT; **TTL** controls caching time.
- DNS routing policies: weighted, latency-based, geolocation, failover.
- **CDN** caches static content at edge locations; reduces latency and origin load; cache-control headers and invalidations manage freshness. Many CDNs also absorb large traffic floods (DDoS protection).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Round robin.** 3 servers, 9 requests → 3 each. **Least connections** would send the next request to the server with the fewest active connections.

**Example 2. CDN hit ratio.** 1,000,000 image requests, 92% cache hits → origin serves only **80,000**.

**Example 3. TTL.** Before migrating a website, lower the DNS TTL (e.g. from 86,400 s to 300 s) a day ahead so the switch propagates quickly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- No health checks (traffic sent to dead servers).
- Storing sessions in server memory, breaking when the LB switches servers.
- Caching personalised pages at the CDN.
- Long TTLs right before a migration.

activity.prompt: A CDN receives 2,500,000 requests with a 96% cache-hit ratio. How many requests reach the origin?

quiz.q: Routing /api to one service and /images to another needs a…
quiz.why: Routing by URL path, such as /api versus /images, needs a layer 7 (application) load balancer that reads HTTP requests.

quiz.q: An alias DNS record type is…
quiz.why: A CNAME record makes one name an alias of another (canonical) name. A records map to IPv4 addresses.

quiz.q: Health checks let a load balancer…
options: Stop sending traffic to unhealthy targets
quiz.why: Health checks let the load balancer detect failed servers and stop sending them traffic, which keeps the service available.
A CDN caches static content at edge locations near users, so it lowers latency for such content. It doesn't speed up database writes.

quiz.q: Lower TTL before a migration because…
quiz.why: DNS records are cached for their TTL. Lowering the TTL before a migration means the change takes effect sooner.

scenes.text: An engineer used to wake at 2 am to check database backups and apply patches.
A managed database handles backups, patching and failover — he now designs schemas and indexes instead.

steps.title: Relational vs NoSQL managed services
steps.body:
- **Relational (SQL)**: MySQL/PostgreSQL/SQL Server managed (RDS, Azure SQL, Cloud SQL); ACID transactions, joins, schemas.
- **NoSQL**: key-value/document (DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, Firestore), wide-column, graph — flexible schemas, horizontal scale, often tunable consistency.
- Data warehouses (Redshift, Synapse, BigQuery) for analytics; caches (Redis/Memcached) for speed.

steps.title: Scaling and resilience
steps.body:
- **Vertical scaling** (bigger machine) vs **horizontal** (more machines).
- **Read replicas** offload reads (replication lag → eventual consistency for those reads).
- **Multi-AZ standby** for automatic failover.
- **Sharding/partitioning** splits data across nodes.
- **CAP theorem**: during a network partition, a distributed store must choose consistency or availability.
- Backups: point-in-time recovery; measure **RPO** (data loss tolerated) and **RTO** (time to recover).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A reporting dashboard slows the main database → add a read replica for reports.

**Example 2. RPO.** Backups every 6 hours → worst-case data loss up to **6 hours** (RPO = 6 h) unless continuous log backups are used.

**Example 3. Cache.** 80% of product-page reads hit Redis → database read load drops to **20%**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting read replicas to be instantly up to date.
- Choosing NoSQL just because it's popular when the data is highly relational.
- Never testing a restore.
- Leaving databases open to the internet or unencrypted.

activity.prompt: Match the need to the cloud database feature.

quiz.why: Adding more servers is horizontal scaling (scaling out). Making one server bigger is vertical scaling.
RPO (recovery point objective) is how much data, measured in time, you can afford to lose. RTO is how long recovery may take.

quiz.q: Read replicas may return slightly old data due to…
quiz.why: Read replicas are usually updated asynchronously, so they can lag behind the primary and return slightly old data.

quiz.q: CAP says during a partition you trade off…
quiz.why: The CAP theorem says that when a network partition happens you must choose between consistency and availability.

quiz.q: The true test of a backup is…
quiz.why: A backup is only proven good when you can restore from it. Test restores regularly.

questions.q: Object storage is accessed mainly via…
questions.why: Object storage is accessed through HTTP (REST) APIs rather than being mounted like a disk.

questions.q: A VM's OS disk is…
questions.why: A VM's OS disk is a block storage volume attached to it, like a virtual hard drive.

questions.q: /22 contains how many addresses?
questions.why: A /22 has 32 − 22 = 10 host bits, so 2¹⁰ = 1,024 addresses.

questions.q: How many /24 subnets fit in a /18?
questions.why: A /18 → /24 is 6 more prefix bits, so 2⁶ = 64 subnets.

questions.q: Assertion: NACLs are typically stateless. Reason: Return traffic must be explicitly allowed by rules.
questions.why: NACLs are stateless, so return traffic must be allowed explicitly by rules. The reason is exactly what stateless means, so both are true and R explains A.

questions.q: Which allows private instances outbound internet without inbound exposure?
questions.why: A NAT gateway lets private instances start outbound connections while blocking unsolicited inbound traffic.

questions.q: Least-connections load balancing sends a request to…
options: The server with the fewest active connections
questions.why: Least-connections load balancing sends each new request to the server that currently has the fewest active connections.

questions.q: CDN with 85% hit ratio and 400,000 requests: origin requests?
questions.why: 85% of requests are served from the cache. The remaining 15% go to the origin: 0.15 × 400,000 = 60,000.

questions.q: Case: users get logged out randomly behind a load balancer. Likely cause?
options: Sessions stored in individual server memory
questions.why: If sessions live in one server's memory, a request that reaches another server won't find the session, so the user seems logged out. Use a shared session store or stateless tokens.

questions.q: Backups every 4 hours, no log shipping: worst-case RPO?
questions.why: Since last backup.

questions.q: Highly relational data with complex joins and transactions → choose…
questions.why: Relational data with complex joins and transactions fits a managed relational database, which gives SQL and ACID transactions.

questions.q: Case: a bucket with student ID scans was found publicly listable. First steps?
options: Block public access, review access logs, rotate links/credentials, notify per policy
questions.why: First contain the leak by blocking public access. Then review access logs to see who accessed it, rotate links and credentials, and notify as required by policy. Renaming the bucket doesn't fix the exposure.

questions.q: Which DNS record maps a name to an IPv6 address?
questions.why: An AAAA record maps a name to an IPv6 address. An A record maps to IPv4.

questions.q: Cache hit rate 75% and DB handles 4,000 reads/s originally. New DB read load?
questions.why: A 75% cache hit rate means only 25% of reads reach the database: 0.25 × 4,000 = 1,000 reads/s.

questions.q: Cloud reserves 5 addresses per subnet. Usable in a /28?
questions.why: A /28 has 2⁴ = 16 addresses. With 5 reserved by the cloud, 16 − 5 = 11 are usable.

questions.q: Case: an analytics team needs to scan 50 TB of logs with SQL weekly. Best service type?
options: Data warehouse / serverless query engine over object storage
questions.why: Scanning 50 TB with SQL fits a data warehouse or serverless query engine over object storage, which scales for analytics. One MySQL VM or a cache wouldn't cope.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Serverless, DevOps and Infrastructure as Code
courses.summary: Serverless functions and event-driven design, message queues, DevOps culture, CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code, and observability.
outcomes: Learners can design event-driven serverless workflows and estimate their cost
Learners can explain queues and pub/sub for decoupling
Learners can describe CI/CD pipelines and deployment strategies
Learners can explain infrastructure as code and the three pillars of observability

scenes.text: Every time a student uploads a profile photo, the app needs a small thumbnail.
A function triggered by the upload event creates it in under a second — and costs nothing when nobody uploads.

steps.title: How FaaS works
steps.body:
- Code runs in response to **events**: HTTP requests, file uploads, queue messages, schedules, database changes.
- Scales automatically from zero; billed per request and per GB-second of execution.
- Limits: maximum execution time, memory, package size; **cold starts** add latency when a new instance initialises.
- Functions should be **stateless** and idempotent (events may be delivered more than once).

steps.title: Decoupling with queues and pub/sub
steps.body:
- **Queue** (SQS, Azure Queue/Service Bus, Pub/Sub pull): producers add messages; consumers process at their own pace — smooths spikes; failed messages go to a **dead-letter queue**.
- **Pub/Sub / event bus**: one event fans out to many subscribers.
- Benefits: resilience, independent scaling, loose coupling.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Cost estimate** (illustrative prices): 3 million requests/month, 200 ms each, 512 MB. GB-seconds = 3,000,000 × 0.2 × 0.5 = **300,000 GB-s**. Multiply by the provider's price per GB-s and add request charges (free tiers may cover part).

**Example 2. Spike smoothing.** 10,000 orders arrive in 1 minute; a worker handles 500/min. With a queue, orders wait safely and are processed in 20 minutes instead of being dropped.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Long-running jobs in functions that hit time limits.
- Non-idempotent handlers (charging a card twice on retry).
- Function-to-function chains that are hard to debug — use workflows/step functions.
- Ignoring cold starts for latency-critical APIs.

activity.prompt: Compute GB-seconds for 3,000,000 requests of 200 ms at 512 MB memory and print it as an integer.
activity.starter:
requests = 3_000_000
seconds = 0.2
memory_gb = 512 / 1024
# gb_s = ...
print(int(gb_s))
activity.solution:
requests = 3_000_000
seconds = 0.2
memory_gb = 512 / 1024
gb_s = requests * seconds * memory_gb
print(int(gb_s))
activity.hint: requests × duration × memory in GB.

options: Extra latency when a new function instance initialises
quiz.why: A cold start is the extra delay when the platform has to create and initialise a new function instance.

options: Events may be delivered more than once
quiz.why: Event systems often deliver at least once, so the same event may arrive twice. An idempotent handler gives the same result when run again.

quiz.q: Messages that repeatedly fail go to…
quiz.why: Messages that keep failing are moved to a dead-letter queue, where they can be inspected without blocking the others.
GB-seconds = requests × duration × memory = 1,000,000 × 0.1 × 1 = 100,000.

quiz.q: Pub/sub differs from a queue by…
options: Fanning out each event to many subscribers
quiz.why: In publish/subscribe, each event is delivered to many subscribers (fan-out). A queue gives each message to a single consumer.

story.title: From monthly to many times a day

scenes.text: A team released once a month with a weekend of manual steps — and frequent rollbacks.
With automated tests and pipelines they now ship small changes daily with fewer failures.

steps.title: DevOps ideas
steps.body:
DevOps joins development and operations through culture, automation, measurement and sharing.

**DORA metrics**: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, time to restore service.
