steps.title: Pipelines and deployment strategies
steps.body:
- **Continuous integration**: every commit builds and runs tests.
- **Continuous delivery**: always deployable; **continuous deployment**: automatically released.
- Strategies: **rolling** (replace gradually), **blue–green** (switch traffic between two environments; instant rollback), **canary** (small % of users first), feature flags.
- Add security checks: dependency scanning, secret scanning, image scanning ('shift left').

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Canary.** Release to 5% of 200,000 users = **10,000** users; if error rate stays normal for an hour, increase to 25%, then 100%.

**Example 2. Change failure rate.** 40 deployments, 3 caused incidents → **7.5%**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Automating a broken manual process without fixing it.
- No rollback plan.
- Skipping tests to 'go faster'.
- Storing deployment credentials in the repository.

activity.prompt: Match deployment strategy to description.
pairs: Two identical environments; switch traffic at once
Replace instances a few at a time
Turn a feature on/off without redeploying

options: Every commit is built and tested automatically
quiz.why: Continuous integration means every commit is built and tested automatically, so problems are found early.

quiz.q: Instant rollback by switching traffic back is a feature of…
quiz.why: In blue–green deployment, the old environment is kept running, so you can roll back at once by switching traffic back.
Change failure rate = failed changes ÷ total deployments = 5/50 = 10%.
The DORA metrics are deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service.

options: Adding security checks early in development and pipelines
quiz.why: 'Shift left' means moving security checks earlier in the process, such as into coding and the CI pipeline, so problems are found sooner and cost less.

scenes.text: Nobody knows why staging behaves differently from production — both were built by clicking in a console.
Rebuilt from version-controlled templates, both environments are identical and reviewable.

steps.title: What IaC is
steps.body:
Infrastructure is defined in code files, stored in version control, reviewed like code and applied by tools.

- **Declarative** (desired end state): Terraform/OpenTofu, CloudFormation, Bicep/ARM, Pulumi (general-purpose languages).
- **Configuration management** (inside servers): Ansible, Chef, Puppet.
- Terraform workflow: `init` → `plan` (preview changes) → `apply`; a **state file** tracks real resources.

steps.title: Benefits and practices
steps.body:
- Repeatable environments, easy disaster recovery, peer review, audit trail.
- **Idempotent**: applying twice changes nothing the second time.
- Detect **drift** (manual changes).
- Use modules, separate environments, remote state with locking, and never commit secrets.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Plan output.** 'Plan: 2 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy' → review the change before apply.

**Example 2. Drift.** Someone manually opens a port in the console; the next `plan` shows a change to revert it to the code's definition.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Committing state files with secrets to public repos.
- Applying without reviewing the plan (accidental deletes).
- Mixing manual console changes with IaC.
- One giant file for every environment.

activity.prompt: Order a safe IaC change.
items: Edit the code in a branch
Open a pull request for review

quiz.why: Declarative IaC describes the desired end state (what you want), and the tool works out how to get there.
terraform plan shows what would change without making any changes, so you can review it first.
Drift is when the real infrastructure no longer matches the code, usually because of manual changes.

options: Running again makes no further changes
quiz.why: Idempotent means applying the same configuration again leaves things unchanged, as nothing more needs doing.

quiz.q: Biggest risk with public state files?
options: They may contain secrets and resource details
quiz.why: State files can contain resource details and even secrets, so they must not be public. Store them securely.

scenes.text: Users complain the app is slow every evening, but servers look 'fine'.
Traces show one database query taking 4 seconds during a nightly report — found in 10 minutes.

steps.title: Three pillars
steps.body:
- **Metrics**: numbers over time (CPU, latency p95/p99, error rate, requests/s).
- **Logs**: timestamped events; structured (JSON) logs are searchable.
- **Traces**: follow one request across services with timings (OpenTelemetry is a vendor-neutral standard).

The 'golden signals': latency, traffic, errors, saturation.

steps.title: SLIs, SLOs and error budgets
steps.body:
- **SLI**: measured indicator (e.g. % of requests under 300 ms).
- **SLO**: target (e.g. 99.5% of requests in 30 days).
- **Error budget** = 100% − SLO; when spent, focus on reliability over features.
- Alerts should be actionable and tied to user impact; runbooks guide responders; blameless post-incident reviews prevent repeats.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Error budget.** SLO 99.9% over 10,000,000 monthly requests → budget = **10,000** failed requests.

**Example 2. Percentiles.** Latencies (ms) for 10 requests: 80, 90, 95, 100, 110, 120, 130, 150, 200, 2000. Mean = 307.5 ms but median ≈ 115 ms; p90 ≈ 200 ms — the mean hides that most are fast and one is very slow.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Alerting on everything (alert fatigue).
- Monitoring only averages.
- Logging passwords or personal data.
- Blame-focused incident reviews that discourage honesty.

activity.prompt: SLO 99.95% for 4,000,000 requests in a month. How many failed requests fit in the error budget?

quiz.q: Following one request across microservices uses…
quiz.why: Distributed tracing follows a single request as it passes through many microservices, showing where time is spent.
The error budget is 100% − SLO = 100% − 99% = 1% of requests or time allowed to fail.

quiz.q: Why watch p99 latency, not just the mean?
options: Mean hides slow tails affecting real users
quiz.why: Averages hide slow outliers. The p99 shows the experience of the slowest 1% of requests, which real users feel.
Passwords and other secrets must never be logged, as logs are widely read and stored. Status codes, request IDs and timestamps are safe.

options: Learn system causes and prevent repeats
quiz.why: Blameless reviews focus on how the system allowed the problem, so the team learns and prevents repeats, without punishing people.

questions.q: Serverless functions scale…
questions.why: Serverless functions scale automatically with the number of events, including down to zero when there is no work.

questions.q: Which smooths traffic spikes between services?
questions.why: A message queue buffers requests, so a sudden spike doesn't overwhelm the consumer. The consumer works through them at its own pace.

questions.q: 2,000,000 requests × 0.5 s × 0.25 GB = GB-s?
Assertion: Function handlers should be idempotent. Reason: Retries can deliver the same event twice.
questions.why: Both are true. Retries can deliver the same event twice, so handlers should be idempotent to avoid doing the work twice.

questions.q: Canary at 2% of 500,000 users =
Blue–green main benefit?
questions.why: The main benefit of blue–green is instant rollback: just switch traffic back to the old (blue) environment.

questions.q: Continuous deployment differs from continuous delivery by…
options: Automatically releasing every passing change to production
questions.why: In continuous deployment every change that passes the tests is released to production automatically. In continuous delivery a person approves the release.

questions.q: Terraform's state file tracks…
questions.why: Terraform's state records which real resources it manages, linking the code to the actual infrastructure.

questions.q: Case: plan shows '0 to add, 0 to change, 3 to destroy' unexpectedly. What do you do?
questions.why: An unexpected 'destroy 3' could delete live resources. Stop and find out why before applying, because applying could cause an outage.

questions.q: SLO 99.5% on 2,000,000 requests: error budget?
questions.why: The error budget is 0.5% of requests: 0.005 × 2,000,000 = 10,000 allowed failures.

questions.q: Latencies 10, 10, 10, 10, 1000 ms: mean vs median?
questions.why: The mean is (10 + 10 + 10 + 10 + 1000)/5 = 208 ms. The median, the middle value, is 10 ms. The outlier pulls the mean up but doesn't affect the median.

questions.q: Which is a golden signal?
questions.why: The four golden signals are latency, traffic, errors and saturation.

questions.q: Case: a payment function retried after timeout charges twice. Best fix?
questions.why: A retry after a timeout can repeat the payment. An idempotency key lets the function recognise a duplicate and not charge again.

questions.q: 10,000 messages arrive at once; consumers process 400/min total. Time to drain?
questions.why: Time = messages ÷ rate = 10,000/400 = 25 minutes.

questions.q: Which tool is configuration management rather than provisioning?
questions.why: Ansible is configuration management, which sets up software and settings on existing servers. Terraform, Bicep and CloudFormation provision infrastructure.

questions.q: Case: error budget for the month is exhausted in week 2. SRE practice suggests…
options: Prioritise reliability work and slow feature releases
questions.why: When the error budget is used up, SRE practice is to focus on reliability and slow down feature releases until things stabilise.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Cloud Security, Identity, Cost and Reliability
courses.summary: The shared responsibility model, identity and access management, encryption and key management, governance and compliance, cost management (FinOps) and well-architected design. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can apply the shared responsibility model to IaaS, PaaS and SaaS
Learners can design least-privilege IAM with roles, groups and MFA
Learners can explain encryption at rest/in transit and key management
Learners can estimate and control cloud costs and apply well-architected pillars

story.title: 'But it's in the cloud, so it's secure'

scenes.text: A company assumed the provider would protect everything — then an employee's weak password let someone into their console.
The provider secures the cloud; the customer secures what they put in it.

steps.title: Security OF the cloud vs IN the cloud
steps.body:
- **Provider**: physical data centres, hardware, host infrastructure, the virtualisation layer, and managed-service internals.
- **Customer** (always): data, identities and access, account configuration, client devices.
- Varies by model: IaaS → customer also owns guest OS, network rules, apps; PaaS → customer owns app code and configuration; SaaS → customer mainly owns users, data and settings.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Unpatched guest OS on a VM → **customer**. A failed disk in the provider's data centre → **provider**. A user given admin rights by mistake → **customer**.

**Example 2.** A publicly readable storage bucket is a customer configuration issue, even though the provider built the storage service.

steps.title: Memory hook
steps.body: The more managed the service, the more the provider handles — but **data and identity are always yours**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming SaaS removes all security duties.
- Ignoring account-level settings such as MFA and logging.
- Treating provider certifications as automatically covering your application.

activity.prompt: Who is responsible (for an IaaS VM workload)?

items.text: Physical security of the data centre

quiz.why: Under the shared responsibility model, the customer is always responsible for their own data and for identity and access, whatever the service model.

quiz.q: Guest OS patching on IaaS is done by…
quiz.why: In IaaS the customer controls the guest operating system, so the customer applies its patches.

quiz.q: In SaaS, the customer still manages…
quiz.why: Even in SaaS the provider runs the app, but the customer still manages users, permissions and their data.

quiz.q: A public bucket leak is mainly a…
quiz.why: Public bucket leaks are usually caused by customer misconfiguration, such as making the bucket public, not by provider failure.
Provider certifications cover only the provider's part of the shared model. You still have to secure and configure what you run.

scenes.text: To 'save time', an intern was given full admin. A mistyped command deleted a production database.
The team switches to role-based, least-privilege access with MFA and approvals for risky actions.

steps.title: IAM building blocks
steps.body:
- **Users** (people), **groups** (collections of users), **roles** (assumable identities for people, services or apps), **policies** (JSON documents allowing/denying actions on resources).
- **Least privilege**: grant only what's needed; start with none.
- **Explicit deny** overrides allow; default is implicit deny.
- **RBAC** (role-based) and ABAC (attribute/tag-based) models.
- Workloads should use roles/managed identities, not long-lived access keys.

steps.title: Strong authentication and governance
steps.body:
- **MFA** for all humans, especially administrators; protect the root/global admin account and use it rarely.
- Single sign-on with an identity provider; remove access when people leave.
- Just-in-time elevation for admin tasks; regular access reviews.
- Audit logs (CloudTrail, Azure Activity Log, Cloud Audit Logs) record who did what.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Policy evaluation.** A user is in a group allowing 'storage:read' on all buckets, and another policy explicitly denies 'storage:read' on the 'payroll' bucket → reading payroll is **denied** (explicit deny wins).

**Example 2. Design.** A web app needs to read one bucket → create a role allowing read on that bucket only and attach it to the app's compute identity — no keys in code.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Sharing one admin login among a team.
- Long-lived access keys in code or repos.
- Wildcard permissions ('*' on '*').
- Not revoking access for leavers.

a.text: A new analyst needs to read reports from one storage bucket. What do you grant?

choices.label: Full administrator, so they never get blocked
Add them to an 'analysts' group with read-only access to that bucket, MFA required

bad.text: Weeks later, a phishing email steals the analyst's password — the attacker gets admin to everything.

good.text: Even if a password is stolen, MFA and narrow permissions limit the damage.

quiz.q: If one policy allows and another explicitly denies an action…
quiz.why: In cloud IAM, an explicit deny overrides any allow, so the action is blocked.

quiz.q: Apps running in the cloud should authenticate with…
quiz.why: Cloud applications should use roles or managed identities, which give short-lived credentials, not hard-coded keys.
Multi-factor authentication adds a second factor, so a stolen password alone isn't enough to log in.

options: Only the permissions needed for the task
quiz.why: Least privilege means giving only the permissions needed for the task, which limits the damage if an account is compromised.

quiz.q: Who did what in the account is recorded by…
quiz.why: Audit logs (like CloudTrail or activity logs) record who did what in an account and when.

scenes.text: A backup copy of a database is accidentally exposed.
Because it was encrypted with a key held in a key-management service, the data remains unreadable.

steps.title: Encryption everywhere
steps.body:
- **In transit**: TLS (HTTPS) between clients and services and between services.
- **At rest**: disks, buckets and databases encrypted (often AES-256), usually on by default.
- **Key management services** (KMS / Key Vault / Cloud KMS) store and control keys; options: provider-managed keys, customer-managed keys, or bring/hold your own keys.
- **Envelope encryption**: data encrypted with a data key, which is encrypted by a master key in KMS.

steps.title: Governance and compliance
steps.body:
- Policies/guardrails enforce rules (e.g. 'no public buckets', 'only India regions').
- Tagging for ownership and cost.
- Compliance frameworks such as ISO/IEC 27001 and SOC 2 reports describe provider controls; customers map them to their own obligations (e.g. India's DPDP Act 2023; CERT-In directions require reporting of specified cyber incidents within 6 hours).
- Secrets managers store passwords and API keys with rotation.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** A regulator requires the company to control key rotation and be able to revoke access → choose **customer-managed keys** in KMS with rotation enabled.

**Example 2.** Database password in app config file → move to a secrets manager, grant the app's role read access to that secret, rotate it every 90 days.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Deleting a KMS key that still protects data (data becomes unrecoverable).
- Plain HTTP between internal services.
- Secrets in environment files committed to Git.
- Treating encryption as a substitute for access control.

statements.s: TLS protects data in transit.
Encryption at rest means you no longer need access controls.
Envelope encryption uses a data key protected by a master key.
Deleting a key has no effect on encrypted data.
Secrets managers can rotate credentials automatically.

quiz.why: HTTPS uses TLS to encrypt data in transit, as it travels over the network. Encryption at rest protects stored data.

quiz.q: A service to create and control encryption keys?
quiz.why: Services like KMS or Key Vault create, store and control access to encryption keys.
Guardrail (policy) controls can enforce rules such as allowed regions or no public buckets across all accounts.

options: More control over rotation and revocation
quiz.why: Customer-managed keys give you control over how keys are rotated, who can use them and when they're revoked.

quiz.q: Where should an app's DB password be stored?
quiz.why: Database passwords belong in a secrets manager, which controls access and can rotate them. Source code, labels and wikis are not safe.

scenes.text: A student club left a large GPU instance running over the vacation and got a huge bill.
Budgets, alerts, auto-shutdown and tagging would have caught it on day one.

steps.title: Cost drivers and FinOps
steps.body:
- Main drivers: compute hours, storage GB-months, data transfer out (egress), requests, managed-service units.
- **FinOps**: shared responsibility for cloud spend — visibility (tags, cost reports), optimisation, governance.
- Tools: pricing calculators, budgets and alerts, cost anomaly detection.
- Optimise: right-size, auto-scale, schedule non-production shutdowns, reserved/savings plans, spot, storage tiers, delete unused resources (idle IPs, orphaned disks, old snapshots).

steps.title: Well-architected pillars
steps.body:
Major providers publish frameworks with similar pillars:

- **Operational excellence** — automate, observe, improve.
- **Security** — identity, protection, detection, response.
- **Reliability** — recover from failure, multi-AZ, backups, tested restores.
- **Performance efficiency** — right resources, caching, scaling.
- **Cost optimisation** — pay only for value.
- **Sustainability** — reduce environmental impact (in some frameworks).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Scheduling dev VMs.** 10 dev VMs at ₹15/h running 24×7 = ₹15 × 10 × 730 = ₹1,09,500/month. Running only 10 h × 22 working days = 220 h → ₹33,000 — saves **₹76,500** (~70%).

**Example 2. Egress.** Serving 5 TB/month of downloads directly vs via a CDN with 90% hit ratio — origin egress drops to 0.5 TB (CDN has its own, often lower, rates).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- No budgets or alerts.
- Ignoring data-transfer costs in architecture.
- Over-provisioning 'just in case'.
- Untagged resources nobody owns.

activity.prompt: Compute the monthly saving from scheduling 10 dev VMs at ₹15/hour to run 220 hours instead of 730. Print the saving as an integer.
activity.starter:
vms, rate = 10, 15
always_on = 730
scheduled = 220
# saving = ...
print(saving)
activity.solution:
vms, rate = 10, 15
always_on = 730
scheduled = 220
saving = vms * rate * (always_on - scheduled)
print(saving)
activity.hint: vms × rate × hours saved.

quiz.q: Which is often a hidden cloud cost?
quiz.why: Data transfer out of the cloud (egress) is charged and often surprises people. Inbound transfer is usually free.

quiz.q: First tool to avoid bill surprises?
quiz.why: Budgets and alerts warn you early when spending goes above plan, which is the first defence against bill surprises.
Reliability is one of the well-architected pillars, with others such as security, cost optimisation, performance and operational excellence.
Tags on resources show who owns them and let costs be allocated to teams or projects.

questions.q: In every service model, the customer is responsible for…
questions.why: In every service model, the customer is responsible for their own data and for managing who can access it. The provider handles things like cooling and physical security.

questions.q: Who patches the OS of a managed PaaS web app platform?
questions.why: In a managed PaaS the provider runs and patches the platform, including its OS.

questions.q: Best authentication for administrators?
questions.why: Administrators have powerful access, so use multi-factor authentication (ideally phishing-resistant). Shared accounts and passwords alone are weak.

questions.q: Policy A allows s3:* on all; Policy B denies delete on 'logs' bucket. Can the user delete from 'logs'?
questions.why: An explicit deny overrides any allow, so the broad allow in policy A doesn't help. The user can't delete from the 'logs' bucket.

questions.q: Assertion: Encrypting data at rest removes the need for IAM. Reason: Authorised identities can decrypt data transparently.
questions.why: The assertion is false: encryption doesn't replace IAM, because access control is still needed. The reason is true, since authorised identities can decrypt transparently, which is why access control still matters.

questions.q: Envelope encryption: the data key is protected by…
questions.why: In envelope encryption, a data key encrypts the data and a master key in KMS encrypts (protects) the data key.

questions.q: Under CERT-In's 2022 directions, specified cyber incidents must be reported within…
questions.why: CERT-In's 2022 directions require specified cyber incidents to be reported within 6 hours of noticing them.

questions.q: Case: an app needs to read one queue. Best credential approach?
options: Role/managed identity with permission on that queue only
questions.why: Give the app a role or managed identity with permission on just that one queue. That follows least privilege, and no keys sit in code.

questions.q: 8 VMs × ₹25/h: always-on (730 h) vs 200 h. Saving?
questions.why: The always-on cost is 730 h and the scheduled cost is 200 h, so the saving is 530 h × ₹25 × 8 VMs = 530 × 200 = ₹1,06,000.

questions.q: Which reduces costs for a steady 24×7 database for 3 years?
questions.why: For a steady 24×7 workload over 3 years, committing with reserved capacity or a savings plan gives a big discount. Spot isn't suitable for a database.

questions.q: Orphaned disks and old snapshots are…
options: A common source of wasted spend
questions.why: Unattached disks and old snapshots keep costing money but are no longer used, so they are a common source of wasted spend.

questions.q: Which pillar covers tested restores and multi-AZ design?
questions.why: The reliability pillar covers recovery, tested restores and designs like multi-AZ.

questions.q: Case: a key in KMS is scheduled for deletion but still encrypts production data. Risk?
questions.why: If a key is deleted while it still encrypts data, that data can no longer be decrypted, so it becomes permanently unreadable. Cancel the deletion before it takes effect.

questions.q: Case: an ex-employee's account still works 3 months after leaving. Which control failed?
questions.why: An old employee's account still working means the identity lifecycle (deprovisioning) and access reviews failed. DNS, CDN and scaling aren't involved.

questions.q: Which is the customer's job in SaaS email?
options: Configure MFA and sharing settings for users
questions.why: In SaaS email the customer still configures MFA and sharing settings for users. The provider patches the servers and runs the data centres.

questions.q: Case: monthly bill doubled; reports show egress from a bucket serving large files directly. Most effective fix?
options: Put a CDN in front and enable caching; review public access
questions.why: Large files served directly from the bucket create high egress charges. A CDN with caching serves repeat requests from the edge, so less data leaves the origin, and public access should be reviewed.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Cloud Computing
courses.summary: Cheat sheets for every unit, an architecture design exercise and a mixed mock paper. Independent practice material; not affiliated with or endorsed by the exam provider. Check the official exam guide for the current skills outline.
outcomes: Learners can recall definitions, models and formulas
Learners can design a secure, resilient three-tier architecture
Learners can solve mixed cloud numericals

scenes.text: You have ten minutes. Read this once, slowly.
Each line is something examiners love to ask.

steps.title: Concepts and models
steps.body:
- NIST 5: self-service, broad access, pooling, elasticity, measured.
- IaaS (you: OS up), PaaS (you: code/data), SaaS (you: users/data), FaaS (functions on events).
- Public, private, hybrid, community, multi-cloud.
- Region → AZs → data centres; edge for CDN.
- Parallel availability 1 − Π(1 − aᵢ); series Π aᵢ; 99.9% ≈ 8.76 h/yr.

steps.title: Platforms and services
steps.body:
- Type 1 vs type 2 hypervisors; containers share kernel (namespaces, cgroups).
- K8s: pod, deployment, service, ingress, HPA ⌈n × m/t⌉.
- Storage: block (VM disks), file (shared), object (buckets).
- CIDR /n → 2^(32−n) addresses.
- SG stateful; NACL stateless; NAT for outbound only.
- RPO = data loss; RTO = recovery time.

steps.title: Ops, security, cost
steps.body:
- Queues, DLQ, idempotent handlers; GB-s = requests × seconds × GB.
- CI/CD; rolling, blue–green, canary.
- IaC: plan before apply; drift.
- Error budget = 1 − SLO.
- Shared responsibility; least privilege; explicit deny; MFA; KMS; secrets manager.
- Budgets, tags, right-size, reserved, spot, schedules; egress costs.

quiz.why: A /27 leaves 32 − 27 = 5 host bits, so 2⁵ = 32 addresses.
Components in series multiply availability: 0.995 × 0.995 ≈ 0.990, so about 99.0%.
desired = ceil(2 × 120/60) = ceil(4) = 4 pods.

lessons.title: Design exercise: a resilient three-tier app

scenes.text: Design an admissions portal that must handle 50,000 applicants on the last day and protect their documents.
Walk through each layer and justify every choice.

steps.title: Reference design
steps.body:
- DNS → CDN (static assets) → Layer-7 load balancer with WAF and TLS.
- App tier: containers or VMs in **private subnets across 2–3 AZs** with auto-scaling.
- Database: managed relational DB, multi-AZ, encrypted, private subnet, automated backups with point-in-time restore.
- Documents: object storage, private, encrypted, accessed via short-lived signed URLs; lifecycle rules after admissions close.
- Queue for email/SMS notifications; functions for document processing.
- IAM roles, MFA for admins, audit logs, budgets, monitoring with SLOs.

steps.title: How to answer design questions
steps.body: State requirements → draw layers → choose services → explain availability, security, scalability and cost for each → mention trade-offs.

steps.title: Red flags examiners look for
steps.body:
- Single AZ.
- Public database.
- Secrets in code.
- No backups or untested restores.
- No cost controls.

activity.prompt: My design includes…
items: Private subnets for app and database
TLS everywhere and encryption at rest

options: Private encrypted object storage with signed URLs
quiz.why: Applicant documents are sensitive, so keep them in private, encrypted object storage and give access through time-limited signed URLs. Public buckets and email aren't safe.
A queue decouples the sender from the processing and absorbs bursts of load, so notifications aren't lost when traffic spikes.

quiz.q: WAF at the load balancer helps by…
quiz.why: A web application firewall (WAF) filters common malicious web requests, such as SQL injection, at layer 7.

scenes.text: Attempt the exam below in 25 minutes.
Revise the units where you lost marks.

steps.title: Numerical types to expect
steps.body:
- Availability (series/parallel, downtime per year/month).
- CIDR sizes and subnet counts.
- HPA replica counts.
- Serverless GB-seconds.
- Cost savings and error budgets.

steps.title: Elimination
steps.body: In scenario MCQs, eliminate options that violate least privilege, put data in public places, or create single points of failure.

steps.title: Traps
steps.body:
- Hybrid vs multi-cloud.
- SG stateful vs NACL stateless.
- Durability vs availability.
- Containers ≠ VMs.

statements.s: Multi-cloud means private + public cloud.
A /16 has 65,536 addresses.
Spot instances can be reclaimed by the provider.
The provider patches your IaaS guest OS.
Explicit deny overrides allow.

quiz.why: Durability is the likelihood that stored data isn't lost over time. It's different from availability, which is about being able to access it right now.
For a steady workload over 3 years, reserved capacity gives a discount in return for the commitment.

quiz.q: Which tier stores data cheapest but slowest to retrieve?
quiz.why: The archive tier has the lowest storage cost but the slowest and most expensive retrieval.

questions.q: Which is SaaS?
questions.why: An online office suite is a complete application delivered over the web, so it's SaaS. A VM is IaaS, and object storage and managed Kubernetes are infrastructure or platform services.

questions.q: A region contains…
questions.why: A region is a geographic area that contains multiple availability zones.

questions.q: Containers isolate processes using…
questions.why: Containers use Linux namespaces to isolate processes, with cgroups limiting resources.

questions.q: /21 has how many addresses?
questions.why: A /21 has 32 − 21 = 11 host bits, so 2¹¹ = 2,048 addresses.

questions.q: Three 99% components in series ≈
questions.why: Three components in series: 0.99³ = 0.9703, about 97.03%. More parts in series lower the availability.

questions.q: Two 99.9% replicas in parallel ≈
questions.why: Two replicas in parallel fail only if both fail: 0.001² = 10⁻⁶. So availability is 1 − 10⁻⁶ = 99.9999%.

questions.q: HPA: 8 pods at 45%, target 60% →
questions.why: desired = ceil(8 × 45/60) = ceil(6) = 6 pods, so the HPA scales down.

questions.q: Assertion: Security groups are stateful. Reason: Return traffic for allowed inbound connections is automatically allowed.
questions.why: Security groups are stateful, which means that return traffic for an allowed inbound connection is allowed automatically. The reason is the definition of stateful.

questions.q: GB-s for 500,000 requests × 0.4 s × 2 GB?
SLO 99.9%, 30-day month — allowed downtime ≈
questions.why: A 99.9% SLO allows 0.1% downtime: 0.001 × 43,200 minutes in 30 days = 43.2 minutes.

questions.q: Case: a team keeps SSH open to the world on all VMs. Better approach?
options: Managed session access / bastion with MFA and restricted IPs
questions.why: Leaving SSH open to the world widens the attack surface. Use managed session access or a bastion host with MFA and restricted IPs. Changing the port only hides it.

questions.q: Case: a function sometimes processes the same order twice. Root cause and fix?
questions.why: Queues and events are usually delivered at least once, so the same order can arrive twice. Fix it by making the handler idempotent.

questions.q: Which is customer responsibility in PaaS?
questions.why: In PaaS the customer is responsible for their application code and its configuration. The provider handles the OS, hypervisor and hardware.

questions.q: Usable addresses in a /24 if 5 are reserved?
questions.why: A /24 has 256 addresses, and 5 reserved by the cloud leaves 256 − 5 = 251 usable.

questions.q: Case: staging differs from production because of manual console changes. Best remedy?
options: Infrastructure as code with drift detection
questions.why: Manual console changes cause drift. Infrastructure as code with drift detection keeps staging and production consistent and reproducible.

questions.q: Case: 12 dev VMs at ₹10/h run 730 h; scheduling to 250 h saves?
questions.why: Each VM saves 730 − 250 = 480 hours. The saving is 12 × ₹10 × 480 = ₹57,600.

questions.q: Case: a design has app servers in 3 AZs but one database instance in a single AZ without standby. Weakness?
options: Database is a single point of failure
questions.why: A single database instance with no standby is a single point of failure. If it or its AZ fails, the whole app goes down, so use a multi-AZ database.

questions.q: Which statement about CDNs and caching personalised pages is correct?
options: Personalised responses must not be cached publicly; use correct cache-control
questions.why: Personalised pages must not be cached publicly, or one user's data could be served to another. Use proper cache-control headers.

uni-cse-cn.title: Computer Networks (B.Tech CSE)
uni-cse-cn.description: From bits on a wire to HTTPS: physical and data-link layers, MAC and LANs, IP and subnetting, routing, TCP/UDP, application protocols and security — with GATE-style numericals and runnable code.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Introduction, Reference Models & Physical Layer
courses.summary: Network types and topologies, OSI and TCP/IP layering, switching, the four delays, bandwidth–delay product, Nyquist and Shannon limits, and line coding.
outcomes: Learners can name each OSI/TCP-IP layer with its PDU and devices
Learners can compute transmission, propagation and end-to-end delays
Learners can apply Nyquist and Shannon formulas
Learners can compare circuit and packet switching

scenes.text: Aman sends a WhatsApp photo from Lucknow to his sister in Toronto.
The photo is wrapped layer by layer — app data, segment, packet, frame, bits — and unwrapped at the other end.

steps.title: Types and topologies
steps.body: By scale: **PAN**, **LAN** (building/campus), **MAN** (city), **WAN** (country/world). Topologies: bus (one cable, cheap, single point of failure), star (central switch; most common LAN), ring, mesh (full mesh needs n(n − 1)/2 links), tree, hybrid.

steps.title: OSI and TCP/IP
steps.body:
OSI (7): **Physical** (bits) · **Data link** (frames; MAC, switches) · **Network** (packets; IP, routers) · **Transport** (segments; TCP/UDP, end-to-end) · **Session** · **Presentation** (encoding, encryption) · **Application**.
TCP/IP (commonly 4 or 5 layers): Application · Transport · Internet · Link (· Physical). Session and presentation functions live inside applications.
Each layer adds a header (**encapsulation**); peers communicate logically at the same layer.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Links in a full mesh
steps.body: 8 routers, full mesh: 8 × 7 / 2 = **28 links**; each router needs **7 ports**. Star with 8 nodes: 8 links.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Overhead of headers
steps.body: Application message 1000 B; TCP header 20 B, IP header 20 B, Ethernet header + trailer 18 B. Frame = 1058 B. Efficiency = 1000/1058 ≈ **94.5%**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing routers at layer 2 or switches at layer 3 (ordinary switches are layer 2; layer-3 switches also route).
- Saying TCP/IP has a separate session layer.
- Confusing logical peer communication with physical data flow (data always goes down and up the stack).

activity.prompt: Match the layer to its PDU or device

quiz.q: Full mesh of 10 nodes needs how many links?
quiz.why: A full mesh joins every pair of nodes, so the links number n(n−1)/2 = 10 × 9/2 = 45.
Routing packets between networks is the job of the network layer (layer 3).

quiz.q: End-to-end reliability is the job of the
quiz.why: Reliable end-to-end delivery between processes is provided by the transport layer, for example by TCP.
In the OSI model, encoding, encryption and compression belong to the presentation layer.
Today's LANs are mostly star networks, with every device connected to a central switch.

scenes.text: Loading a truck's cargo onto the road takes time (transmission); driving to the city takes time (propagation).
Waiting at the toll plaza is queuing; checking documents is processing.

steps.title: Four delays
steps.body:
- **Transmission** Tt = L / R (packet length / link rate).
- **Propagation** Tp = d / s (distance / signal speed, ≈ 2 × 10⁸ m/s in copper/fibre).
- **Queuing** (variable; traffic intensity La/R → near 1 means huge delays).
- **Processing** (header checks, lookup).
Store-and-forward over N links (N − 1 routers), one packet: N·Tt + ΣTp (ignoring queuing). P packets pipelined over N equal links: (N + P − 1)·Tt + ΣTp.
**Bandwidth–delay product** R × Tp = bits 'in flight' on the link.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · One link
steps.body:
L = 1000 bytes = 8000 bits, R = 1 Mbps, d = 2000 km, s = 2 × 10⁸ m/s.
- Tt = 8000 / 10⁶ = **8 ms**.
- Tp = 2 × 10⁶ / 2 × 10⁸ = **10 ms**.
- Total ≈ **18 ms** (one packet, no queuing).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Store-and-forward pipeline
steps.body: 10 packets of 1500 B over 3 links of 10 Mbps (ignore propagation). Tt = 12000 / 10⁷ = 1.2 ms. Time = (3 + 10 − 1) × 1.2 = **14.4 ms**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 · Bits in flight
steps.body: R = 100 Mbps, Tp = 20 ms → R × Tp = 2 × 10⁶ bits = **250 KB** on the wire at once.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting to convert bytes to bits.
- Using Mbps = 2²⁰ bps (data rates use powers of 10: 1 Mbps = 10⁶ bps).
- Assuming transmission delay depends on distance (it does not).

activity.prompt: A 2500-byte packet goes over a 10 Mbps link of length 4000 km (signal speed 2 × 10⁸ m/s). Transmission + propagation delay in ms?

quiz.why: Transmission delay is the time to push all the packet's bits onto the link: packet length ÷ link rate (L/R).
Propagation delay is the time for a signal to travel along the link: distance ÷ signal speed.
Link rates use decimal prefixes, so 1 Mbps = 10⁶ bits per second. 2²⁰ is used for memory sizes.
When traffic intensity nears 1, packets arrive almost as fast as the link can send them, so queues grow very long and queuing delay becomes very large.

options: bits in flight on the link
quiz.why: The bandwidth–delay product (rate × propagation delay) is the number of bits that can be in flight on the link at once.

story.title: How fast can a phone line go?

scenes.text: An old phone line passes about 3 kHz of bandwidth.
Nyquist and Shannon tell us the ceilings for noiseless and noisy channels.

steps.title: Capacity limits
steps.body:
- **Nyquist (noiseless):** max bit rate = 2B log₂ L (B = bandwidth in Hz, L = signal levels).
- **Shannon (noisy):** C = B log₂(1 + SNR), with SNR as a ratio; SNR_dB = 10 log₁₀ SNR.
Shannon gives the absolute limit; Nyquist tells how many levels are needed to approach it.

steps.title: Line coding and media
steps.body:
- **NRZ-L / NRZ-I:** simple; long runs lose synchronisation.
- **Manchester:** transition in the middle of every bit (self-clocking; needs 2× bandwidth) — classic 10 Mbps Ethernet. **Differential Manchester.**
- **4B/5B, 8B/10B** block codes ensure transitions.
Media: twisted pair (Cat5e/6), coaxial, optical fibre (single/multi-mode; immune to EMI), wireless (radio, microwave, infrared).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Nyquist
steps.body: B = 3000 Hz, 4 levels: 2 × 3000 × log₂ 4 = **12 kbps**. To reach 24 kbps on the same line noiselessly: 2 × 3000 × log₂ L = 24000 → log₂ L = 4 → **16 levels**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Plugging dB directly into Shannon's formula (convert first).
- Thinking more levels beat Shannon's limit — noise caps it.
- Forgetting Manchester's doubled baud rate.

activity.prompt: Bandwidth 1 MHz, SNR = 63 (ratio). Shannon capacity in Mbps?

quiz.q: SNR of 20 dB is a ratio of
quiz.why: dB = 10 log₁₀(ratio), so 20 dB means a ratio of 10^(20/10) = 10² = 100.

quiz.q: Nyquist rate with B = 4 kHz and 2 levels
quiz.why: Nyquist rate = 2B log₂L = 2 × 4000 × 1 = 8000 bps = 8 kbps for 2 levels.
Manchester encoding puts a transition in the middle of every bit, so the receiver can recover the clock from the signal. It is self-clocking.

quiz.q: Which medium is immune to electromagnetic interference?
quiz.why: Optical fibre carries light, not electric current, so it isn't affected by electromagnetic interference.
Shannon's formula C = B log₂(1 + SNR) gives the maximum error-free capacity of a noisy channel.

scenes.text: A classic phone call reserves a path end to end for the whole call.
The Internet sends postcards (packets) that share links and may take different roads.

steps.title: Comparison
steps.body:
- **Circuit switching:** setup phase, dedicated resources (FDM/TDM slots), constant rate, no queuing after setup; wasteful for bursty data.
- **Packet switching:** store-and-forward, statistical multiplexing, efficient for bursty traffic; variable delay, possible loss. **Datagram** (each packet routed independently — IP) vs **virtual circuit** (path set up, labels — e.g. MPLS, older ATM/Frame Relay).
- **Message switching:** whole message stored and forwarded (historic).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · How many users?
steps.body:
1 Mbps link; each user needs 100 kbps when active and is active 10% of the time.
- Circuit switching: **10 users**.
- Packet switching with 35 users: P(more than 10 active at once) is about 0.0004 — so about **35 users** share the link with rare congestion.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Setup cost
steps.body: File of 640,000 bits over a circuit with 24 TDM slots on 1.536 Mbps → each slot 64 kbps; setup 500 ms. Time = 0.5 + 640,000 / 64,000 = **10.5 s**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the Internet is circuit-switched.
- Ignoring setup time in circuit-switched calculations.
- Thinking virtual circuits reserve bandwidth by definition (they may or may not).

statements.s: IP is a datagram (connectionless) network.
Circuit switching suits bursty data well.
Packet switching can have variable delay.
TDM gives each circuit periodic time slots.
Virtual circuits need no setup phase.
statements.why: They set up a path first.

quiz.q: Statistical multiplexing is a feature of
quiz.why: Packet switching shares link capacity on demand, which is statistical multiplexing. Circuit switching reserves fixed capacity.
In a datagram network each packet is routed independently, so packets of one flow may take different paths and arrive out of order.
Circuit switching reserves a path, so after setup, you get a constant rate. The price is wasted capacity when the circuit is idle.
MPLS sets up label-switched paths, like virtual circuits, where packets follow a pre-set route using labels.

quiz.q: In the example, circuit switching supports how many users?
quiz.why: Circuit switching reserves 100 kbps per user on a 1 Mbps link, so it can support 1 Mbps ÷ 100 kbps = 10 users.

questions.q: The layer responsible for routing is
questions.why: Routing is the job of the network layer, layer 3.

questions.q: Switches work at
questions.why: Switches work at the data link layer, layer 2, forwarding frames by MAC address.

questions.q: Transmission delay formula
questions.why: Transmission delay = packet length L ÷ rate R. Propagation delay is d/s.

questions.q: Full mesh of 6 nodes: links
questions.why: Links in a full mesh = n(n−1)/2 = 6 × 5/2 = 15.

questions.q: SNR 30 dB ratio
Manchester encoding used in
questions.why: Manchester encoding was used in classic 10 Mbps Ethernet, since it carries its own clock.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Transmission delay does not depend on distance. Reason (R): It is the time to push all bits onto the link. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: transmission delay is the time to push the bits onto the link, so it doesn't depend on distance. R states exactly that, so it explains A.

questions.q: 1500 B packet, 100 Mbps link: Tt
Nyquist: B = 8 kHz, 8 levels
questions.why: Nyquist rate = 2B log₂L = 2 × 8000 × log₂8 = 2 × 8000 × 3 = 48,000 bps = 48 kbps.

questions.q: Case: a satellite link has Tp = 270 ms and R = 10 Mbps. Bits in flight
questions.why: Bits in flight = rate × propagation delay = 10 × 10⁶ × 0.27 = 2.7 × 10⁶ bits = 2.7 Mb.

questions.q: 5 packets of 1000 B over 4 links of 8 Mbps, propagation ignored: total time
questions.why: 1000 B = 8000 bits, so Tt = 8000/8×10⁶ = 1 ms. With store-and-forward over 4 links, the time is (4 + 5 − 1) × 1 ms = 8 ms.

questions.q: Shannon: B = 2 MHz, SNR 15 → C
questions.why: C = B log₂(1 + SNR) = 2 MHz × log₂16 = 2 × 4 = 8 Mbps.

questions.q: Levels needed for 36 kbps over B = 3 kHz (noiseless)
questions.why: 2B log₂L = 36,000 gives log₂L = 36,000/6,000 = 6, so L = 2⁶ = 64 levels.

questions.q: Which statement is TRUE?
options: Shannon limit can be exceeded with more levels
Noise sets an upper bound on capacity
questions.why: Shannon's formula shows that noise sets an upper limit on capacity, which more signal levels can't exceed. Hubs don't route and propagation delay doesn't depend on packet size.

questions.q: A 1 Gbps link 3000 km long (s = 2 × 10⁸ m/s): how many 1500-byte packets fit 'in flight' one way?
questions.why: Tp = 3×10⁶ m / 2×10⁸ = 15 ms. Bits in flight = 10⁹ × 0.015 = 1.5×10⁷, and each packet is 12,000 bits, so 1.5×10⁷/12,000 = 1250 packets.

questions.q: 1000 packets of 1000 bytes each go over 2 store-and-forward links of 8 Mbps (ignore propagation and headers). Total time?
questions.why: Each packet's Tt = 8000/(8×10⁶) = 1 ms. With 2 store-and-forward links, the total is (2 + 1000 − 1) × 1 ms = 1001 ms = 1.001 s.

courses.note: topic order may differ by university syllabus

courses.title: Unit 2 · Data Link Layer — Framing, Errors & Flow Control
courses.summary: Framing with byte and bit stuffing, error detection (parity, checksum, CRC), Hamming codes, and reliable delivery with stop-and-wait, Go-Back-N and Selective Repeat including efficiency and sequence-number limits.
outcomes: Learners can perform bit stuffing and CRC division
Learners can build and correct a Hamming(7,4) codeword
Learners can compute stop-and-wait and sliding-window efficiency
Learners can find minimum sequence-number bits for GBN and SR

scenes.text: Bits arrive as an endless stream. The receiver must find where each frame starts and stops.
A special flag marks the edges — but what if the data contains the flag?

steps.title: Framing methods
steps.body:
- **Character count:** header gives length (one error desynchronises everything).
- **Byte stuffing:** flag byte (e.g. 0x7E) marks boundaries; an ESC byte is inserted before any flag/ESC inside data (PPP).
- **Bit stuffing (HDLC):** flag 01111110; the sender inserts a 0 after every five consecutive 1s in data; the receiver removes it.
- Physical-layer coding violations.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Bit stuffing
steps.body:
Data: 0111111111100 (a 0, then ten 1s, then 00). Insert a 0 after every run of five 1s:
- 0 | 11111 | **0** | 11111 | **0** | 00
- Stuffed: **011111011111000** (13 bits → 15 bits).
The receiver deletes any 0 that follows five consecutive 1s.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Byte stuffing
steps.body: Data bytes: A FLAG B ESC C. Stuffed: A **ESC** FLAG B **ESC** ESC C. The receiver drops each ESC and keeps the next byte literally.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Stuffing after six 1s instead of five.
- Forgetting to stuff a 0 even if the next data bit is already 0 (always stuff after five 1s).
- Not escaping the ESC byte itself.

activity.prompt: Bit-stuff the data 11111111 (eight 1s) using HDLC rules.

quiz.why: The HDLC frame flag is 01111110, six 1s with a 0 at each end.
To keep data from looking like the flag, bit stuffing inserts a 0 after every five consecutive 1s.
Byte stuffing inserts an escape (ESC) byte before any flag byte or ESC byte that appears in the data.

options: a corrupted count desynchronises later frames
quiz.why: If the count field is corrupted, the receiver can't find where the frame ends, so all later frames get out of step and there's no way to resynchronise.
PPP is byte-oriented, so it uses byte stuffing, with a flag byte 0x7E and an escape byte.

scenes.text: A lightning strike flips a few bits on a long cable.
The receiver recomputes a check value; a mismatch means 'ask again'.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
- **Single parity bit:** detects any odd number of bit errors.
- **2-D parity:** detects all 1-, 2- and 3-bit errors and can correct single-bit errors.
- **Internet checksum:** 16-bit one's-complement sum of words, then complemented (IP header, TCP, UDP).
- **CRC:** treat data as a polynomial; append r zeros (r = degree of generator G); divide by G using XOR (mod-2); the remainder is the CRC. Detects all single-bit errors, all double-bit errors (for suitable G), all odd-count errors if (x + 1) is a factor, and all **bursts of length ≤ r**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Checksum
steps.body: Two 16-bit words 0x4500 and 0x0073 (simplified to two words). Sum = 0x4573 (no carry). One's complement = **0xBA8C**. Receiver adds all words + checksum = 0xFFFF → complement 0 → OK.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Appending r + 1 zeros (append degree r, i.e. generator length − 1).
- Doing ordinary subtraction instead of XOR.
- Thinking parity detects all 2-bit errors (it misses them).

activity.prompt: CRC remainder: line 1 = data bits, line 2 = generator bits. Print the remainder (length = generator length − 1).
activity.starter:
data = input().strip()
g = input().strip()
n = len(g) - 1
bits = list(data + '0' * n)
# XOR-divide: whenever the leading bit is 1, XOR the generator in
activity.hint: XOR of two bit characters: equal → '0', different → '1'.

quiz.why: A parity bit detects odd numbers of bit errors. With an even number of flips the parity looks right again, so they go unnoticed.

quiz.q: CRC with generator of degree 16 detects all bursts of length up to
quiz.why: A CRC with an r-bit (degree r) generator detects all burst errors of length up to r, here 16.

quiz.q: Number of zeros appended for generator 10011
quiz.why: The generator 10011 has degree 4 (five bits), so you append 4 zeros before the division.
The Internet checksum adds 16-bit words using one's-complement addition and complements the sum.
CRC division is done with modulo-2 arithmetic, where subtraction is the same as XOR.

scenes.text: A Mars rover can't wait 20 minutes for every retransmission.
Error-correcting codes let the receiver repair a flipped bit on its own.

steps.title: Hamming distance and codes
steps.body:
**Hamming distance** = number of differing bits. A code with minimum distance d_min can **detect** d_min − 1 errors and **correct** ⌊(d_min − 1)/2⌋.
**Hamming code:** for m data bits choose the smallest r with 2^r ≥ m + r + 1. Parity bits at positions 1, 2, 4, 8…; parity bit at position 2^k covers positions whose binary index has bit k set. The **syndrome** (recomputed parities read as binary) gives the position of a single-bit error.

steps.title: Solved example 3 · Parity bits needed
steps.body: m = 7: r = 3 gives 8 ≥ 11? No. r = 4: 16 ≥ 12 ✓ → **4 parity bits** (11-bit codeword). m = 4 → r = 3 (Hamming(7,4)).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing data bits at positions 1, 2, 4.
- Reading the syndrome in the wrong bit order (c4 c2 c1).
- Claiming Hamming(7,4) corrects 2-bit errors (it corrects 1).

activity.prompt: Minimum number of Hamming parity bits for 16 data bits?

quiz.why: A code can correct t errors if d_min ≥ 2t + 1. For d_min = 5, t = ⌊(5−1)/2⌋ = 2.

quiz.q: To detect up to 3 errors, d_min must be at least
quiz.why: To detect up to d errors you need d_min ≥ d + 1, so for 3 errors d_min must be at least 4.
Compare bit by bit: 10110 and 11011 differ at positions 2, 3 and 5, so the Hamming distance is 3.

quiz.q: Parity bits in Hamming code sit at positions
quiz.why: In a Hamming code the parity bits sit at positions that are powers of two: 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on.
A syndrome of 000 means all parity checks pass, so no single-bit error is detected. Several errors could still cancel out.

scenes.text: If you wait for a reply after every letter to a far city, most of your time is spent waiting.
Send several letters before waiting — a sliding window — and the courier stays busy.

steps.title: Efficiency
steps.body:
Let a = Tp / Tt.
- **Stop-and-wait:** η = Tt / (Tt + 2Tp) = **1 / (1 + 2a)** (ignoring ACK transmission and processing).
- **Sliding window** with window W: η = min(1, **W / (1 + 2a)**). Throughput = η × R.
- Window needed for 100%: W ≥ 1 + 2a.

steps.title: GBN vs SR
steps.body:
- **Go-Back-N:** receiver window 1; cumulative ACKs; on loss/timeout resend that frame and all after it. With k-bit sequence numbers, **sender window ≤ 2^k − 1**.
- **Selective Repeat:** receiver buffers out-of-order frames; resend only the lost ones; **window ≤ 2^(k − 1)** (sender = receiver window).
- Stop-and-wait needs 1-bit sequence numbers (alternating-bit protocol).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Stop-and-wait
steps.body:
R = 1 Mbps, frame 1000 bits → Tt = 1 ms; Tp = 10 ms → a = 10.
η = 1/21 ≈ **4.76%** → throughput ≈ 47.6 kbps. For full utilisation, W ≥ 21 frames → need sequence numbers: GBN k with 2^k − 1 ≥ 21 → **k = 5**; SR 2^(k−1) ≥ 21 → **k = 6**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · GBN retransmissions
steps.body:
GBN with window 4 must send frames 0–6; frame 2 is lost once. The sender transmits 0–5 (window full: 2, 3, 4, 5 outstanding), the receiver discards 3, 4, 5, the timer for 2 expires and the sender resends 2, 3, 4, 5 and then sends 6.
- Total transmissions = 6 + 5 = **11**.
- Selective Repeat resends only frame 2 → 7 + 1 = **8**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a = Tt/Tp (it is Tp/Tt).
- Allowing SR window 2^k − 1 (causes old/new frame confusion).
- Forgetting the 2 in 2a (round trip).

activity.prompt: Tt = 2 ms, Tp = 19 ms. Sliding window of 7 frames. Efficiency in % (W/(1+2a) × 100, 1 decimal)?

quiz.why: Stop-and-wait sends one frame and waits a round trip (2Tp), so efficiency = Tt/(Tt + 2Tp) = 1/(1 + 2a), where a = Tp/Tt.

quiz.q: GBN with 3-bit sequence numbers: max sender window
quiz.why: Go-Back-N with k-bit sequence numbers can have at most 2ᵏ − 1 frames outstanding. For k = 3, that is 7.

quiz.q: SR with 3-bit sequence numbers: max window
quiz.why: Selective Repeat's window can be at most half the sequence space, 2ᵏ⁻¹ = 4 for 3 bits, so the receiver can tell new frames from retransmissions.
A Go-Back-N receiver accepts frames only in order, so its window size is 1.
Selective Repeat (SR) retransmits only the frames that were lost or damaged. Go-Back-N resends everything from the error onwards.

questions.q: HDLC uses
questions.why: HDLC is a bit-oriented protocol, so it uses bit stuffing with the 01111110 flag.

questions.q: Parity detects
questions.why: A single parity bit detects any odd number of bit errors, but even numbers go unnoticed.

questions.q: CRC division uses
questions.why: CRC division uses modulo-2 arithmetic, which is carried out with XOR.

questions.q: Hamming(7,4) has how many parity bits?
questions.why: Hamming(7,4) has 7 total bits and 4 data bits, so 7 − 4 = 3 parity bits.

questions.q: d_min needed to correct 2 errors
questions.why: To correct t errors you need d_min = 2t + 1. For t = 2 that's 5.

questions.q: GBN with 4-bit sequence numbers: max window
questions.why: Go-Back-N with k-bit sequence numbers has a maximum window of 2ᵏ − 1. For k = 4 that's 15.

questions.q: Assertion (A): SR's window must be at most half the sequence space. Reason (R): Otherwise the receiver cannot tell a retransmitted old frame from a new one. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: the window of SR must be at most half the sequence space. R is true and explains it: if the window were larger, the receiver couldn't tell a retransmitted old frame from a new frame that reuses the same number.
After the first five 1s insert 0 (01111101…), and after the second run of five insert 0 again.

questions.q: Stop-and-wait: Tt = 4 ms, Tp = 8 ms: efficiency
Case: a satellite link with a = 50 uses SR. Minimum sequence-number bits for 100% efficiency
questions.why: For 100% efficiency the window must be at least 1 + 2a = 101. SR needs a window of 2ᵏ⁻¹ ≥ 101, so 2ᵏ⁻¹ = 128 and k = 8.

questions.q: CRC of data 1101011111 with generator 10011
questions.why: Append 4 zeros and divide by the generator 10011 using XOR. The remainder, which is the CRC, comes out as 0010.

questions.q: Received Hamming word 1110011 (even parity, positions 1–7). Error position
1 Gbps link, 1000-byte frames, Tp = 50 µs. GBN window for 100% efficiency (min W)
questions.why: Tt = 8000 bits/10⁹ = 8 µs, so a = 50/8 = 6.25. Efficient window W ≥ 1 + 2a = 13.5, so the minimum is 14 frames.

questions.q: GBN window 5, frames 0–9 sent, frame 4 lost once (timeout resends from 4). Total transmissions
questions.why: With window 5, frames 0–8 are sent before frame 4's timer expires (4–8 outstanding). Then 4–9 are sent: 9 + 6 = 15.

questions.q: 2-D parity can always
questions.why: With 2-D parity, a single bit error makes exactly one row and one column parity fail, and their intersection pinpoints the bit, so it can be corrected.

questions.q: Throughput of stop-and-wait on 2 Mbps with a = 4.5
questions.why: Efficiency = 1/(1 + 2a) = 1/(1 + 9) = 0.1, so the throughput is 0.1 × 2 Mbps = 0.2 Mbps = 200 kbps.

courses.note: topic order may differ by university syllabus

courses.title: Unit 3 · MAC Sublayer, Ethernet & Wireless LANs
courses.summary: Multiple-access protocols (ALOHA, slotted ALOHA, CSMA, CSMA/CD, CSMA/CA), Ethernet frames and minimum frame size, switches and learning bridges, VLANs and spanning tree, and IEEE 802.11.
outcomes: Learners can compute ALOHA throughput
Learners can derive the minimum Ethernet frame size
Learners can explain how a learning switch fills its table
Learners can explain hidden terminals and RTS/CTS

scenes.text: In a group call with no moderator, people talk whenever they like and collide.
If they first listen before talking, collisions drop — that's carrier sensing.

steps.title: ALOHA
steps.body:
With offered load G frames per frame-time:
- **Pure ALOHA:** S = G e^(−2G); vulnerable period 2 frame-times; max **1/(2e) ≈ 18.4%** at G = 0.5.
- **Slotted ALOHA:** S = G e^(−G); vulnerable period 1 slot; max **1/e ≈ 36.8%** at G = 1.

steps.title: CSMA family
steps.body:
- **1-persistent:** sense; if idle send immediately; if busy wait and send as soon as idle (collisions likely).
- **Non-persistent:** if busy, wait a random time before sensing again.
- **p-persistent:** slotted; if idle send with probability p.
Collisions still occur due to propagation delay.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Pure ALOHA
steps.body: A 200 kbps channel, 1000-bit frames → frame time 5 ms → 200 frames/s capacity. Network offers 100 frames/s → G = 0.5 → S = 0.5 e^(−1) ≈ **0.184** → ≈ 36.8 successful frames/s.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Slotted ALOHA
steps.body: Same channel slotted, G = 1 (200 frames/s offered): S = e^(−1) ≈ 0.368 → ≈ **73.6 frames/s**. G = 2: S = 2e^(−2) ≈ 0.27.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up e^(−2G) and e^(−G).
- Forgetting to convert frames/s into G (multiply by frame time).
- Believing carrier sensing eliminates collisions.

activity.prompt: Slotted ALOHA throughput S = G·e^(−G) at G = 0.5 (3 decimals)?

quiz.why: Pure ALOHA's maximum efficiency is 1/(2e) ≈ 18.4%. Slotted ALOHA doubles it to 1/e ≈ 36.8%.
In slotted ALOHA frames start only at slot boundaries, so the vulnerable period is one slot, half of pure ALOHA's two frame times.

quiz.q: Max of slotted ALOHA occurs at G =
quiz.why: Slotted ALOHA throughput S = G·e^(−G) has its maximum where the derivative is zero, at G = 1.

quiz.q: Which CSMA waits random time when busy?
quiz.why: Non-persistent CSMA, if the channel is busy, waits a random time before sensing again instead of continuously sensing.

quiz.q: Collisions in CSMA happen because of
quiz.why: Collisions happen in CSMA because of propagation delay: a station may not yet have heard another station's transmission and so sends anyway.

scenes.text: In a long hall, two people start speaking at once and only notice when their voices meet.
To notice in time, each must keep speaking at least as long as a round trip of the hall.

steps.title: CSMA/CD
steps.body:
Transmit while listening; on collision send a jam signal and back off using **binary exponential backoff**: after the n-th collision choose K from {0, …, 2^m − 1}, m = min(n, 10), wait K × 512 bit times; give up after 16 attempts.
To detect a collision before finishing, **Tt ≥ 2 Tp** → **L_min = 2 × Tp × R**. Classic 10 Mbps Ethernet: slot time 51.2 µs → **512 bits = 64 bytes** minimum frame.

steps.title: Ethernet frame
steps.body: Preamble (7 B) + SFD (1 B) | Destination MAC (6) | Source MAC (6) | Type/Length (2) | Data **46–1500 B** | CRC (4). Header + CRC = 18 B, so the frame is 64–1518 B. MAC addresses are 48 bits; FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF is broadcast. Modern switched full-duplex Ethernet has no collisions, but the format remains.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Minimum frame
steps.body: R = 1 Gbps, cable 1 km, s = 2 × 10⁸ m/s → Tp = 5 µs. L_min = 2 × 5 × 10⁻⁶ × 10⁹ = **10,000 bits = 1250 bytes**. (Gigabit Ethernet solved this with carrier extension / mostly full-duplex.)

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Efficiency
steps.body: Approximate CSMA/CD efficiency = 1 / (1 + 6.44a), a = Tp/Tt. With a = 0.1 → 1/1.644 ≈ **61%**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using Tp instead of 2Tp for the minimum frame.
- Counting the preamble in the 64-byte minimum (it is excluded).
- Saying CSMA/CD is used in Wi-Fi (Wi-Fi uses CSMA/CA).

activity.prompt: CSMA/CD on 100 Mbps, max distance 500 m, signal speed 2 × 10⁸ m/s. Minimum frame size in bits?

quiz.why: The minimum Ethernet payload is 46 bytes. Shorter data is padded to 46.
Minimum frame = 46 bytes payload + 18 bytes of header and CRC = 64 bytes (the preamble isn't counted).

quiz.q: After the 3rd collision K is chosen from
quiz.why: With binary exponential backoff, after the nth collision K is chosen from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1. For the 3rd collision that's 0 to 7.
A MAC address is 6 bytes, which is 48 bits, written as six hex pairs such as 00:1A:2B:3C:4D:5E. 32 bits is an IPv4 address and 128 bits an IPv6 address.
For CSMA/CD the sender must still be transmitting when a collision signal returns, which takes up to a round trip, 2 × Tp. So the minimum frame is L_min = 2 × Tp × R bits.

scenes.text: A new receptionist doesn't know which desk each employee sits at. Each time someone calls out, she notes their desk.
Soon she forwards calls directly — like a learning switch.

steps.title: Learning switches
steps.body: For each incoming frame: record (source MAC → incoming port, time); look up the destination: if known and on another port → forward there; if on the same port → filter (drop); if unknown or broadcast → **flood** to all other ports. Entries age out. Each switch port is its own **collision domain**; the whole switched LAN is one **broadcast domain** (unless VLANs/routers split it). Hubs repeat bits to every port (one collision domain).

steps.title: VLANs and STP
steps.body:
**VLANs (IEEE 802.1Q)** split one switch into several broadcast domains; trunk links carry a 4-byte tag with a 12-bit VLAN ID. Traffic between VLANs needs a router/layer-3 switch.
**Spanning Tree Protocol (802.1D)** disables redundant links to prevent broadcast storms: elect the **root bridge** (lowest bridge ID), each switch picks a root port (least cost), each segment a designated port; others block.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Table filling
steps.body: Switch ports 1–3. A (port 1) → B: table {A:1}; B unknown → flood to 2, 3. B (port 2) → A: table {A:1, B:2}; A known → forward only to 1. C (port 3) → broadcast: table adds C:3; flood to 1, 2.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Counting domains
steps.body:
A router has 2 interfaces. Interface 1 connects to switch S1 with 8 PCs; interface 2 connects to a hub with 5 PCs.
- Broadcast domains = **2** (the router separates them).
- Collision domains: S1's 8 PC ports + its uplink port to the router = 9; the hub side is a single collision domain = 1 → **10** in total.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying switches split broadcast domains (only VLANs/routers do).
- Forgetting the switch learns from the **source** address.
- Thinking STP deletes links — it blocks ports and can unblock on failure.

activity.prompt: Order what a learning switch does with an incoming frame
items: Record source MAC with incoming port
Look up destination MAC in the table
If unknown or broadcast, flood to all other ports
If known on another port, forward only there

quiz.q: A switch learns from the frame's
quiz.why: A learning switch reads the source MAC address of each incoming frame and records it against the port, so it knows where that device is. It forwards using the destination MAC.
Routers operate at layer 3 and don't forward broadcasts, so each router interface is its own broadcast domain. Switches and hubs keep one broadcast domain.
The 802.1Q VLAN ID field is 12 bits, giving 4096 values, of which 4094 are usable because 0 and 4095 are reserved.

quiz.q: STP root bridge is the one with
quiz.why: In spanning tree protocol, the switch with the lowest bridge ID (priority first, then MAC address) becomes the root bridge.
A hub repeats every signal out of all its ports, so everything attached shares one collision domain.

scenes.text: Two students at opposite ends of a hall can both hear the teacher but not each other.
Both answer at once and the teacher hears noise — the hidden-terminal problem.

steps.title: Why not CSMA/CD?
steps.body: A radio cannot reliably listen while transmitting (its own signal drowns others), and **hidden terminals** mean the sender may not hear a collision at the receiver. So 802.11 uses **CSMA/CA**: sense; wait DIFS; random backoff counted down only while idle; transmit the whole frame; receiver sends ACK after SIFS. Optional **RTS/CTS** reserves the medium: other stations set their NAV (virtual carrier sense).

steps.title: 802.11 details
steps.body: Infrastructure mode (access point, BSS) vs ad hoc. Frames have up to **four address fields** (e.g. receiver, transmitter, destination/source for distribution). Exposed-terminal problem: a station needlessly defers. Generations: 802.11n (Wi-Fi 4), ac (Wi-Fi 5), ax (Wi-Fi 6/6E), be (Wi-Fi 7).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Hidden terminal
steps.body: A — AP — C; A and C cannot hear each other. A sends RTS; AP replies CTS heard by both; C sets NAV for the announced duration and stays quiet → collision avoided.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Why ACKs?
steps.body: On Ethernet the sender detects collisions; on Wi-Fi it cannot, so every unicast data frame is **acknowledged**; a missing ACK triggers a retransmission with a larger backoff window.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Wi-Fi uses collision detection.
- Confusing hidden (cannot hear the other sender) with exposed (hears an irrelevant sender).
- Thinking RTS/CTS is mandatory for every frame.

statements.s: 802.11 uses CSMA/CA rather than CSMA/CD.
statements.why: Collision detection is impractical on radio.

statements.s: RTS/CTS helps with the hidden-terminal problem.
statements.why: Everyone near the receiver hears CTS.

statements.s: Wi-Fi unicast data frames are acknowledged.
An exposed terminal cannot hear the sender.
NAV is a form of virtual carrier sensing.

quiz.why: SIFS is the shortest interframe space in Wi-Fi, shorter than DIFS, so ACKs and CTS frames get priority over new data transmissions.

quiz.q: Hidden terminals cause collisions at the
quiz.why: Hidden terminals can't hear each other but both reach the same receiver, so their signals overlap and collide at the receiver.
The network allocation vector (NAV) is set from the duration field in RTS/CTS frames, so stations that hear them wait for that time before sending.
Wi-Fi 6 is the name for the IEEE 802.11ax standard. 802.11ac is Wi-Fi 5 and 802.11n is Wi-Fi 4.

quiz.q: Max address fields in an 802.11 frame
quiz.why: An 802.11 frame can carry up to four address fields (for example in a wireless distribution system), though most frames use three.

questions.q: Slotted ALOHA max throughput
questions.why: Slotted ALOHA has a vulnerable period of one slot, which doubles pure ALOHA's efficiency to 1/e ≈ 36.8%.

questions.q: Ethernet uses
questions.why: Classic Ethernet uses CSMA/CD (collision detection). CSMA/CA is used in Wi-Fi.

questions.q: A broadcast MAC address is
questions.why: The Ethernet broadcast address has all 48 bits set to 1, written FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF, so every device on the LAN accepts the frame.

questions.q: Switch floods a frame when
questions.why: A switch floods a frame out of all ports except the one it arrived on when the destination MAC isn't in its table (or the frame is a broadcast). If the destination is known, it forwards on one port.

questions.q: Max Ethernet payload
questions.why: The standard Ethernet MTU, the maximum payload, is 1500 bytes. With header and CRC the frame is 1518 bytes.

questions.q: Pure ALOHA vulnerable time
questions.why: In pure ALOHA a frame can collide with any frame sent from one frame time before to one frame time after, so the vulnerable time is 2 frame times.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Wi-Fi uses ACKs for unicast frames. Reason (R): A wireless sender cannot detect collisions at the receiver. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: Wi-Fi uses ACKs for unicast frames. R is true and explains it: a wireless sender can't detect a collision at the receiver, so it needs the ACK to know that the frame arrived.

questions.q: Pure ALOHA S at G = 1
questions.why: Pure ALOHA throughput is S = G·e^(−2G). At G = 1, S = e^(−2) ≈ 0.135. The maximum, 0.184, occurs at G = 0.5.

questions.q: Number of broadcast domains: 3 VLANs on one switch, no router
questions.why: Each VLAN is its own broadcast domain, and without a router they can't talk to each other. Three VLANs give three broadcast domains.

questions.q: Case: a 10 Mbps Ethernet is extended to 10 km of cable. Problem?
options: collisions may go undetected for 64-byte frames
questions.why: A 10 km cable makes the round-trip delay longer than the 51.2 µs slot time that a 64-byte frame lasts. A sender may finish transmitting before the collision signal returns, so the collision goes undetected.

questions.q: CSMA/CD: 1 Gbps, 2 km, s = 2 × 10⁸ m/s. Min frame
Channel 50 kbps, frames 1000 bits, 30 stations each sending 1 frame/s, pure ALOHA. G =
questions.why: The frame time is 1000 bits/50 kbps = 20 ms. The stations send 30 frames/s, so G = 30 × 0.02 = 0.6 frames per frame time.

questions.q: For G = 0.6 above, pure ALOHA throughput S ≈
questions.why: Pure ALOHA S = G·e^(−2G) = 0.6 × e^(−1.2) = 0.6 × 0.301 ≈ 0.181. Only about 18% of the channel time carries successful frames.

questions.q: After 12 collisions, binary exponential backoff picks K from
questions.why: The backoff exponent stops growing at 10, so after 12 collisions K is chosen from 0 to 2¹⁰ − 1 = 1023.

questions.q: Which device both separates collision domains and keeps one broadcast domain?
questions.why: A layer-2 switch gives each port its own collision domain but forwards broadcasts, so the LAN stays one broadcast domain. A router splits both, and a hub splits neither.

questions.q: A station hears another sender that is not near its intended receiver and defers unnecessarily. This is
questions.why: An exposed terminal hears a transmission that wouldn't actually interfere with its own intended receiver, and wrongly defers. A hidden terminal is the opposite problem: it doesn't hear a sender that would collide at the receiver.
