courses.title: Unit 2 · Computer Arithmetic
courses.summary: Half and full adders, ripple-carry and carry-lookahead adders with delay analysis, Booth's multiplication algorithm, restoring and non-restoring division, and floating-point add/multiply steps.
outcomes: Learners can compute ripple-carry and carry-lookahead delays
Learners can multiply signed numbers with Booth's algorithm
Learners can trace restoring division
Learners can list the steps of floating-point addition

lessons.title: Adders: ripple carry and carry lookahead

scenes.text: In a ripple-carry adder, bit 31 can't finish until the carry crawls from bit 0.
Carry lookahead predicts carries in parallel.

steps.title: Building blocks
steps.body:
Half adder: S = A ⊕ B, C = AB. Full adder: S = A ⊕ B ⊕ Cin, Cout = AB + Cin(A ⊕ B).
**Ripple-carry (n bits):** carry passes through n full adders; with 2 gate delays per carry stage, carry-out after ≈ **2n** gate delays.
**Carry lookahead:** generate Gᵢ = AᵢBᵢ, propagate Pᵢ = Aᵢ ⊕ Bᵢ; Cᵢ₊₁ = Gᵢ + PᵢCᵢ, expanded so every carry is a 2-level sum of products: C₂ = G₁ + P₁G₀ + P₁P₀C₀ … Delay ≈ 1 (G, P) + 2 (carry) + 1 (sum XOR) = **4 gate delays** independent of n (fan-in grows). Real designs use 4-bit CLA blocks with a second-level lookahead unit.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Ripple delay
steps.body: 32-bit ripple adder, full-adder carry delay 2 ns and sum delay 3 ns. Last sum ready after the carry reaches stage 31 (31 × 2 = 62 ns) + 3 ns = **65 ns**; carry-out after 32 × 2 = 64 ns.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Carry lookahead
steps.body:
A = 1011, B = 0110, C₀ = 0. G = A·B = 0010 (only G₁ = 1); P = A ⊕ B = 1101 (P₃ = 1, P₂ = 1, P₁ = 0, P₀ = 1).
- C₁ = G₀ + P₀C₀ = 0
- C₂ = G₁ + P₁C₁ = 1
- C₃ = G₂ + P₂C₂ = 0 + 1·1 = 1
- C₄ = G₃ + P₃C₃ = 0 + 1·1 = 1
Sum Sᵢ = Pᵢ ⊕ Cᵢ: with C₃C₂C₁C₀ = 1100, S = 1101 ⊕ 1100 = **0001** and carry-out 1 → 10001 = 17 = 11 + 6 ✓.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing Pᵢ = Aᵢ + Bᵢ but then using it in the sum (sum needs XOR).
- Forgetting the last sum's own delay after the carry arrives.
- Claiming CLA delay is constant for any n with no cost (gate fan-in explodes).

activity.prompt: 16-bit ripple-carry adder: each full adder has carry delay 2 gate delays. Carry-out delay in gate delays?

quiz.why: A full adder's sum is A XOR B XOR Cin. It is 1 when an odd number of inputs are 1.
A bit position generates a carry by itself when both inputs are 1, so Gᵢ = Aᵢ·Bᵢ (AND).
A ripple-carry adder passes the carry through the stages one after the other, so its delay grows linearly with the number of bits n.

quiz.q: C₁ in terms of G, P
quiz.why: The carry into stage 1 is C₁ = G₀ + P₀·C₀: either stage 0 generates a carry or it propagates the incoming one.
A half adder's carry is the AND of the two inputs, AB. Its sum is the XOR.

scenes.text: Multiplying by 0111 1110 needs six additions with shift-and-add.
Booth notices a run of 1s: 0111 1110 = 1000 0000 − 0000 0010 — just one add and one subtract.

steps.title: Shift-and-add and Booth
steps.body:
Unsigned: for each multiplier bit, add the multiplicand if 1, shift.
**Booth (2's complement):** registers A (0), Q (multiplier), Q₋₁ (0), M (multiplicand). Repeat n times: look at Q₀Q₋₁ — **10 → A = A − M**, **01 → A = A + M**, 00/11 → nothing; then **arithmetic shift right** A, Q, Q₋₁. Result in AQ.
Booth recoding: bit pair (Qᵢ, Qᵢ₋₁): 10 → −1, 01 → +1, 00/11 → 0. Worst case is alternating 0101… (many operations).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Recoding
steps.body: Multiplier 0011 1100 (append 0 on the right): pairs from the right give 0, 0, −1, 0, 0, 0, +1, 0 → 2⁶ − 2² = 64 − 4 = **60** ✓ — only 2 operations instead of 4 additions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a logical shift (must preserve the sign of A).
- Forgetting to initialise Q₋₁ = 0.
- Mixing up which pair means add vs subtract (10 = subtract).

activity.prompt: Order one Booth iteration
items: If 10 subtract M from A; if 01 add M to A
Arithmetic-shift right A, Q, Q₋₁ together
Stop after n iterations; read the product from A:Q

quiz.why: In Booth's algorithm, the bit pair Q₀Q₋₁ = 01 marks the end of a run of 1s, so you add the multiplicand (A + M) and then shift.
Booth's algorithm uses an arithmetic right shift, which keeps the sign bit, so signed products stay correct.

quiz.q: Booth recoding of a long run of 1s needs
quiz.why: A long run of 1s needs just one subtraction at the start of the run and one addition after its end, since the middle bits give no operation.
The worst case is an alternating pattern 0101…, where every bit pair differs, so each step needs an add or subtract.

quiz.q: Product register size for n-bit operands
quiz.why: Multiplying two n-bit numbers gives up to 2n bits, held in the A and Q registers together.

scenes.text: Binary long division only ever asks: does the divisor fit — yes (1) or no (0)?
Restoring division tries a subtraction and undoes it if it went negative.

steps.title: Restoring and non-restoring
steps.body:
**Restoring (unsigned, n bits):** A = 0, Q = dividend, M = divisor. Repeat n times: shift A:Q left; A = A − M; if A < 0 → Q₀ = 0 and **restore** A = A + M; else Q₀ = 1. Quotient in Q, remainder in A.
**Non-restoring:** if A < 0 after a step, next step shift and **add** M instead of subtract (skips the restore); a final correction may be needed for the remainder.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Count operations
steps.body: Restoring division of n-bit numbers does n subtractions and up to n restoring additions (worst case 2n add/sub). Non-restoring does exactly **n** add-or-subtract operations (+ possible final correction).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Setting Q₀ before checking the sign of A.
- Forgetting to shift A and Q together.
- Treating non-restoring as producing a different quotient (same result, fewer operations).

activity.prompt: Restoring division of 13 by 4 (unsigned). What remainder ends up in A?

quiz.why: In restoring division, if subtracting makes A negative, the subtraction is undone (restored) by adding the divisor back, and the quotient bit is 0.
The division loop produces one quotient bit in each iteration.
Non-restoring division skips the restoring addition: when A goes negative, the next step adds instead of subtracting, which saves work.
7 = 2 × 3 + 1, so the quotient is 2 and the remainder is 1.

quiz.q: For n-bit division the loop runs
quiz.why: For n-bit division, the loop runs n times, once per quotient bit.

scenes.text: Scientific notation needs equal exponents before adding — the same in hardware.
Align, add, normalise, round.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
**Addition/subtraction:** (1) compare exponents; (2) shift the smaller number's significand right by the difference (alignment); (3) add/subtract significands; (4) normalise (shift and adjust exponent; check overflow/underflow); (5) round (guard, round and sticky bits; round-to-nearest-even default); renormalise if needed.
**Multiplication:** add exponents and subtract the bias; multiply significands; XOR signs; normalise and round.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Biased exponents in multiplication
steps.body: Multiply numbers with stored exponents 130 and 125 (bias 127): true exponents 3 and −2 → product exponent 1 → stored = 130 + 125 − 127 = **128**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adding the two biased exponents without subtracting the bias.
- Shifting the larger operand instead of the smaller.
- Expecting floating-point addition to be associative (it is not, due to rounding).

activity.prompt: Stored exponents 140 and 120 (bias 127) are multiplied. Stored exponent of the product before normalisation?

quiz.why: Floating-point addition first aligns the exponents, shifting the smaller number's fraction right, and then adds the fractions. Normalising and rounding come afterwards.
To multiply floating-point numbers you add the exponents. But both biased exponents already include the bias, so the sum has it twice, and you subtract it once: e₁ + e₂ − bias.

options: round to nearest, ties to even
quiz.why: The IEEE 754 default is round to nearest, ties to even. It is unbiased, so rounding errors don't build up in one direction.

quiz.q: Is (a + b) + c always equal to a + (b + c) in FP?
quiz.why: Floating-point addition isn't associative, since each addition is rounded. (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) can differ, for example when adding a tiny number to a huge one.

quiz.q: Which operand is shifted during alignment?
quiz.why: To align exponents, the number with the smaller exponent has its fraction shifted right. The larger number stays as it is, so least precision is lost.

questions.q: Half adder carry is
questions.why: A half adder adds two bits. The carry is 1 only when both are 1, which is the AND of A and B. The sum is the XOR.

questions.q: Booth's algorithm multiplies
questions.why: Booth's algorithm multiplies signed numbers in two's complement form, so it handles negative operands without special cases.

questions.q: Carry lookahead reduces
questions.why: Carry lookahead computes carries in parallel from generate and propagate signals, so it removes the delay of waiting for a carry to ripple through all stages.

questions.q: Pᵢ in CLA (for sum) is
questions.why: The propagate signal is Pᵢ = Aᵢ ⊕ Bᵢ. It's 1 when a stage passes an incoming carry along (exactly one input is 1).

questions.q: Booth: Q₀Q₋₁ = 10 →
questions.why: In Booth's algorithm, the bit pair 10 marks the start of a run of 1s, so you subtract the multiplicand (A − M) and then shift.

questions.q: Restoring division of 9 by 2: quotient
questions.why: 9 ÷ 2: 2 goes into 9 four times with 1 left over, since 9 = 4 × 2 + 1. So the quotient is 4 and the remainder is 1.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Floating-point addition is not associative. Reason (R): Results are rounded at each step. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: FP addition isn't associative. R is true and explains it: each addition is rounded, so the order of operations changes the rounding errors.

questions.q: 32-bit ripple adder, 1 ns per carry stage: carry-out after
questions.why: In a ripple-carry adder, the carry passes through each of the 32 stages one after another, so the carry-out is ready after 32 × 1 ns = 32 ns.

questions.q: Booth recoding of multiplier 0111 (append 0)
Case: a DSP chip multiplies many constants like 0111 1111. Booth helps because
options: it uses fewer add/subtract operations for runs of 1s
questions.why: A constant like 0111 1111 is a run of 1s. Booth turns a run into one subtraction and one addition (128 − 1), instead of an add for every 1 bit.

questions.q: CLA C₂ expanded
questions.why: Expanding C₂ = G₁ + P₁C₁ and C₁ = G₀ + P₀C₀ gives C₂ = G₁ + P₁G₀ + P₁P₀C₀. It is a two-level sum of products with no waiting for C₁.

questions.q: A = 0111, B = 0101, C₀ = 0: carry C₃ by lookahead
questions.why: G = 0101, P = 0010. C₁ = G₀ = 1; C₂ = G₁ + P₁C₁ = 0 + 1 = 1; C₃ = G₂ + P₂C₂ = 1 → 1.

questions.q: Booth 4-bit: 3 × (−2) final AQ
questions.why: 3 × (−2) = −6. In 8 bits, 6 is 0000 0110, so −6 is the invert 1111 1001 plus 1 = 1111 1010. The product register AQ holds 11111010.

questions.q: FP add: 1.000 × 2⁴ + 1.000 × 2⁰ with a 4-bit significand (1 hidden + 3 fraction), truncating
questions.why: Aligned addend 0.0001 is lost beyond 3 fraction bits → 1.000 × 2⁴ (a classic absorption error).

questions.q: Non-restoring division needs per iteration
questions.why: Non-restoring division does exactly one add or subtract per iteration, since a negative result is corrected in the next step instead of restoring now.

questions.q: Overflow of a 2's complement adder is detected by
questions.why: Two's complement overflow is detected when the carry into the most significant bit differs from the carry out of it: Cin(MSB) XOR Cout(MSB). Carry-out alone only indicates unsigned overflow.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Instruction Set Architecture & Performance
courses.summary: Instruction formats and number of addresses, expanding opcodes, addressing modes with effective-address calculation, RISC vs CISC, stack/accumulator/register machines, and performance metrics (CPI, MIPS, CPU time, Amdahl).
outcomes: Learners can compute effective addresses for every addressing mode
Learners can design and count instructions with expanding opcodes
Learners can compare RISC and CISC
Learners can compute CPU time, average CPI and MIPS

story.title: Fitting orders on a small card

scenes.text: Every instruction must fit into, say, 16 bits — opcode plus operand fields.
Rarely used formats can borrow unused opcode patterns: expanding opcodes.

steps.title: Formats
steps.body:
Instruction = opcode + operand specifiers. Number of explicit addresses: **3-address** (ADD R1, R2, R3), **2-address** (ADD R1, R2), **1-address** (accumulator: ADD X), **0-address** (stack: ADD).
Fixed length (RISC, easy decode) vs variable length (x86: 1–15 bytes, dense code).
With k-bit opcode: up to 2^k instructions. Register field bits = log₂(number of registers).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Field sizes
steps.body: 32-bit instructions, 64 registers, 3-register format: register fields 3 × 6 = 18 bits → opcode **14 bits** → up to 16,384 opcodes.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Expanding opcode
steps.body: 16-bit instructions, 6-bit address fields. Two-address instructions use a 4-bit opcode (16 patterns). If 12 two-address instructions exist, 4 patterns remain; each frees 6 more bits → 4 × 2⁶ = **256 one-address instructions** possible.

steps.title: Solved example 3 · Zero-address code
steps.body: Evaluate X = (A + B) × C on a stack machine: PUSH A, PUSH B, ADD, PUSH C, MUL, POP X → 6 instructions. On a 3-address machine: ADD T, A, B; MUL X, T, C → 2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting that expanding opcodes reuse *unused* patterns only.
- Using number of registers instead of log₂ for field width.
- Thinking 0-address machines have no operands at all (they are implicit on the stack).

activity.prompt: A 24-bit instruction has two 8-bit address fields and the rest opcode. 200 two-address instructions are defined. Maximum number of one-address instructions?

quiz.why: You need 2ⁿ ≥ 120 opcodes. 2⁶ = 64 is too few, and 2⁷ = 128 is enough, so 7 bits.
Naming one of 32 registers needs log₂32 = 5 bits.
A stack machine takes its operands from the top of the stack implicitly, so arithmetic instructions need no explicit addresses (0-address).
Fixed-length instructions make decoding simple and fast and fit pipelining, since the next instruction's position is known. This is a RISC advantage.
An accumulator machine has one implicit operand (the accumulator) and one explicit address, so it uses 1-address instructions.

scenes.text: 'The parcel is X' (immediate), 'in locker 50' (direct), 'locker 50 has a note pointing to locker 80' (indirect)…
Addressing modes are the CPU's ways to find an operand.

steps.title: Modes and effective address (EA)
steps.body:
- **Immediate:** operand in the instruction (no memory access).
- **Direct/absolute:** EA = address field.
- **Indirect:** EA = M[address field] (one extra access).
- **Register:** operand in a register.
- **Register indirect:** EA = R.
- **Indexed:** EA = address field + index register (arrays).
- **Base (displacement):** EA = base register + offset (relocation, structs).
- **PC-relative:** EA = PC + offset (branches; position-independent code). Note PC usually already points to the *next* instruction.
- **Auto-increment/decrement:** EA = R then R ± size (stacks, strings).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Same instruction, many modes
Solved example 2 · PC-relative branch
steps.body: A 2-word branch instruction at address 1000 (word-addressed) with offset −20. After fetch PC = 1002 → target = 1002 − 20 = **982**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the address of the current instruction instead of the updated PC in relative mode.
- Counting no memory access for indirect (it needs two).
- Confusing indexed (big constant + small register) with base (big register + small offset) — the arithmetic is the same.

activity.prompt: Match the mode to its typical use

quiz.q: Which needs no memory access for the operand?
quiz.why: With immediate addressing, the operand is part of the instruction itself, so no memory access is needed to get it.

quiz.q: Indirect addressing needs how many memory accesses to get the operand?
quiz.why: Indirect addressing first reads memory to get the operand's address, then reads again to get the operand: 2 memory accesses.
In base (displacement) addressing, the effective address is the content of a base register plus an offset from the instruction.

quiz.q: Branch at 2000 (instruction size 4 bytes), offset +16, PC-relative: target
quiz.why: PC-relative addressing adds the offset to the PC after the instruction has been fetched. The PC is already 2000 + 4 = 2004, so the target is 2004 + 16 = 2020.
Position-independent code uses PC-relative addressing, so references stay correct wherever the program is loaded in memory.

lessons.title: RISC vs CISC and CPU organisations

scenes.text: Kitchen A has a few simple tools used very fast; kitchen B has gadgets for every dish.
RISC and CISC are the same trade-off for instruction sets.

steps.title: Comparison
steps.body:
**RISC:** few simple instructions, fixed length, load/store architecture (only loads/stores touch memory), many registers, mostly one-cycle execution, hardwired control, easy pipelining — ARM, RISC-V, MIPS.
**CISC:** many complex instructions, variable length, memory operands in ALU instructions, fewer registers historically, microprogrammed control — x86 (modern x86 cores decode into RISC-like micro-ops).
CPU organisations: accumulator, general-register, stack.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Load/store code
steps.body: C = A + B on RISC: LOAD R1, A; LOAD R2, B; ADD R3, R1, R2; STORE R3, C → 4 instructions. CISC (memory-to-memory): ADD C, A, B → 1 instruction, but several memory accesses and cycles.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Which is RISC-like?
steps.body: Features: 32 registers, all instructions 32 bits, only LW/SW access memory → **RISC** (e.g. RISC-V RV32I).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying RISC programs are always shorter (usually longer, but faster per instruction).
- Assuming CISC cannot be pipelined (modern x86 pipelines micro-ops deeply).
- Calling ARM CISC.

activity.prompt: RISC or CISC trait?

quiz.why: In a load/store architecture, only load and store instructions access memory. All other instructions work on registers. This is typical of RISC.
x86 is a CISC instruction set, though modern chips translate instructions into simpler RISC-like micro-operations inside.
RISC-V is an open RISC instruction set architecture.
RISC designs usually have simple, regular instructions, so hardwired control is practical and fast. CISC often uses microprogrammed control.
A CISC instruction does more work and can be variable length, so programs are usually more compact, with higher code density.

scenes.text: Laptop A runs at 3 GHz, laptop B at 2.4 GHz. Is A faster?
Not necessarily — instructions per program and cycles per instruction matter too.

steps.title: Iron law
steps.body:
**CPU time = Instruction count × CPI × Clock period = IC × CPI / f.**
Average CPI = Σ (fraction of class i × CPIᵢ).
**MIPS = f / (CPI × 10⁶)** — misleading across ISAs.
**Speedup** = old time / new time. **Amdahl:** speedup = 1 / ((1 − f) + f/s) when a fraction f of time is sped up by s.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Average CPI and time
steps.body: Mix: ALU 50% (CPI 1), load 20% (CPI 5), store 10% (CPI 3), branch 20% (CPI 2). CPI = 0.5 + 1.0 + 0.3 + 0.4 = **2.2**. At 2 GHz with 10⁹ instructions: time = 10⁹ × 2.2 / (2 × 10⁹) = **1.1 s**; MIPS = 2000 / 2.2 ≈ **909**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Amdahl
steps.body: Floating-point code is 40% of run time; a new FPU makes it 8× faster. Speedup = 1 / (0.6 + 0.4/8) = 1 / 0.65 ≈ **1.54**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing clock rates alone.
- Weighting CPI by time fractions instead of instruction-count fractions.
- Applying Amdahl to the wrong fraction (fraction of *time*, not of code lines).

activity.prompt: Program: 2 × 10⁹ instructions, CPI 1.5, clock 3 GHz. CPU time in seconds?

quiz.why: The iron law of performance: CPU time = instruction count × cycles per instruction × clock period.
MIPS = clock rate/(CPI × 10⁶) = 1000 MHz/2 = 500.

quiz.q: Halving CPI with the same IC and clock
quiz.why: CPU time is proportional to CPI when IC and the clock are fixed. Halving CPI halves the time.
If half the work is sped up infinitely, the other half remains: speedup = 1/(1 − 0.5) = 2×. That's Amdahl's law.

quiz.q: MIPS is a poor cross-ISA metric because
options: instruction counts and work per instruction differ
quiz.why: MIPS depends on how much work each instruction does, which differs between instruction sets. A machine with simpler instructions may show a higher MIPS but not finish a task sooner.

questions.q: Number of explicit addresses in a stack ADD
questions.why: In a stack machine ADD takes both operands from the top of the stack, so it needs 0 explicit addresses.

questions.q: Immediate operand is
questions.why: An immediate operand is a constant stored in the instruction itself.

questions.q: RISC instructions are typically
questions.why: RISC instructions typically have a fixed length (for example 32 bits), which simplifies decoding and pipelining.

questions.q: Opcode bits for 300 instructions
questions.why: For 300 instructions you need 2ⁿ ≥ 300. 2⁸ = 256 is too small and 2⁹ = 512 is enough, so 9 bits.

questions.q: EA for indexed mode
questions.why: In indexed mode, the effective address is a base address from the instruction plus the contents of an index register. It suits array access.

questions.q: CPI 2, 4 GHz: MIPS
Assertion (A): MIPS can rank machines wrongly. Reason (R): Different ISAs need different instruction counts for the same task. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: MIPS can rank machines wrongly. R is true and explains it: different instruction sets need different numbers of instructions for the same task, so MIPS doesn't measure work done.

questions.q: Field = 300, R = 200, M[300] = 500, M[500] = 700, M[200] = 900. Operand under indirect
questions.why: With indirect addressing, the field (300) holds the address of the address: M[300] = 500, and the operand is M[500] = 700.

questions.q: 32-bit instruction, 32 registers, 3 register fields + 11-bit opcode... remaining bits for an immediate field
questions.why: Three register fields of 5 bits take 15 bits. With an 11-bit opcode that leaves 32 − 15 − 11 = 6 bits for an immediate.

questions.q: Case: compiler change cuts instruction count 20% but raises CPI from 1.5 to 1.7. Speedup
questions.why: Old time ∝ 1 × 1.5 = 1.5. New time ∝ 0.8 × 1.7 = 1.36. Speedup = 1.5/1.36 ≈ 1.10, so the fewer instructions win, despite the higher CPI.

questions.q: 16-bit instructions, 4-bit address fields, three-address format with 15 three-address instructions defined. Max two-address instructions
questions.why: With 4-bit opcode space, the 15 three-address instructions use 15 of the 16 opcodes. The one unused opcode can be extended using the freed 4-bit field to give 1 × 2⁴ = 16 two-address instructions.

questions.q: Machine A: 2 GHz, CPI 2; B: 1.5 GHz, CPI 1.2; same IC. Faster and by how much
questions.why: Time per instruction: A = CPI/f = 2/2 GHz = 1 ns. B = 1.2/1.5 GHz = 0.8 ns. B is faster by 1/0.8 = 1.25×.

questions.q: Amdahl: 90% parallel on 10 cores
Branch at address 400, 4-byte instructions, target 340, PC-relative. Offset field value
questions.why: The PC is already 400 + 4 = 404 when the offset is added. The offset is 340 − 404 = −64.

questions.q: Instruction mix: 40% CPI 1, 40% CPI 2, 20% CPI 4; 1.6 GHz; IC 4 × 10⁹. Time
Auto-increment mode is ideal for
questions.why: Auto-increment updates the pointer by itself after each access, which is ideal for stepping through arrays and strings.

courses.title: Unit 4 · CPU Datapath & Control Unit
courses.summary: Register transfer notation, micro-operations, single-bus and multi-bus datapaths, instruction cycle (fetch–decode–execute), hardwired versus microprogrammed control, horizontal and vertical microcode, and control-word sizing.
outcomes: Learners can write micro-operation sequences for fetch and execute
Learners can compare single-bus and three-bus datapaths
Learners can contrast hardwired and microprogrammed control
Learners can size control memory for horizontal and vertical microcode

scenes.text: The CPU is a kitchen: registers are counters, the ALU is the stove, buses are the paths between them.
Each tiny step — move, add, shift — is a micro-operation.

steps.title: Key registers
steps.body:
PC (address of next instruction), IR (current instruction), MAR (memory address), MDR/MBR (memory data), general registers, flags/status register, SP.
Register transfer notation: R2 ← R1 + R3; MAR ← PC; MDR ← M[MAR].
Micro-operation types: register transfer, arithmetic, logic, shift.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Fetch on a single bus
steps.body:
T1: MAR ← PC, (start read), PC ← PC + 1 (via ALU/Z register)
T2: MDR ← M[MAR] (wait for memory)
T3: IR ← MDR
Then decode. On a single internal bus, only one value moves per step, so steps that need two operands take longer.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Execute ADD R1, R2 (single bus)
steps.body:
T4: Y ← R1
T5: Z ← Y + R2 (ALU)
T6: R1 ← Z
Three steps because the ALU's second operand must be held in Y while the bus carries R2. With **three buses** (two source, one destination): R1 ← R1 + R2 in **one** step.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting two different values on one bus in the same step.
- Forgetting the temporary registers Y and Z in single-bus designs.
- Incrementing PC after the instruction executes (it is done during fetch).

activity.prompt: Order the fetch micro-operations

quiz.why: The memory address register (MAR) holds the address of the memory location to be read or written.
The instruction register (IR) holds the instruction currently being executed.

quiz.q: Single-bus ADD R1, R2 needs temporary register
quiz.why: A single bus can carry only one value at a time, so one operand is held in a temporary register Y while the ALU output goes to Z.

options: two sources and a destination in one step
quiz.why: A three-bus datapath has two source buses and one destination bus, so it can read two registers and write a result in the same step.
The PC is incremented during the fetch step so that it points to the next instruction.

scenes.text: The CPU's life: fetch, decode, execute, check for interrupts, repeat.
A doorbell (interrupt) is checked between instructions, not in the middle of one.

steps.title: Cycle
steps.body: Fetch → decode → (fetch operands: indirect cycle if needed) → execute → (write back) → **interrupt check**. If an enabled interrupt is pending: save PC (and status) — e.g. on the stack — load the ISR address from the **interrupt vector**, disable further interrupts as needed, run the ISR, return (restore PC/status).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Cycles per instruction
steps.body: An instruction with an indirect operand: fetch (1 memory read) + indirect cycle (1 read for the address) + execute (1 read for the operand) = **3 memory reads**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Interrupt overhead
steps.body: ISR entry/exit costs 20 cycles and the ISR body 80 cycles; 10,000 interrupts per second on a 100 MHz CPU → 10⁶ cycles/s = **1%** of CPU time.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Checking interrupts in the middle of an instruction (except for page faults/restartable instructions).
- Forgetting to save the status register.
- Mixing up vectored (address supplied) and polled interrupts.

activity.prompt: 10,000 interrupts per second, each costing 200 cycles, on a 50 MHz CPU. Percentage of CPU time spent on interrupts?

quiz.why: The CPU checks for interrupts at the end of each instruction, between instructions, so each instruction completes cleanly.

options: the device supplies/identifies the ISR address
quiz.why: In a vectored interrupt the device supplies or identifies the address (vector) of its service routine, so the CPU jumps there directly without polling.

quiz.q: Before running the ISR the CPU must save
quiz.why: Before the ISR runs, the CPU saves the PC and status register so that it can resume the interrupted program afterwards.
An indirect cycle makes an extra memory read to fetch the operand's address when indirect addressing is used.
ISR stands for interrupt service routine, the handler code that runs when an interrupt occurs.

story.title: Wired switches vs a recipe book

scenes.text: A hardwired controller is a fixed web of gates — fast but hard to change.
A microprogrammed controller reads a recipe (microcode) from control memory — slower, easy to modify.

steps.title: Two designs
steps.body:
**Hardwired:** control signals generated by combinational logic from opcode, step counter (timing signals) and flags. Fast; complex to design/modify; RISC.
**Microprogrammed:** each machine instruction maps to a sequence of **microinstructions** in **control memory (ROM)**; a **control address register (CAR)** and sequencer pick the next microinstruction (increment, branch on condition, map from opcode). Flexible, easier for complex ISAs; slower; CISC (historically).

steps.title: Horizontal vs vertical microcode
steps.body:
- **Horizontal:** one bit per control signal → wide words, high parallelism, no decoding, fast.
- **Vertical:** signals encoded into fields and decoded → narrow words, less parallelism, extra decode delay.
Microinstruction = control field + next-address field (+ condition select).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Control word size
steps.body: 48 control signals, horizontal format, control memory of 256 words with a next-address field → next address needs 8 bits; plus a 3-bit condition field selecting among 8 flags → word = 48 + 3 + 8 = **59 bits**; memory = 256 × 59 bits.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Vertical encoding
steps.body: The 48 signals fall into mutually exclusive groups of sizes 15, 15, 10, 8. Encoding each group in a field (with one 'none' code): ⌈log₂ 16⌉ + ⌈log₂ 16⌉ + ⌈log₂ 11⌉ + ⌈log₂ 9⌉ = 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = **16 bits** instead of 48.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the 'no signal' code when encoding groups.
- Saying microprogrammed control is faster.
- Confusing control memory (microcode) with main memory.

activity.prompt: A horizontal microinstruction has 40 control bits, a 4-bit condition field, and control memory has 512 words. Word width with a next-address field?

quiz.why: Hardwired control uses logic gates directly, which is faster but harder to change. Microprogrammed control is slower but more flexible.
The control memory in microprogrammed control stores the microinstructions that make up each instruction's steps.
Horizontal microcode has one bit per control signal, so words are wide and many signals can be active in parallel, with no decoding.
The CAR is the control address register, which acts as the microprogram counter by holding the address of the next microinstruction.
Vertical microcode encodes the signals in fields, which makes words narrower but needs decoders to produce the actual control signals.

scenes.text: Students in a lab build a toy CPU on an FPGA with ALU, register file and memory.
The clock period must fit the slowest step.

steps.title: Single-cycle vs multi-cycle
steps.body:
**Single-cycle:** every instruction finishes in one long clock cycle sized for the slowest instruction (usually load: fetch + register read + ALU + memory + write back).
**Multi-cycle:** each step is one short cycle; instructions take different numbers of cycles; hardware units (ALU, memory) can be reused across steps.
Pipelining (next unit) overlaps the steps of different instructions.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Clock periods
steps.body:
Step delays: fetch 200 ps, decode/register read 100 ps, ALU 150 ps, memory 200 ps, write back 100 ps.
- Single-cycle clock = 200 + 100 + 150 + 200 + 100 = **750 ps** for every instruction.
- Multi-cycle clock = max step = **200 ps**; a load needs 5 cycles = 1000 ps, an R-type 4 cycles = 800 ps, a branch 3 cycles = 600 ps.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Which wins?
steps.body: Mix: 25% loads (5 cycles), 10% stores (4), 50% ALU (4), 15% branches (3). Average multi-cycle CPI = 1.25 + 0.4 + 2.0 + 0.45 = 4.1 → 4.1 × 200 = 820 ps per instruction vs 750 ps single-cycle → **single-cycle slightly faster here**; multi-cycle wins when step delays are more balanced or instructions vary more.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming multi-cycle is always faster.
- Sizing the single-cycle clock by the average instruction.
- Forgetting register-file write time in the critical path.

activity.prompt: Single-cycle CPU steps: 250, 150, 200, 250, 100 ps. Clock period of the single-cycle design (ps)?

quiz.why: In a single-cycle design, every instruction takes one clock cycle, so the clock period must suit the slowest instruction.
In a multi-cycle design each step takes one cycle, so the clock must be long enough for the slowest step.
Multi-cycle designs can reuse hardware, such as one ALU for different steps (address calculation, execution and PC update).
A branch needs fetch, decode and an ALU compare to decide the target, which takes 3 cycles in this multi-cycle design.

quiz.q: Overlapping steps of different instructions is
quiz.why: Overlapping the stages of different instructions is called pipelining.

questions.q: PC holds
questions.why: The program counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction to fetch.

questions.q: MDR holds
questions.why: The memory data register (MDR) holds the data read from or to be written to memory.

questions.q: Microprogrammed control stores signals in
questions.why: Microprogrammed control keeps its microinstructions, and so the control signals, in a control memory (usually a ROM).

questions.q: Horizontal vs vertical: which is faster?
questions.why: Horizontal microcode is faster because its signals need no decoding. Vertical microcode must decode the encoded fields first.

questions.q: Single-bus ADD R1, R2 steps (after fetch)
questions.why: After the fetch, ADD R1, R2 on a single bus takes 3 steps: Y ← R1; Z ← Y + R2; R1 ← Z.

questions.q: Interrupt vector gives
questions.why: The interrupt vector gives the address of the interrupt service routine for that interrupt.

questions.q: Assertion (A): RISC processors commonly use hardwired control. Reason (R): Simple, regular instructions make fast combinational decoding practical. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: RISC processors usually use hardwired control. R is true and explains it: simple, regular instructions allow fast combinational decoding without microcode.

questions.q: Control memory 1024 words, 30 control bits, 2-bit condition: horizontal word width
questions.why: Horizontal word width = control signals 30 + condition bits 2 + next-address bits log₂1024 = 10, which is 42 bits.

questions.q: Groups of 7, 7, 3 mutually exclusive signals encoded vertically (with a none code): bits
questions.why: Each mutually exclusive group, including a 'none' code, needs ⌈log₂(n + 1)⌉ bits: 7 signals + none = 8 values → 3 bits; again 3; 3 signals + none = 4 → 2 bits. Total 3 + 3 + 2 = 8.

questions.q: Case: a vendor must patch an instruction bug after shipping. Which control style makes this easiest?
questions.why: Microprogrammed control stores the instruction steps in (writable) microcode, so a bug can be patched with a microcode update. Hardwired logic would need a hardware change.

questions.q: Multi-cycle: steps 200, 100, 150, 200, 100 ps; ALU instr uses 4 steps. Its time
questions.why: In a multi-cycle design every step takes one clock, and the clock is set by the slowest step, 200 ps. Four steps give 4 × 200 = 800 ps.

questions.q: Indirect-address instruction memory reads: fetch + ? + operand
questions.why: Indirect addressing adds one extra memory read, to get the operand's address, between the instruction fetch and the operand read.

questions.q: 5000 interrupts/s × 400 cycles on 200 MHz: CPU share
questions.why: Cycles spent per second = 5000 × 400 = 2×10⁶. The CPU does 2×10⁸ cycles per second, so the share is 2×10⁶/2×10⁸ = 1%.

questions.q: Single-cycle 800 ps vs multi-cycle clock 200 ps with average CPI 4.4: faster
questions.why: Multi-cycle time per instruction = 4.4 × 200 = 880 ps, which is more than the single-cycle 800 ps. So the single-cycle design is faster here.

questions.q: Microinstruction sequencing using the opcode to find the routine start is called
questions.why: Mapping uses the opcode to find the starting address of the micro-routine in control memory, through mapping logic or a ROM.

questions.q: Which signal group can be encoded in one field?
questions.why: Only mutually exclusive signals (never active together) can share one encoded field, since the field can specify just one of them at a time.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Pipelining & Hazards
courses.summary: Pipeline timing and speedup, non-uniform stages and latch overhead, structural, data and control hazards, forwarding and stalls, branch penalties and prediction, and an introduction to superscalar and out-of-order execution.
outcomes: Learners can compute pipelined execution time, speedup and throughput
Learners can classify RAW, WAR and WAW hazards
Learners can count stalls with and without forwarding
Learners can compute effective CPI with branch penalties

scenes.text: Washing, drying and folding one load takes 3 hours. Four loads one after another take 12 hours.
Start the next wash while the first dries — four loads finish in 6 hours.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
k stages, n instructions, cycle τ:
- Pipelined time = **(k + n − 1) τ**
- Non-pipelined time = n × (sum of stage delays) (or n × k × τ if stages are equal)
- Speedup = non-pipelined / pipelined → approaches k for large n (ideal CPI = 1)
- With unequal stages: **τ = max stage delay + latch (register) delay**
- Throughput = 1 instruction per τ (ideal).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Equal stages
steps.body: k = 5, τ = 2 ns, n = 100: pipelined = (5 + 99) × 2 = **208 ns**; non-pipelined = 100 × 10 = 1000 ns → speedup ≈ **4.81**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Unequal stages
steps.body: Stages 150, 120, 160, 140, 130 ps, latch 10 ps → τ = 170 ps. 1000 instructions: (5 + 999) × 170 = **170,680 ps**. Non-pipelined per instruction: 700 ps → 700,000 ps. Speedup ≈ **4.10** (less than 5 due to imbalance and latches).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using (k × n) τ for the pipelined time.
- Forgetting latch delay in τ.
- Adding latch delay to the non-pipelined design (it has no inter-stage latches).

activity.prompt: Pipeline time: input k (stages), n (instructions) and the k stage delays on the next line, then latch delay. Print the total pipelined time (integer) = (k + n − 1) × (max stage + latch).
activity.starter:
k = int(input())
n = int(input())
d = list(map(int, input().split()))
latch = int(input())
activity.solution:
k = int(input())
n = int(input())
d = list(map(int, input().split()))
latch = int(input())
print((k + n - 1) * (max(d) + latch))
activity.hint: The slowest stage sets the clock.

quiz.why: An ideal pipeline completes one instruction every cycle, so its CPI is 1.
Pipelined time = (k + n − 1)τ = (4 + 20 − 1) × 1 ns = 23 ns. The first instruction takes k cycles and each of the others adds one more.

quiz.q: Maximum speedup of a k-stage pipeline
quiz.why: The ideal maximum speedup of a k-stage pipeline is k, when all stages are balanced and nothing stalls.

quiz.q: Clock with stages 10, 20, 15 ns and latch 2 ns
quiz.why: The clock must fit the slowest stage plus the latch delay: 20 + 2 = 22 ns.
With unbalanced stages, the clock is set by the slowest, so faster stages sit idle, which cuts the speedup.

scenes.text: The next cook needs the sauce the previous cook is still making.
Pass the sauce directly across the counter instead of waiting for it to reach the fridge — forwarding.

steps.title: Hazard types
steps.body:
- **RAW (read after write, true dependence):** I2 reads what I1 writes — the real hazard in simple in-order pipelines.
- **WAR (anti-dependence)** and **WAW (output dependence):** name dependences; matter with out-of-order execution; removed by register renaming.
- **Structural:** two instructions need the same unit (e.g. one memory port for IF and MEM).
- **Control:** branches.

steps.title: Resolving RAW in a 5-stage pipeline (IF ID EX MEM WB)
steps.body:
- Without forwarding (register written in first half of WB, read in second half of ID): dependent instruction right after → **2 stalls**.
- With **forwarding** (EX/MEM → EX): ALU-to-ALU dependence → **0 stalls**.
- **Load-use hazard:** a load followed immediately by a use → **1 stall** even with forwarding (data available after MEM). Compilers schedule an independent instruction into the slot.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Classify
steps.body:
I1: ADD R1, R2, R3; I2: SUB R4, R1, R5; I3: MUL R1, R6, R7; I4: OR R6, R8, R9.
- I1→I2 on R1: **RAW**
- I1→I3 on R1: **WAW**
- I2→I3 on R1 (I2 reads, I3 writes): **WAR**
- I3→I4 on R6 (I3 reads, I4 writes): **WAR**

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Count cycles
steps.body:
LW R1, 0(R2); ADD R3, R1, R4; SUB R5, R3, R6 on a 5-stage pipeline with forwarding.
- LW→ADD load-use → 1 stall; ADD→SUB forwarded → 0.
- Cycles = 5 + (3 − 1) + 1 = **8**. Without forwarding: 2 + 2 stalls → 5 + 2 + 4 = **11**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking forwarding removes the load-use stall.
- Calling WAR a RAW hazard.
- Counting stalls for independent instructions.

activity.prompt: 5-stage pipeline with full forwarding: LW R1, 0(R2); ADD R3, R1, R1; ADD R4, R3, R2; SW R4, 4(R2). Total cycles?

quiz.why: A true data dependence is read after write (RAW): an instruction needs a value that an earlier one hasn't yet produced.
Register renaming removes the false (name) dependences, WAR and WAW, by giving each result its own register. True RAW dependences remain.

quiz.q: Load followed by dependent ALU op with forwarding
quiz.why: A load's data is available only after the MEM stage, so even with forwarding a dependent instruction right after it must wait 1 cycle (the load-use stall).

quiz.q: One shared memory for IF and MEM causes
quiz.why: When IF and MEM both need the same single memory in the same cycle, that's a structural hazard, a resource conflict.
For an ALU result used by the next ALU instruction, forwarding from the EX/MEM register supplies the value in time, so no stall is needed.

scenes.text: A driver at a fork must choose before seeing the signboard clearly.
Guess well (prediction) or wait (stall) — waiting costs time every time.

steps.title: Branch penalty
steps.body:
If a branch is resolved in stage s, (s − 1) instructions may be fetched wrongly → penalty up to s − 1 cycles.
**Effective CPI = 1 + (branch fraction × misprediction or stall rate × penalty) + other stalls.**
Techniques: stall/flush, predict not-taken, **delayed branch** (fill delay slots), static prediction (backward taken), **dynamic prediction** (1-bit, **2-bit saturating counters**, branch target buffer, global history).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Stall on every branch
steps.body: 20% branches, resolved in EX (stage 3) → penalty 2 cycles. CPI = 1 + 0.2 × 2 = **1.4**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · With prediction
steps.body: Same pipeline, predictor accuracy 90%, penalty only on mispredictions: CPI = 1 + 0.2 × 0.1 × 2 = **1.04**. A 2-bit counter on a loop running 10 iterations mispredicts only at loop exit (once per run after warm-up), whereas a 1-bit predictor mispredicts twice (exit and first iteration of the next run).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Multiplying by the taken fraction when the pipeline stalls on *every* branch.
- Forgetting that the penalty depends on where the branch resolves.
- Assuming delay slots are always filled usefully.

activity.prompt: 25% of instructions are branches, misprediction rate 20%, penalty 3 cycles, base CPI 1. Effective CPI?

quiz.q: Branch resolved in stage 4: max penalty
quiz.why: If a branch is resolved in stage s, the instructions fetched in the meantime are wasted. The maximum penalty is s − 1 = 3 cycles.
A 2-bit predictor must be wrong twice in a row before it flips its prediction. This hysteresis helps with loop branches.

options: the instruction(s) after the branch always execute
quiz.why: With a delayed branch, the instruction(s) in the delay slot after the branch always execute, which hides the branch delay.

quiz.q: CPI with 10% branches, 1-cycle penalty, always stall
quiz.why: CPI = 1 + (branch frequency × penalty) = 1 + 0.10 × 1 = 1.1.
A branch target buffer (BTB) stores predicted branch target addresses, so fetch can redirect immediately.

scenes.text: Two cooks can each start a dish every minute (superscalar).
A smart kitchen starts whichever dish has its ingredients ready, not strictly in menu order (out-of-order).

steps.title: ILP techniques
steps.body:
- **Superscalar:** issue m instructions per cycle (ideal CPI = 1/m, IPC = m).
- **Out-of-order execution** with **Tomasulo-style** reservation stations, **register renaming** and a **reorder buffer** (in-order commit for precise exceptions).
- **Speculative execution** past predicted branches.
- **VLIW:** compiler packs independent operations into long instructions.
- **Multithreading / SMT** hides stalls using other threads.
Deep pipelines raise clock rate but increase branch penalties and power.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Superscalar CPI
steps.body: A 4-wide superscalar achieves an average IPC of 2.5 at 3 GHz → instructions per second = 7.5 × 10⁹; CPI = 0.4.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Deeper isn't free
steps.body: Going from 5 to 15 stages raises the clock 2.5×, but branch penalty rises from 2 to 10 cycles. With 20% branches and 5% mispredicts: CPI 5-stage = 1 + 0.2 × 0.05 × 2 = 1.02; 15-stage = 1 + 0.2 × 0.05 × 10 = 1.10. Time per instruction ratio = (1.10 / 2.5) / 1.02 ≈ **0.43** → still faster here, but with diminishing returns.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying out-of-order CPUs commit out of order (they commit in order).
- Treating IPC and CPI as the same number (they are reciprocals).
- Thinking superscalar requires VLIW instructions.

statements.s: A reorder buffer allows precise exceptions in out-of-order cores.
Register renaming eliminates RAW dependences.
statements.why: It removes WAR and WAW; RAW are true dependences.

statements.s: A 2-wide superscalar can reach CPI 0.5 ideally.
VLIW relies mainly on the compiler for scheduling.
Deeper pipelines always improve performance.

quiz.why: IPC is the reciprocal of CPI. An IPC of 2 means CPI = 1/2 = 0.5.
Tomasulo's algorithm schedules instructions dynamically using reservation stations and register renaming.
SMT is simultaneous multithreading, in which a core runs instructions from several threads at once (like Intel's Hyper-Threading).

quiz.q: Speculative work on a mispredicted path is
quiz.why: Work done on a mispredicted path is squashed (discarded) when the misprediction is found, so it doesn't change the program state.
VLIW processors rely on the compiler to schedule instructions statically, so the hardware stays simpler.

questions.q: Pipelined time formula
questions.why: Pipelined time for n instructions in k stages is (k + n − 1)τ: k cycles to fill the pipeline, then one more cycle per further instruction.

questions.q: RAW hazard is
questions.why: A RAW hazard is a true (flow) dependence: the later instruction reads a value written by the earlier one.

questions.q: Branches cause
questions.why: Branches create control hazards, because the next instruction address isn't known until the branch is resolved.

questions.q: 5 stages, 1 ns each, 10 instructions
Load-use stalls with forwarding
questions.why: Even with forwarding, a load followed immediately by a dependent instruction needs 1 stall cycle.

questions.q: Max speedup of 6-stage ideal pipeline
questions.why: The ideal speedup of a k-stage pipeline is k, so 6 for a 6-stage pipeline.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Forwarding cannot fully hide a load-use hazard in the classic 5-stage pipeline. Reason (R): Load data is available only after the MEM stage. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: forwarding can't fully hide a load-use hazard in the classic pipeline. R is true and explains it: loaded data appears only after the MEM stage, which is too late for the next instruction's EX stage in the very next cycle.

questions.q: Stages 200, 250, 150, 300, 100 ps, latch 20: clock
questions.why: The clock period is the slowest stage plus latch overhead: 300 + 20 = 320 ps.

questions.q: 30% branches, always 2-cycle stall: CPI
questions.why: 30% of instructions suffer 2 stall cycles, so the extra CPI is 0.3 × 2 = 0.6. CPI = 1 + 0.6 = 1.6.

questions.q: Case: a compiler puts an independent instruction between a load and its use. Effect
questions.why: Placing an independent instruction between the load and its use fills the delay, so the load-use stall disappears. This is instruction scheduling by the compiler.

questions.q: Speedup for n = 1000 with stages above vs non-pipelined 1000 ps per instruction
questions.why: Non-pipelined: 1000 × 1000 ps = 10⁶ ps. Pipelined: (5 + 999) × 320 = 321,280 ps. Speedup = 10⁶/321,280 ≈ 3.11.

questions.q: I1: ADD R1,R2,R3; I2: LW R4,0(R1); I3: SUB R5,R4,R1; with forwarding: total cycles
questions.why: Without stalls, 3 instructions take 5 + 2 = 7 cycles. I3 uses R4 loaded by I2, so there's 1 load-use stall even with forwarding, giving 8 cycles.

questions.q: Without forwarding (2 stalls per adjacent RAW), I1→I2→I3 chain of 3 dependent ALU instructions: cycles
questions.why: Three instructions take 5 + 2 = 7 cycles without stalls. Each adjacent dependent pair needs 2 stalls without forwarding: 2 pairs × 2 = 4, so 11 cycles.

questions.q: Branch resolved in MEM (stage 4) of a 5-stage pipeline, 15% branches, 60% taken, predict not-taken: CPI
questions.why: Only taken branches (60%) cost a penalty when predicting not-taken, and a branch resolved in MEM wastes 3 cycles. Extra CPI = 0.15 × 0.6 × 3 = 0.27, so CPI = 1.27.

questions.q: Which dependency remains after renaming?
options: I1 reads R1, I2 writes R1
R1 written by I1 then read by I2
I1 writes R1, I2 writes R1
questions.why: Renaming removes WAR and WAW, but a value that is written and then read (RAW) is a true dependence and remains.

questions.q: A 3-wide superscalar at 2 GHz with IPC 1.8 executes per second
questions.why: Instructions per second = IPC × clock rate = 1.8 × 2×10⁹ = 3.6×10⁹. Issue width 3 is only the maximum.

courses.note: topic order may differ by university syllabus

courses.title: Unit 6 · Memory Hierarchy & Cache
courses.summary: Locality, the memory hierarchy, SRAM vs DRAM, memory chip organisation, cache mapping (direct, fully associative, set-associative) with address breakdown, hit/miss simulations, AMAT and multilevel caches, replacement and write policies.
outcomes: Learners can split an address into tag, index and offset for any cache
Learners can simulate hits and misses for direct-mapped and set-associative caches
Learners can compute AMAT for single and multilevel caches
Learners can build a memory of given size from smaller chips

scenes.text: Books you use often stay on your desk; others are on the shelf; rare ones in the library.
Programs behave the same — that's locality, and it's why caches work.

steps.title: Hierarchy
steps.body:
Registers → L1 (≈1 ns, KB) → L2 → L3 (MB) → DRAM main memory (≈50–100 ns, GB) → SSD/disk. Faster = smaller and costlier per bit.
**Temporal locality:** recently used data is likely reused. **Spatial locality:** nearby data is likely used soon.
**SRAM** (6 transistors/bit, fast, caches) vs **DRAM** (1 transistor + capacitor, dense, needs refresh, main memory).

steps.title: Building memory from chips
steps.body: Required size W × B from chips w × b: chips = (W / w) × (B / b). Address lines for W words = log₂ W; a decoder selects among W / w rows of chips. **Interleaving** spreads consecutive addresses across banks to overlap accesses.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Chips needed
steps.body: Build 32K × 8 from 1K × 4 chips: (32K / 1K) × (8 / 4) = 32 × 2 = **64 chips**. Address lines: 15 total; 10 go to each chip, 5 drive a **5-to-32 decoder**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Locality in code
steps.body: `for (i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += a[i];` — `sum` and `i` show temporal locality; walking through `a[i]` shows spatial locality. Traversing a 2-D C array column by column destroys spatial locality (row-major layout) → many more misses.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying DRAM is used for L1 caches.
- Multiplying only the word ratio when building wider memory.
- Forgetting that C arrays are row-major.

activity.prompt: Build a 64K × 16 memory from 4K × 8 chips. How many chips?

quiz.why: Caches are built from SRAM, which is fast but expensive. Main memory uses DRAM.

quiz.q: Reusing the same variable often is
quiz.why: Using the same data again soon is temporal locality, with reuse over time. Spatial locality is about nearby addresses.
DRAM stores bits as charge on capacitors, which leak, so it needs periodic refresh.
1M = 2²⁰ words, so 20 address lines are needed.

quiz.q: Column-wise traversal of a C 2-D array hurts
quiz.why: C stores 2-D arrays row by row, so going column by column jumps through memory and loses spatial locality.

scenes.text: Direct mapping: every ticket has exactly one seat. Fully associative: sit anywhere. Set-associative: sit anywhere in your row.
The address says which row (index) and who you are (tag).

steps.title: Breaking down an address
steps.body:
Block (line) size B → **offset = log₂ B** bits. Number of lines L = cache size / B. Associativity k → sets S = L / k → **index = log₂ S** bits. **Tag = address bits − index − offset**.
- Direct-mapped: k = 1.
- Fully associative: S = 1 → no index bits.
Tag directory size = L × (tag + valid [+ dirty] [+ LRU] bits). Comparators: k for k-way (one per way), L for fully associative.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Three organisations
steps.body:
32-bit addresses, 64 KB cache, 64 B blocks → L = 1024 lines, offset 6.
- Direct-mapped: index 10, tag **16**.
- 4-way: sets 256, index 8, tag **18**.
- Fully associative: index 0, tag **26**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Which line?
steps.body: Direct-mapped, 128 lines, 16-byte blocks. Address 0x0001_2345: offset = 0x5 (low 4 bits); block number = 0x12345 >> 4 = 0x1234 = 4660 → line = 4660 mod 128 = **52**; tag = 4660 / 128 = 36.

steps.title: Solved example 3 · Tag memory
steps.body: Direct-mapped case above with 1 valid bit: 1024 × (16 + 1) = **17,408 bits** ≈ 2.1 KB of tag storage.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using cache size instead of number of sets for index bits.
- Forgetting byte vs word addressing.
- Counting index bits in fully associative caches.

activity.prompt: Cache address split: input 'addr_bits cache_bytes block_bytes ways' on one line. Print tag, index and offset bits separated by spaces.
activity.starter:
a, c, b, w = map(int, input().split())
# offset = log2(b); sets = c // (b * w); index = log2(sets)
activity.solution:
a, c, b, w = map(int, input().split())
off = b.bit_length() - 1
sets = c // (b * w)
idx = sets.bit_length() - 1
print(a - idx - off, idx, off)
activity.hint: For a power of two p, p.bit_length() − 1 = log₂ p.

quiz.why: A 32-byte block needs log₂32 = 5 offset bits.
A fully associative cache lets a block go in any line, so there's no index field; the whole block address is the tag.
256 KB/64 B = 4096 lines. With 8 lines per set, 4096/8 = 512 sets.

quiz.q: Comparators in a 4-way set-associative cache lookup
quiz.why: A 4-way set-associative lookup compares the tag with all 4 lines of the set at once, so it needs 4 comparators.
A direct-mapped cache is the special case with 1 way, since each block can go in only one line.

scenes.text: A small hotel (cache) is full; a new guest (block) arrives.
Policy decides who leaves: least recently used, first in, or random.

steps.title: Misses and policies
steps.body:
**3 Cs:** compulsory (first reference), capacity (cache too small), conflict (too many blocks map to one set; zero in fully associative).
Replacement: LRU, FIFO, random, pseudo-LRU. Direct-mapped needs no choice.
Write policies: **write-through** (update memory on every write; write buffer) vs **write-back** (dirty bit; write on eviction). Write miss: **write-allocate** (fetch block) usually with write-back; **no-write-allocate** usually with write-through.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Direct-mapped simulation
steps.body: 4 lines, block addresses 0, 4, 0, 8, 4 (all map to line 0 since b mod 4 = 0): miss, miss, miss, miss, miss → **5 misses** (conflict misses).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Same sequence, other caches
steps.body:
- 2-way, 2 sets, LRU: 0, 4, 8 all map to set 0. 0 miss, 4 miss, 0 hit, 8 miss (evicts 4), 4 miss (evicts 0) → **4 misses**.
- Fully associative, 4 lines: 0 m, 4 m, 0 h, 8 m, 4 h → **3 misses** (all compulsory).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting the first access to a block as a conflict miss (it is compulsory).
- Forgetting to update LRU on hits.
- Writing back clean blocks in write-back caches (only dirty ones).

activity.prompt: Direct-mapped cache with 8 lines; block address sequence 3, 11, 3, 19, 11, 3. How many misses?

quiz.q: Misses in a fully associative cache of infinite size are
quiz.why: In an infinitely large fully associative cache, nothing is ever evicted, so the only misses are the first touches of each block: compulsory misses.
A write-back cache updates memory only when a line is evicted, so it needs a dirty bit to mark lines that were modified.
A fully associative cache lets any block use any line, so there are no conflict misses. Only compulsory and capacity misses remain.
Write-through caches are commonly paired with no-write-allocate, since writes go straight to memory and there's no need to bring the block in on a write miss.

quiz.q: In the 2-way example, 0 is evicted when
quiz.why: With LRU in the 2-way set, block 0 is the least recently used when 4 arrives again. So the second arrival of 4 evicts 0.

scenes.text: Most errands take a minute in the house; a few need a drive to the market.
The average time per errand depends on how often you must drive — the miss rate.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
**AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty.**
Two levels: AMAT = H₁ + m₁ × (H₂ + m₂ × P_mem), where m₂ is the **local** miss rate of L2 (misses in L2 / accesses to L2). **Global** L2 miss rate = m₁ × m₂.
CPU stall cycles per instruction = memory accesses per instruction × miss rate × miss penalty; CPI_eff = CPI_base + stalls.
Block transfer penalty example: penalty = latency + (block size / bus width) × transfer time per word.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Single level
steps.body: Hit 1 cycle, miss rate 5%, penalty 100 cycles → AMAT = 1 + 0.05 × 100 = **6 cycles**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Two levels
steps.body: L1 hit 1, L1 miss rate 5%; L2 hit 10, L2 local miss 20%; memory 100. AMAT = 1 + 0.05 × (10 + 0.2 × 100) = 1 + 0.05 × 30 = **2.5 cycles**. Global L2 miss rate = 0.05 × 0.2 = **1%**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 · Effect on CPI
steps.body: Base CPI 1, 1.3 memory accesses per instruction (1 fetch + 0.3 data), miss rate 2%, penalty 100 → stalls = 1.3 × 0.02 × 100 = 2.6 → CPI = **3.6**: memory dominates.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using global instead of local miss rate inside the L2 term.
- Adding the hit time twice for misses (the formula already counts it once).
- Ignoring instruction fetches in memory accesses per instruction.

activity.prompt: L1 hit 2 cycles, miss rate 10%; L2 hit 12 cycles, local miss rate 25%; memory 200 cycles. AMAT in cycles?

quiz.why: Average memory access time = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty.

quiz.q: Global L2 miss rate with m₁ = 4%, m₂ = 50%
quiz.why: The global L2 miss rate is the fraction of all accesses that miss both levels: 0.04 × 0.5 = 0.02 = 2%.
Larger blocks bring in more nearby data per miss, using spatial locality, so compulsory misses fall (up to a point, after which pollution and longer penalties hurt).
Higher associativity gives a block more places to go, which reduces conflict misses.

questions.q: Fastest storage level
questions.why: Registers are at the top of the memory hierarchy and are the fastest storage, then L1, L2, L3, DRAM and SSD.

questions.q: Spatial locality refers to
questions.why: Spatial locality means that if you access one address, nearby addresses are likely to be accessed soon.

questions.q: Direct-mapped cache has associativity
questions.why: A direct-mapped cache has associativity 1: each block maps to exactly one line.

questions.q: Offset bits for 128-byte block
questions.why: A 128-byte block needs log₂128 = 7 offset bits.

questions.q: Lines in 32 KB cache with 32 B blocks
questions.why: Lines = 32 KB/32 B = 2¹⁵/2⁵ = 2¹⁰ = 1024.

questions.q: Dirty bit is needed for
questions.why: A dirty bit is needed in a write-back cache, to know whether a line must be written to memory when it's evicted.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Fully associative caches have no conflict misses. Reason (R): Any block can occupy any line. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: fully associative caches have no conflict misses. R is true and explains it: any block can go in any line, so a block is evicted only when the whole cache is full.

questions.q: 32-bit address, 128 KB 2-way cache, 32 B blocks: tag bits
questions.why: 128 KB/32 B = 4096 lines, and with 2 ways that's 2048 sets, so 11 index bits. Offset is 5 bits. Tag = 32 − 11 − 5 = 16 bits.

questions.q: Hit 1, miss rate 3%, penalty 80: AMAT
Case: a matrix program runs 5× faster after swapping loop order. Why?
questions.why: Swapping loop order makes the program walk through memory in row-major order, so consecutive accesses hit the same cache block. That's better spatial locality, not fewer instructions.

questions.q: Build 256K × 32 from 64K × 8 chips: chips
questions.why: 256K × 32 needs 4 rows of 64K words (256K/64K) and 4 chips side by side for the width (32/8). Total is 4 × 4 = 16 chips.

questions.q: Direct-mapped 4 lines, block refs 1, 5, 9, 1, 5: misses
questions.why: Blocks 1, 5 and 9 all map to line 1 (mod 4), so each access evicts the previous one. All 5 accesses miss.

questions.q: 2-way set-associative (2 sets, LRU), refs 0, 2, 4, 0, 2: misses
questions.why: 0, 2, 4 all map to set 0 (even); LRU thrashes: 0 m, 2 m, 4 m (evict 0), 0 m (evict 2), 2 m (evict 4).

questions.q: Base CPI 1.2, 1.4 accesses/instr, miss 1.5%, penalty 120: CPI
questions.why: Stall cycles per instruction = 1.4 × 0.015 × 120 = 2.52. CPI = 1.2 + 2.52 = 3.72.

questions.q: Tag directory bits: direct-mapped, 512 lines, 20-bit tag, valid + dirty bits
questions.why: Each line needs a 20-bit tag plus valid and dirty bits, which is 22 bits. 512 × 22 = 11,264 bits.

questions.q: L1 2 cycles, 5% miss; L2 10 cycles, 40% local miss; memory 100: AMAT
questions.why: AMAT = L1 hit + L1 miss rate × (L2 hit + L2 local miss rate × memory) = 2 + 0.05 × (10 + 0.4 × 100) = 2 + 0.05 × 50 = 4.5 cycles.

courses.note: topic order may differ by university syllabus

courses.title: Unit 7 · I/O Organisation, Interrupts, DMA & Buses
courses.summary: I/O interfaces and ports (memory-mapped vs isolated), programmed I/O, interrupt-driven I/O with priority schemes, DMA modes and CPU overhead calculations, buses and arbitration, and secondary storage timing.
outcomes: Learners can compare programmed, interrupt-driven and DMA I/O
Learners can compute CPU overhead for each I/O method
Learners can explain daisy-chain and vectored interrupts
Learners can compare bus arbitration schemes

scenes.text: Programmed I/O is walking to the letterbox every minute to check for mail.
Interrupts are a doorbell; DMA is a helper who files the mail for you.

steps.title: Interfaces
steps.body:
Each device has a controller with **data, status and control registers**.
- **Memory-mapped I/O:** device registers share the memory address space; ordinary load/store instructions access them.
- **Isolated (port-mapped) I/O:** separate address space with IN/OUT instructions (x86).
**Programmed I/O (polling):** CPU loops reading the status register until ready, then transfers each word. Simple, wastes CPU cycles.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Polling cost
steps.body: A keyboard is polled 100 times/s; each poll costs 500 cycles on a 1 GHz CPU → 50,000 cycles/s = **0.005%** — fine for slow devices.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Polling a fast device
steps.body: A device delivers 4-byte words at 40 MB/s → 10⁷ words/s. If each poll+transfer costs 100 cycles at 1 GHz → 10⁹ cycles/s = **100%** of the CPU. Polling is impractical; use DMA.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking memory-mapped I/O needs special instructions.
- Forgetting that polling cost scales with the poll rate, not the data actually present.
- Mixing up status and data registers.

activity.prompt: A device is polled 2000 times per second, 400 cycles per poll, on a 400 MHz CPU. Percentage of CPU used?

quiz.why: Memory-mapped I/O gives devices addresses in the normal address space, so ordinary load and store instructions are used.
Polling means the CPU keeps checking the device's status until it's ready.

quiz.q: A device controller's status register tells
quiz.why: A device's status register tells the CPU whether the device is ready, busy or in error.
Isolated I/O has a separate I/O address space with special instructions, such as IN and OUT on x86.
Polling wastes CPU time, so it's acceptable only for slow devices that are checked infrequently.

scenes.text: An office has many doorbells ringing at once — the fire alarm must beat the courier.
Priority decides who is served first.

steps.title: Interrupt handling
steps.body:
Device raises an interrupt request; CPU finishes the current instruction, acknowledges, saves context, gets the ISR address (vectored: device supplies a vector number; non-vectored: fixed address + polling), runs the ISR, restores context.
Priority schemes: **daisy chaining** (acknowledge passes device to device; nearest has highest priority; simple, can starve far devices), **parallel priority** with a priority encoder/interrupt controller (e.g. APIC/GIC), software polling. **Nested interrupts**: higher priority can preempt a lower-priority ISR. **Masking** disables selected interrupts (NMI cannot be masked).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Interrupt overhead
steps.body: Disk sends an interrupt per 4-byte word at 1 MB/s → 250,000 interrupts/s; each costs 2 µs → 0.5 s per second = **50%** CPU.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Daisy chain
steps.body: Devices D1 (nearest the CPU), D2, D3 on a daisy chain request together. Acknowledge reaches D1 first → **D1 served**, D2 and D3 wait; if D1 keeps requesting, D3 may starve.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the CPU stops mid-instruction for ordinary interrupts.
- Forgetting the non-maskable interrupt exists.
- Confusing interrupt latency (time to start the ISR) with ISR duration.

activity.prompt: Order the steps of servicing a vectored interrupt
items: CPU acknowledges; device supplies vector number
Context restored; return to the program

quiz.why: In a daisy chain, the device nearest to the CPU sees the interrupt acknowledge first, so priority depends on position in the chain.
A non-maskable interrupt (NMI) can't be disabled by the CPU, so it's used for critical events.

options: polling devices to find the source
quiz.why: A vectored interrupt identifies the source directly, so the CPU needn't poll every device to find out which one interrupted.

options: a higher-priority interrupt to preempt an ISR
quiz.why: Nested interrupts allow a higher-priority interrupt to preempt a lower-priority ISR that is already running.

quiz.q: Interrupt per word at high data rates is
quiz.why: At high data rates, one interrupt for every word costs so much overhead that the CPU spends most of its time on interrupts. DMA is better.

scenes.text: Instead of carrying every book one by one, you give the librarian's helper the list and the trolley.
The helper tells you only when the whole trolley is shelved — one interrupt per block.

steps.title: DMA
steps.body:
CPU programs the DMA controller with source/destination address, count and direction, then continues; the DMA controller becomes bus master and transfers data; one interrupt at the end.
Modes:
- **Burst (block) mode:** DMA holds the bus for the whole block — fast, CPU locked out of memory meanwhile.
- **Cycle stealing:** DMA takes one bus cycle per word, interleaved with the CPU.
- **Transparent (hidden):** uses only cycles when the CPU is not using the bus.
Cache coherence: DMA writes must invalidate/update cached copies.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · DMA vs interrupts
steps.body: Same disk (1 MB/s) with DMA in 4 KB blocks: 1 MB / 4 KB = 256 blocks/s; setup + completion interrupt = 10 µs each → 2.56 ms/s = **0.256%** CPU (vs 50% with per-word interrupts).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Cycle-stealing slowdown
steps.body: Memory cycle 100 ns; device transfers a word every 2 µs by cycle stealing → it steals 1 of every 20 memory cycles → CPU memory bandwidth reduced by **5%**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking DMA needs no CPU at all (CPU sets it up and handles the completion interrupt).
- Confusing burst mode with cycle stealing.
- Ignoring cache-coherence issues with DMA buffers.

activity.prompt: A device transfers 8 KB blocks by DMA at 2 MB/s (1 KB = 1024 B, 1 MB = 1024 KB). Each block costs the CPU 20 µs. CPU time percentage (3 decimals)?

quiz.why: With DMA, the controller moves the whole block on its own and interrupts the CPU once, at completion.

options: DMA holds the bus for the whole block
DMA takes single bus cycles between CPU cycles
quiz.why: In cycle stealing, the DMA controller takes single bus cycles between CPU cycles, so the CPU is slowed only slightly.

quiz.q: Who sets up a DMA transfer?
quiz.why: The CPU (through the driver) sets up the DMA transfer by programming the memory address, device and count. Then the DMA controller does the work.

quiz.q: Fastest DMA mode for one block
quiz.why: Burst mode gives DMA exclusive use of the bus for the whole block, so a single block moves fastest, but the CPU is blocked meanwhile.

quiz.q: DMA into memory requires care with
quiz.why: DMA writes straight to memory, bypassing the cache, so a cache may hold stale copies. Cache coherence needs care.

scenes.text: CPU, memory, GPU and devices share buses and links.
An arbiter decides who drives next.

steps.title: Buses
steps.body:
Address, data and control lines. **Synchronous** (shared clock) vs **asynchronous** (handshake: request/acknowledge). Bandwidth = width × transfer rate.
Arbitration: **centralised** (daisy chain, polling, independent request/grant lines) vs **distributed** (self-selection with priority codes, collision detection).
Modern systems use point-to-point serial links: **PCIe** lanes (×1, ×4, ×16), USB, SATA/NVMe.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Bus bandwidth
steps.body: 64-bit bus at 200 MHz, one transfer per cycle: 8 B × 200 × 10⁶ = **1.6 GB/s**. Double data rate (2 transfers/cycle) → 3.2 GB/s.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Disk access time
steps.body: 7200 RPM, average seek 6 ms, transfer rate 100 MB/s, controller overhead 0.2 ms, 4 KB read: rotation period 8.33 ms → average latency 4.17 ms; transfer 0.04 ms → total ≈ 6 + 4.17 + 0.04 + 0.2 = **10.4 ms**. SSDs avoid seek and rotation (~0.1 ms).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using full rotation time instead of half for average latency.
- Forgetting DDR doubles transfers per clock.
- Thinking PCIe is a shared parallel bus (it is point-to-point serial lanes).

activity.prompt: A 32-bit synchronous bus at 100 MHz transfers once per cycle. Bandwidth in MB/s (10⁶ bytes)?

quiz.why: Asynchronous buses have no shared clock; they coordinate with handshaking signals (request and acknowledge).
With independent request and grant lines for each device, a central arbiter decides who gets the bus, so it's centralised arbitration.
PCIe ×16 means 16 serial lanes are used together for higher bandwidth.
At 10,000 RPM one rotation takes 60/10,000 s = 6 ms. Average rotational latency is half a rotation, 3 ms.
DDR (double data rate) memory transfers data on both the rising and falling clock edges, so 2 transfers per clock.

questions.q: DMA reduces
questions.why: DMA moves data between a device and memory without the CPU handling each word, which reduces CPU involvement.

questions.q: Polling is
questions.why: In polling, the CPU repeatedly checks the device's status, which is busy-waiting.

questions.q: Memory-mapped I/O uses
questions.why: With memory-mapped I/O, devices sit in the memory address space, so regular memory instructions (loads and stores) access them.

questions.q: Daisy chain highest priority
questions.why: In a daisy chain, the device closest to the CPU gets the highest priority, as the signal reaches it first.

questions.q: Burst-mode DMA
options: holds the bus for the block
questions.why: Burst-mode DMA holds the bus and transfers the whole block before releasing it.

questions.q: Bus 64-bit, 100 MHz, 1 transfer/cycle
questions.why: A 64-bit bus carries 8 bytes per transfer. At 100 MHz that is 8 × 10⁸ = 800 MB/s.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Interrupt-per-word I/O is unsuitable for high-speed disks. Reason (R): Interrupt overhead per word would consume most CPU time. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A is true: per-word interrupts don't suit high-speed disks. R is true and explains it: the interrupt overhead for every word would consume most of the CPU's time.

questions.q: Interrupt per 2-byte word at 500 KB/s (10³), 4 µs each: CPU
questions.why: 500,000 bytes/s with 2-byte words is 250,000 interrupts/s. Each takes 4 µs, so 250,000 × 4 µs = 1 s of CPU time every second: 100%.

questions.q: DMA 4 KB blocks at 4 MB/s (binary units), 50 µs per block: CPU
questions.why: 4 MB/s ÷ 4 KB = 1024 blocks/s. At 50 µs of CPU time per block, 1024 × 50 µs ≈ 51.2 ms per second, about 5%.

questions.q: Case: a network card at 10 Gbps interrupts per packet and the CPU saturates. A common fix
options: interrupt coalescing / polling mode (NAPI) with DMA rings
questions.why: At 10 Gbps a per-packet interrupt overwhelms the CPU. Interrupt coalescing (batching) or polling mode (like NAPI), with DMA rings, cuts the overhead.

questions.q: Cycle stealing: memory cycle 50 ns, word every 1 µs: CPU memory bandwidth lost
questions.why: The device takes one 50 ns memory cycle for each word every 1 µs, which is 1 cycle out of 20: 5% of the CPU's memory bandwidth.

questions.q: Disk 15,000 RPM, seek 4 ms, transfer 200 MB/s, 1 MB read (10⁶ B), no overhead
questions.why: 15,000 RPM is 4 ms per rotation, so average rotational latency is 2 ms. Transfer is 1 MB/200 MB/s = 5 ms. Total = 4 + 2 + 5 = 11 ms.

questions.q: Polling 1000×/s at 300 cycles on 300 MHz CPU
questions.why: Polling takes 1000 × 300 = 3×10⁵ cycles per second out of 3×10⁸. That's 0.1% of the CPU.

questions.q: Which arbitration has no single point of failure?
questions.why: Distributed arbitration has no central arbiter, so no single failure can stop it. Daisy chain and central arbiters have a single point of failure.

questions.q: An NMI is typically used for
questions.why: A non-maskable interrupt can't be disabled, so it's used for critical hardware errors such as memory parity failures or power loss.

questions.q: DMA transferring into a buffer that the CPU has cached, with no coherence support, risks
questions.why: If DMA writes to memory behind the cache, the CPU may read an old cached copy. The cache lines must be invalidated or kept coherent.

courses.title: Revision & Practice · Computer Organisation & Architecture
courses.summary: COA formula sheet, a mixed numerical drill and two mock papers covering representation, arithmetic, ISA, control, pipelining, caches and I/O.
outcomes: Learners can recall every COA formula
Learners can solve mixed GATE-style COA numericals
Learners can avoid the classic traps

scenes.text: Meera condenses COA into one page before the exam.
Each formula has its trap next to it.

steps.title: Representation and arithmetic
steps.body:
- 2's complement range −2ⁿ⁻¹ … 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1; overflow V = C_in(MSB) ⊕ C_out
- IEEE single: (−1)^s × 1.f × 2^(e − 127); double bias 1023
- Ripple delay ∝ n; CLA Cᵢ₊₁ = Gᵢ + PᵢCᵢ
- Booth: 10 → A − M, 01 → A + M, then arithmetic shift

steps.title: ISA and performance
steps.body:
- CPU time = IC × CPI / f; MIPS = f / (CPI × 10⁶)
- Expanding opcode: free patterns × 2^(freed bits)
- PC-relative target = updated PC + offset
- Amdahl 1 / ((1 − f) + f/s)

steps.title: Pipelines
steps.body:
- Time = (k + n − 1)τ; τ = max stage + latch
- Load-use: 1 stall with forwarding; RAW without forwarding: 2 stalls (split-cycle register file)
- CPI = 1 + branch% × miss% × penalty

steps.title: Memory and I/O
steps.body:
- offset = log₂ B; sets = lines / k; tag = A − index − offset
- AMAT = H₁ + m₁(H₂ + m₂P)
- Chips = (W/w) × (B/b)
- I/O overhead = events/s × cost per event ÷ cycles or time per second

steps.title: Top traps
steps.body:
- hidden 1 in IEEE
- subtract bias when multiplying FP
- local vs global L2 miss rate
- latch delay in τ
- KB = 1024 in memory sizes, MB/s = 10⁶ in rates (unless stated)

quiz.why: Double precision uses an 11-bit exponent, so the bias is 2¹⁰ − 1 = 1023. Single precision's bias is 127.

quiz.q: τ with stages 3, 5, 4 ns and latch 1 ns
quiz.why: The clock must fit the slowest stage plus latch delay: 5 + 1 = 6 ns.
AMAT = hit time + miss rate × penalty = 1 + 0.1 × 20 = 1 + 2 = 3.
16K × 8 from 4K × 4 chips needs 4 rows (16K/4K) and 2 chips for width (8/4): 4 × 2 = 8 chips.

scenes.text: Time yourself: three minutes each.
Check each against the worked steps.

steps.title: Drill 4 · Pipeline
steps.body: 6 stages, τ = 1.5 ns, 200 instructions, 10% need 1 stall each → (6 + 199) × 1.5 + 20 × 1.5 = 307.5 + 30 = **337.5 ns**.

steps.title: Drill 5 · Cache
steps.body: 40-bit address, 1 MB 16-way cache, 128 B blocks: lines 8192, sets 512 → index 9, offset 7, tag **24**.

steps.title: Drill 6 · I/O
steps.body: 1000 interrupts/s × 5000 cycles on a 2 GHz CPU → 5 × 10⁶ / 2 × 10⁹ = **0.25%**.

activity.prompt: 40-bit address, 2 MB 8-way cache, 64 B blocks: how many tag bits?

quiz.why: 1011 in two's complement is −8 + 3 = −5. Booth's recoding gives the same value, −5.
CPU time follows the iron law, IC × CPI/clock rate. Applying it to the numbers in the drill gives 3.2 s.
Tag bits = address bits − index bits − offset bits = 40 − 9 − 7 = 24.
CPU share = cycles spent ÷ cycles available = 5×10⁶/2×10⁹ = 0.0025 = 0.25%.
